docs/components/chrome-extension.html.summary: Chrome Extension src/chrome-extension is a Manifest V3 extension written in TypeScript and bundled with esbuild. It is a member of the npm workspace at src/ (see The npm workspace), and its platform-free logic lives in the shared @passel/core package. What it does Popup: sign in and out, send the current page, send typed text or a link, and browse the live packet feed. Tiles can be opened, copied or deleted, and a delete can be undone for 4 seconds. All feedback (send and sign-in results, copies, deletes with their undo) goes through one snackbar that overlays the bottom of the popup, so nothing shifts the layout. Side panel: the popup's page, laid out for a tall, narrow panel that stays open beside the page while you move between tabs and open links. Open it with the panel button in the popup's header, the Open Passel in the side panel shortcut, or Chrome's own side panel menu. The composer stays at the top while the feed scrolls under it, and notes show twice as many lines before "Show more". The popup stays the quick way to send. Keyboard shortcuts: open the popup, send the page you're on (or the text selected on it), and open the side panel. See Keyboard shortcuts. Address bar: type passel, a space and some text, then press Enter to send it: a link if it's a web address, otherwise a note. See The passel keyword. Context menus: send a link, the selected text, or an image's URL. Sends from a shortcut, the address bar or a context menu show their outcome on the toolbar icon: a green tick, or a red ! when nothing could be sent. Modules File Responsibility background.ts The service worker. Handles context menus, routes messages from the popup, schedules deletes so they still happen after the popup closes, shows badge feedback, and tells every open page when someone signs in or out. commands.ts The keyboard commands the service worker handles: sending the page or its selection, and opening the side panel. omnibox.ts The passel address bar keyword: the suggestion that says what Enter will send, and sending it. popup.ts The entry point of the popup and the side panel, which are the same page; it starts popup/controller.ts. Every API call and sign-in request goes to the service worker. popup/controller.ts The popup's session: who is signed in, the live connection to the service worker, sign-in and sign-out, sending, and moving into the side panel, handing off to the parts below. popup/feed-view.ts The feed as the popup shows it: tiles, the row after the oldest packet, the sync label, paging, copying, and deleting with undo, on top of FeedStore. popup/composer.ts Sending the current page and typed text or links, and pasting into the composer. popup/toast.ts, popup/dom.ts The one snackbar all feedback goes through; the popup's fixed elements, whether the page is the side panel, the message channel to the service worker, and the element and icon builders. popup.css The styles of the popup and, under body.side-panel, of the side panel. It imports the design tokens from @passel/ui, and esbuild inlines them into dist/popup.css. auth.ts Google sign-in through chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow, using the implicit flow with response_type=id_token; in a development build with DEV_SIGN_IN, also signing in as a development user through the API's Dev scheme. api.ts Authenticated fetches. On a 401 it refreshes the token and retries once. Also the packet endpoints and the server-sent events (SSE) stream. live.ts Keeps one SSE connection open while a popup or the side panel is open, reconnects with backoff, and opens it again with the new session after a sign-in or sign-out. cache.ts The feed cache in chrome.storage.local. From @passel/core (src/packages/core), shared with the web app: feed.ts (FeedStore: the feed's state, including paging, merging live events and undo), packets.ts (parsing the wire format), sse.ts (the SSE parser), authorization.ts (Bearer for a Google ID token, Dev <user> for a development user) and types.ts (the wire, message and cache types). None of them touches chrome.* or the DOM, and their tests run there. The ID token is kept in chrome.storage.session, which is cleared when the browser closes. Only a login hint goes in local storage, so the extension can sign the user back in silently. A development user (Run without Google) is kept in local storage until sign-out, along with the name last used, which the popup offers again. The feed cache holds only the first page (50 packets) and the cursor after it, so it never grows as the user scrolls through older pages; the in-memory list keeps every page loaded while the popup is open. The side panel build.mjs writes dist/sidepanel.html from static/popup.html, with a side-panel class on the body, so the side panel runs the popup's own script and markup and the two can't drift apart. The class is all that differs: popup.css sizes the page to the panel and keeps the composer in view, the popup's button for opening the side panel is hidden, and the composer asks for the tabs permission before sending the page (see Permissions). The side panel holds a live connection to the service worker like the popup, so the feed stays live for as long as the panel is open. Because the panel stays open, a sign-in or sign-out can happen elsewhere while it shows a feed: in a popup opened beside it, or through a shortcut, the passel keyword or a context menu that needed a sign-in. auth.ts reports every sign-out, and every sign-in that the user saw or that brought another account (a silent refresh of the same account is not reported). The service worker then starts the event stream again with the new session, since the stream it had open was opened with the previous token and the API would keep it open until that token expires. It also sends a sessionChanged message to every open page, signed in or not. Each page asks for the auth state again. If the account it shows has changed, it forgets its feed, shows the new session and fetches that account's feed, so one account's packets are never shown or cached under another. Keyboard shortcuts Command Suggested key Mac What it does Open the popup (_execute_action) Alt+Shift+P Control+Shift+P Opens the popup, as the toolbar button does Send this page, or the selected text (send-current-page) Alt+Shift+S (Alt+Shift+Y on ChromeOS) Control+Shift+S Sends the text selected on the page as a note if there is any, otherwise the page as a link, without opening anything Open Passel in the side panel (open-side-panel) Alt+Shift+O Control+Shift+O Opens the side panel in the current window The keys avoid Chrome's own shortcuts: Chrome uses Alt+Shift with T, I, A and N on Windows and Linux, ChromeOS uses Alt+Shift+S for its quick settings, and on a Mac the suggestions use the Control key, which Chrome's own shortcuts leave alone. Chrome only assigns a suggested key when the extension is first installed and the key is free, so one can be missing; anyone can change them at chrome://extensions/shortcuts. A command that reads the page works on the tab it was pressed on, through the activeTab grant the shortcut gives. The passel keyword The manifest's omnibox keyword is passel. Typing passel and a space in the address bar hands the rest of the line to the extension. Its suggestion says what Enter will send ("Send link: …" or "Send note: …"), or how to use it while nothing is typed yet, and Enter sends it through the service worker: a link if it's an http or https address and a note otherwise, the same rule as the popup's text field. An empty line sends nothing and shows the red !. Permissions Permission Why activeTab Reading the address and title of the page the user asked to send, from the popup, a shortcut or a context menu. Granted only for that tab, only by that action. contextMenus The three send entries in the page's context menu identity Google sign-in through chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow storage The ID token (session storage), the login hint, the feed cache and whether the tabs permission was declined (local storage) sidePanel The side panel. No install warning. scripting Reading the text selected on the page for the send shortcut, by running one function in the tab. It only works where activeTab has been granted, so it reaches no page the user didn't act on. No install warning. tabs, optional Asked for by the side panel the first time it sends the page: the panel stays open across tabs, and the activeTab grant doesn't follow it to the next one. Chrome shows its "Read your browsing history" prompt then, never at install. Chrome doesn't remember a refusal, so the panel does: once the prompt is declined, the panel doesn't ask by itself again, even in a panel opened later. It can still send a page Passel was opened from. For other pages it says why it can't send them and offers Allow, which shows the prompt again and sends the page once the permission is granted. The only host permission is the API's origin (see Build). The side panel and sidePanel.open need Chrome 116, so the manifest's minimum_chrome_version is 116. Build build.mjs bundles src/background.ts, src/popup.ts and src/popup.css into dist/, following the workspace packages into the bundle, copies static/ alongside them, and writes sidepanel.html from popup.html. It needs two values and takes a third. Values already in the environment take precedence over a local .env: Variable Value API_URL The packets endpoint (for example https://localhost:7030/api/packets), not the API root. The extension appends /events and /{id} to it. GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID The extension's OAuth client id DEV_SIGN_IN true lets a development build sign in as a development user through the API's Development-only Dev scheme, without Google; GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID may then be left empty, and the popup offers only the development sign-in. A minified build never has it. The AppHost sets it. The manifest's host_permissions are generated from the API_URL origin, so the extension can only call its own API. Run npm install once in src/ (the workspace root, not the extension folder), then, in src/chrome-extension: Command What it does npm run dev / npm run dev:watch Unminified build with source maps (the AppHost runs dev:watch) npm run build Type-check, then a minified build npm run typecheck The TypeScript check of the extension npm run harness Serves the built popup with chrome.* stubbed; see The popup harness dotnet atom BuildChromeExtension Release build, zipped into atom-publish/ChromeExtension The tests of the platform-free logic live with it in @passel/core; the extension's own modules, the ones that call chrome.*, are tested in test/ against a stubbed chrome (see Testing). npm test in src/ runs every package's tests, npm run test:coverage adds the coverage reports, and dotnet atom TestChromeExtension runs the type-checks and the tests of the whole workspace with coverage. Load dist/ unpacked; see Running Locally. The source folder deliberately has no manifest, so it can't be loaded by mistake. The popup harness harness/ serves the built popup in an ordinary browser tab, with a stand-in for the chrome.* APIs (harness/chrome-stub.js) and canned packets, so the popup can be looked at and clicked through without loading the extension or running the API. Build first with npm run dev, then run npm run harness and open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ for the popup or http://127.0.0.1:8765/sidepanel.html for the side panel, framed at Chrome's default panel width and the height of the tab. On either page, ?state=signedout shows the signed-out popup, ?state=empty an empty feed, and &lastDevUser=alice offers that development user. The stub behaves like the service worker where the popup can tell: sends echo the packet, deletions wait out the undo window and a cancel stops them, and passel.created({...}) in the console makes a packet arrive live. The npm workspace src/package.json declares an npm workspace with one lockfile, src/package-lock.json, for every TypeScript project: Member What it holds packages/core (@passel/core) The client logic with no platform APIs, and its tests, including the contract checks against contracts/ packages/ui (@passel/ui) The design tokens as CSS custom properties chrome-extension The extension, consuming both web The web app, consuming both The packages are consumed from source: their exports point at the TypeScript and CSS files, and each app's bundler compiles them, so nothing is built in a package. @passel/core also holds a fetch-based API client (api.ts), a reconnecting event stream (live.ts) and JWT helpers (jwt.ts), which the web app uses; the extension still has its own in its service worker, and can move onto them later. The key in static/manifest.json pins the extension id to aikjdmilnbdacmaeahelifppjjgppemj. The OAuth redirect URI depends on that id.

docs/components/mobile-app.html.title: Mobile App | Passel
docs/components/mobile-app.html.summary: Mobile App src/mobile_app is a Flutter app (package passel_mobileapp). Android is the supported platform. The iOS project is scaffolding only and isn't configured. Structure Folder Contents lib/config/ AppConfig, the compile-time configuration, and the page shown when a required value is missing lib/api/ The error types (ApiException, NetworkException, SessionExpiredException, SignInException) and describeError, which turns any of them into user-facing text lib/auth/ Google Sign-In (google_sign_in 7), ID token refresh, the DEV_USER sign-in through the API's Dev scheme (authorization.dart maps a token to its Authorization header), the API HTTP client (ApiClient: never follows redirects, sends the tunnel token when there is one) and helpers that retry once on a 401 lib/packets/ The packet model, repository (HTTP and SSE), offline cache, Riverpod providers and widgets lib/settings/ The settings page, the theme choice and the app version lib/theme/ The Material 3 theme, used when the device doesn't provide dynamic colour State lives in Riverpod providers. packetsProvider serves the cached feed first, then refreshes it. It keeps the whole loaded list in memory across sign-in and an expired session, and drops it when the user's local data is cleared (userDataGenerationProvider, bumped on sign-out and when a different account signs in). packetLiveUpdatesProvider keeps the server-sent events stream open while the feed is visible, the user is signed in, and the app is in the foreground. Every resync event triggers a fresh fetch of the latest packets: immediately for the first one after the stream (re)starts, after a random delay of up to 3 seconds for later ones, and reconnects back off exponentially with full jitter (a random share of the backoff, up to a minute), so clients that lose the server together don't all come back in the same instant. The feed is cached in shared_preferences, so it can still be browsed offline. On a cold start StartupRouter shows the cached feed as soon as the cache has been read, before Google Sign-In has initialised; the full-screen login page is only shown when there is no cache and the user turns out to be signed out. The cache holds the first page only: at most 50 packets (PacketCache.maxPackets) and the cursor that followed the first page, so older pages are fetched again when the user scrolls to them. Writes are debounced by 300 ms (packetCacheWriteDelayProvider), so a burst of live events is written once, and the cache is parsed once at start-up by cachedPacketsProvider, which the start-up router and the feed share. Sign-in asks Google for a token for the web client (SERVER_CLIENT_ID), which the API accepts as its main audience. The token is kept in memory only. Errors validateResponse (in lib/auth/auth_helpers.dart) turns a failure response into an ApiException with the status and, when the server sent application/problem+json, its title, detail and the validation messages keyed by field. Transport failures thrown by package:http and dart:io (no connection, timeouts) become a NetworkException, a 401 that survives the token retry a SessionExpiredException, and Google Sign-In failures a SignInException whose message is already written for the user. Every snackbar and error row (push, refresh, delete, the feed's error state, the login page and sheet, the start-up auth error) shows describeError(error): client errors (4xx) use the server's detail or field messages, everything else a short generic sentence, so no exception text reaches the screen. Sharing into the app The app is an Android share target. AndroidManifest.xml declares an activity alias, SendToPassel, on MainActivity with intent filters for ACTION_SEND with text/plain (the share sheet) and ACTION_PROCESS_TEXT (the text selection menu); its label, "Send to Passel" (or "Send to Passel Dev"), comes from the flavor's resValue, so the launcher label is untouched. MainActivity.kt takes the shared text from the intent and hands it to Dart over the passel/share method channel: text that arrives before Dart is ready waits until ShareIntent.takePendingText asks for it, text that arrives while the app runs comes through ShareIntent.sharedText. PacketFeedPage opens the send sheet filled in with the text; the user sends or edits it. No share-receiving plugin is involved. Images wait for parcels. Settings The feed page's app bar has a settings action beside the sign-in or sign-out action; it opens SettingsPage (lib/settings/), which works signed in and signed out. Account shows who is signed in: the Google account's name and email (AuthService.currentAccount, an AccountInfo the repository takes from the Google sign-in and drops on sign-out) or the development user (currentDevUser), with a Sign out tile. Signed out it offers Sign in, through the same sheet as the feed. Appearance chooses the theme: system default, light or dark. themeModeProvider (theme_mode_setting.dart) holds the choice, MyApp passes it to MaterialApp as the themeMode on top of the device's dynamic colours, and it is saved in shared_preferences (settings_theme_mode) so it survives a restart; until the saved choice has been read the app follows the device. About shows the version and build number (package_info_plus, read once by appVersionProvider), in a development build the flavor and the API URL, and the privacy policy and terms of service at passel.link/privacy and passel.link/terms. Those two tiles stay disabled (legalPagesPublished in settings_page.dart) until the pages, which the web app has (roadmap 1.E3), are hosted at passel.link, a follow-up of roadmap 0.A2; see Hosting. Configuration Values are compiled in with --dart-define or --dart-define-from-file. Nothing is bundled as an asset. Key Required Value API_BASE_URL Yes The API root, as the device can reach it: http://localhost:5218 for a phone on USB (with adb reverse), http://10.0.2.2:5218 for an emulator, or the dev tunnel URL. See Running Locally. SERVER_CLIENT_ID Unless DEV_USER is set The Google web client id APP_CLIENT_ID No The Android client id TUNNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN No A Dev Tunnels access token, for a tunnel that doesn't allow anonymous access. Development flavor only. DEV_USER No Signs in as this user through the API's Development-only Dev scheme instead of Google, so no Google client is needed. The login page can sign in as any other user, and each user is a separate account. Development flavor only. See Run without Google. Copy .env.example to .env for local runs. If a value is passed both in the file and with --dart-define, the --dart-define value wins. AppConfig checks the values at start-up and shows ConfigErrorPage instead of the app when one is missing or can't be used in the flavor: the production flavor needs an https:// API URL and refuses a tunnel token and a development user, and the development flavor allows an http:// URL only to localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 10.0.2.2, the hosts its network security configuration permits cleartext to. Flavors Flavor Application id App name Signing development com.invex.passel.mobileapp.dev Passel Dev The release key if one is configured, otherwise debug keys production com.invex.passel.mobileapp Passel The release keystore, from the SIGNING_RELEASE_* environment variables The development flavor also carries a network security configuration (android/app/src/development/res/xml/network_security_config.xml, applied by that flavor's manifest) that permits plain HTTP to localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 10.0.2.2, so a phone on USB and an emulator reach the local API without a tunnel or a trusted certificate. The production flavor has no such configuration and keeps the platform default, which blocks cleartext everywhere. dotnet atom BuildMobileAppAndroid --mobile-app-flavor production builds an obfuscated app bundle and packages its symbols. The development flavor builds a debug APK. See Build Targets.

docs/components/web-api.html.title: Web API | Passel
docs/components/web-api.html.summary: Web API src/webapi holds five projects: Project Purpose Invex.Passel.WebApi The API Invex.Passel.WebApi.Tests Unit tests (xUnit v3 on Microsoft.Testing.Platform) Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests Integration tests against PostgreSQL and Azurite in Docker; see Integration tests Invex.Passel.AppHost The Aspire AppHost that runs the local environment, and describes the Azure deployment (Releasing and Deploying) Invex.Passel.ServiceDefaults OpenTelemetry (to the Aspire dashboard locally, Application Insights in Azure), health checks, service discovery and HTTP resilience, shared Aspire-style Request pipeline Program.cs adds the service defaults and the web defaults (Extensions/HostWebExtensions.cs). Those cover JSON options, ProblemDetails, compression, authentication, rate limiting and API versioning, plus the edge: a Kestrel connection limit, forwarded headers when a proxy is declared, host filtering, and HSTS outside Development. CORS allows the web app's origins only (Cors:AllowedOrigins, see Configuration), with no credentials, and answers preflights ahead of authentication (Extensions/CorsExtensions.cs). It then maps the packet, device and parcel endpoints (Endpoints/EndpointMapper.cs). In development it also maps OpenAPI, Scalar and the browser login endpoints (Extensions/HostDevExtensions.cs), in one route group that only answers to the localhost host (RequireHost), so they are not served through the dev tunnel; the packet, device and parcel endpoints answer to any host. Every packet endpoint lives under /api/packets, every device endpoint under /api/devices and every parcel (uploaded file) endpoint under /api/parcels; all of them require authentication and are API version 1. The parcel group also runs ParcelResponseHeadersFilter on every request, which adds the sandboxing and caching headers to whatever the endpoint answers; see Parcels. The user id is the Google sub claim. See HTTP API for the endpoints themselves. A body that cannot be read (malformed JSON, a missing or unknown discriminator, an unknown enum name, a missing required property) is a 400 in every environment: the web defaults turn off RouteHandlerOptions.ThrowOnBadRequest, which Development otherwise sets, so the request never reaches the exception handler as a 500, and the status code pages write the problem. A union body without its $type needs one more step, because System.Text.Json cannot create the union's abstract base and reports that with a NotSupportedException, which body binding does not count as a bad request. A type info modifier on the HTTP JSON options (HostWebExtensions.RequireTypeDiscriminator) gives every such base a factory that throws a JsonException instead. Abuse controls Each endpoint opts into one of six rate-limiting policies (Extensions/RateLimitingExtensions.cs): packet creates, reads (the packet list and delete endpoints, and the device list), event-stream connections, device writes (every other device endpoint), parcel uploads (uploads and discards) and parcel reads (downloads and thumbnails, generous because a feed page can show fifty thumbnails). The limiter runs after authentication so requests are counted per user; requests that fail authentication are counted per remote address instead. Rejections are 429 problems with Retry-After. The limits come from the RateLimits configuration section; see Configuration. Before a create, PacketQuotaService reads the caller's usage with one aggregate over the packet table (count(*) and the summed pg_column_size of the documents, through the leading member of the index on UserId and Id), and PacketQuota.Exceeded compares it with the Quotas configuration. A user at the packet limit gets 429, a packet that would pass the byte limit gets 413, and both messages say to delete packets. Two creates that race can both pass the check, so the quotas are approximate by a packet. The device cap works the same way (DeviceQuota.Exceeded against a count of the user's devices, 429 when reached), but only for an installation that registers for the first time; see Device registry. Nothing ties the count to the insert, so every registration of a new installation in a burst can pass it: a user one below the cap can get past it by as many registrations as the device-writes limit admits at once, RateLimits:DeviceWritesPerMinute less one, and more behind several API instances, since each instance counts the limit in memory. The rate limit bounds the excess; enforcing the cap exactly would mean serialising a user's registrations in the database, which a bound on rows of a few dozen does not justify. Uploaded files have a quota of their own, separate from the packet byte quota, which counts packet documents only (a File packet counts its name and a fixed 64 bytes there). ParcelQuotaService reads it with one aggregate over the parcel table: the number of files uploaded but not sent (still uploading, or uploaded and in no packet) and the summed Size of every file not deleted, through the index on UserId. ParcelQuota.Exceeded refuses an upload with 429 at Quotas:MaxPendingParcelsPerUser unsent files and with 413 when it would pass Quotas:MaxParcelBytesPerUser; ParcelQuota.TooLarge gives the 413 for one file over Parcels:MaxParcelBytes. An upload is checked twice: before its body is read, against the size it declares (or the largest file allowed, for a body without a length), which it then reserves by recording the parcel at once; and again with its exact size once it is stored. Two uploads that race the first check can both pass it, so this quota is approximate too, by the uploads that arrive in the same moment. Storage: Marten documents Packets are stored with Marten on PostgreSQL, as plain documents (ADR 0001). Each packet is one Packet document (Domain/Packet.cs) in the mt_doc_packet table: Id, UserId, CreatedAt and the Content union (Link, Text or File, stored with a $type discriminator). The id is a version 7 Guid, so id order is creation order; the feed and its cursor rely on that. A Link also carries its Preview once one has been fetched; see Link previews. PacketStoreService handles creating and deleting packets, and attaching a link's preview: one upsert to create, one delete to remove, one update for the preview. Deleting checks ownership first. A missing packet and someone else's packet both return 404, so ids can't be probed. A delete removes the document, and nothing else keeps the content. A File packet is the exception in both directions: creating one also attaches its parcel, and deleting one also marks its parcel deleted, each in the same commit; see Parcels. The documents carry one composite computed index on UserId and Id, which serves the feed query. See The feed index. In Development, Marten applies the schema at startup (ApplyAllDatabaseChangesOnStartup), so the table exists before the first request; the quota check reads it with plain SQL, which Marten's on-first-use creation would not cover. Everywhere else the deployment applies it; see Schema in production. The data source comes from Aspire.Azure.Npgsql (Extensions/HostDatabaseExtensions.cs): a connection string with a password is used as it is, and one without signs in with a Microsoft Entra token for the managed identity, as the Azure deployment does. The bytes of uploaded files are not in the database: each upload is one Parcel document (Domain/Parcel.cs, table mt_doc_parcel) whose bytes are in the parcel store (Azure Blob Storage, or a directory on the server's disk when self-hosted), and a File packet refers to it by id. See Parcels. A database from before the move still has the event-sourcing tables (mt_doc_packetaggregate, mt_events, mt_streams); nothing reads them, and they can be dropped. Marten does not migrate the old packets into the new table. Schema in production Outside Development the API never changes the schema (ADR 0003): The store uses AutoCreate.None, so nothing is created or altered at runtime, and the API's database role needs no more than DML. At startup, before anything else starts, it checks that the database has every schema, table, column and function its configuration declares (Services/DatabaseSchemaCheck.cs) and refuses to start otherwise, so a revision whose migration didn't run never becomes ready. What it finds beyond that, such as a column or an index a newer release's migration added or a Marten function it changed, is logged and accepted: the previous revision keeps serving, and restarting, on that schema until the new one is ready, and for good if the deployment fails after its migration. Marten's own AssertDatabaseMatchesConfigurationOnStartup refuses any difference, so it isn't used; db-assert still runs that strict comparison. The deployment's migration job applies the schema before each new revision starts, by running the API's image with the db-migrate command. db-migrate (Extensions/MigrateDatabaseCommand.cs, Services/DatabaseMigrator.cs) logs in as a role that may change the schema, and then: Applies the configured schema with AutoCreate.CreateOrUpdate, with every table marked add-only (Weasel's AddOnlyMigrations). It creates what is missing, alters what changed and replaces Marten's functions, but never drops a table, or a column, index or foreign key that the configuration no longer declares: it logs each one it leaves in place. Plain CreateOrUpdate would drop them, and with them the data in a column, so rolling back to an older release would delete what a newer one added. Creates the role passel_app if it doesn't exist (no login), and grants it select, insert, update and delete on the tables in the store's schema, use of its sequences and execution of its functions, now and, through default privileges, on what the migration creates later. If Database:ApiRole is set, makes that role a member of passel_app. If Database:ApiRoleObjectId is set too, it first creates the role as a Microsoft Entra principal of that managed identity (a login role carrying the pgaadauth security label), so the API can sign in with tokens. Every step is idempotent, so the job runs on every deployment. The API's role can then read and write packets, listen and notify, and run the quota query, but not create, alter or drop anything; the integration tests check both sides. Program.cs runs JasperFx's command line when the first argument names a command, and the API otherwise. Besides db-migrate, db-assert checks a database against the configuration, db-patch <file> writes the statements a migration would run without running them, and help lists the rest. Both use Marten's plain comparison, so db-patch also lists the drops db-migrate leaves out, which makes it the way to write one by hand. For example, against the database in appsettings.Development.json: dotnet run --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi -- db-patch patch.sql There is no code generation step. Marten 9 removed runtime code generation, so there is nothing for codegen write to produce and nothing to regenerate when a document type is added. A unit test (DatabaseSetupTests) fails if a package ever registers code that would need generating ahead of time; that is when to add codegen write to the build, with a check that its committed output is current. The feed index GET /api/packets runs where UserId = ? and Id < ? order by Id desc limit 51. With the index declared as .Index([p => p.UserId, p => p.Id]), Marten emits the identity member as the id column rather than a JSON expression, so the query becomes a backward range scan of at most 51 index entries however many packets the user has: CREATE INDEX mt_doc_packet_idx_user_id_id ON public.mt_doc_packet USING btree ((data ->> 'UserId'), (id)); Program.cs sets the name; the one Marten derives runs the members together as user_idid. The single-column index on UserId that the API used to declare is gone, because the leading member of this one serves the same lookups, including the quota aggregate. Measured on PostgreSQL 18.3 with 15,021 packets seeded through the API (one user with 5,001, fifty users with 200 each), EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) of the exact statements Marten emits, warm, after ANALYZE. The measurements were taken on the snapshot table of the event-sourced model; the document table has the same columns and the same index, so the plans are the same: Query Index on UserId only Index on UserId, Id First page, user with 200 packets Index Scan Backward on the primary key, filtering on the JSON expression: 7,322 rows discarded, 7,399 buffers, 0.89 ms Index Scan Backward on the composite index: 53 buffers, 0.03 ms Cursor page, same user The same walk from the cursor: 2,551 rows discarded, 2,608 buffers, 0.35 ms Index Cond on both members: 50 buffers, 0.03 ms First and cursor page, user with 5,001 packets Primary-key walk: 53 buffers, 0.02 to 0.03 ms Unchanged. A third of the table is this user's, so the walk finds 51 rows at once and the planner keeps it Quota aggregate, user with 200 packets Bitmap scan on the index: 172 buffers, 0.07 ms Bitmap scan on the composite index: 173 buffers, 0.07 ms The primary-key walk reads every newer packet of every other user until it has 51 of the caller's, so it gets worse with every user added; the composite index reads 51 entries whatever the table holds. Two things to know: the planner only prefers the index once it has statistics on the expression, so run ANALYZE after creating it on a database that already has data (autovacuum gets there eventually), and the index is larger than the single-column one was (744 kB against 120 kB for these rows), because PostgreSQL deduplicated the old one's fifty-one distinct keys. Public ids Packet, device and parcel ids are never exposed as raw Guids. IdEncodingService encodes the Guid's two 64-bit halves with Sqids (minimum length 10). The alphabet comes from Encoding:Alphabet. Changing it invalidates every id that clients have stored. Live updates GET /api/packets/events streams server-sent events to signed-in clients: After a create, a delete or a preview update commits, PacketStoreService sends a PostgreSQL NOTIFY on the passel_packet_events channel. The payload carries the user id, packet id and the change (Created, Deleted or Updated). Each API instance runs PacketNotificationListener, a hosted service that LISTENs on that channel on its own connection. It reconnects after 5 seconds if the connection fails, and sends a keep-alive query when the connection is idle. Npgsql raises one notification per wait on the connection, so the connection loop only queues what it parses, and a dispatch loop takes everything queued at once as a batch: it loads the created and updated packets of users with a stream open on the instance with one query, publishes per user in arrival order (packet-created or packet-updated, each carrying the packet as it is now), and publishes deletes without a load. If the query fails, each affected user gets a resync instead. The listener publishes to PacketEventHub, an in-memory hub on that instance. The hub fans events out to each user's open streams through bounded channels of 64 events. Because every instance listens, events reach clients connected to any instance. The stream doesn't support resuming. Instead, clients reconnect, receive resync, and fetch GET /api/packets again. The server also sends resync when it may have missed events: after the listener reconnects, every open stream on the instance gets one, spread at random over three seconds so that the re-fetches don't all reach a database that may just have recovered at the same moment. If a stream's buffer fills, the server closes the stream rather than drop events. A stream sends a ping after 20 seconds without events. The wait is a delay that completes rather than a timeout that throws, because every idle stream times out every 20 seconds. The first event of a stream carries an SSE retry value drawn per stream between 2 and 6 seconds, so clients that honour it (a browser EventSource does; the extension and the mobile app use their own jittered backoff) reconnect spread out after a restart. Event-stream requests are left out of request tracing in ServiceDefaults, next to the health endpoints, because a stream's request lasts up to a day and its trace would hold an activity open for all of it. Streams are capped by the EventStreams configuration. The hub keeps at most five per user on an instance: subscribing a sixth removes the oldest from the hub and completes its channel, so that client's stream ends cleanly and it reconnects. Beyond the per-instance total, Subscribe returns null and the endpoint answers 503 with Retry-After. The subscription is registered for disposal with the response, so the hub releases it when the stream ends however it ends. A stream never outlives the token that opened it: the endpoint reads the exp claim and cancels the stream at exp plus the bearer handler's clock skew (PacketEndpoints.StreamLifetime), with a ceiling of a day for principals without an expiry. The clients already reconnect with a fresh token. Link previews When a link packet is created, its page is fetched in the background and what the page says about itself is stored on the link (LinkPreview on PacketContent.Link: title, description, image URL and when they were read). The fetch never runs inside the request: PacketStoreService queues it on LinkPreviewQueue, a bounded in-memory channel, once the create has committed, and LinkPreviewWorker, a hosted service, runs the queued fetches a few at a time. A fetch still queued when the instance stops is lost, and the link then keeps no preview, which is the same outcome as a page that gave none. The API is fetching URLs that users chose, so LinkPreviewFetcher is held to rules that no configuration loosens: Only absolute http and https URLs without credentials are requested, on the URL the user sent and on every redirect. Nothing else is ever fetched: not the image a page names, not the links on it. The fetcher resolves each host itself and checks every address it gets with LinkPreviewAddressPolicy, which allows public unicast addresses only: no loopback, private (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), carrier-grade NAT (100.64/10), link-local (169.254/16, where the cloud metadata services live), multicast, reserved or documentation ranges, in IPv4 or IPv6. An IPv6 address that stands for an IPv4 one (IPv4-mapped, NAT64) is judged by that address; the deprecated IPv4-compatible and 6to4 forms are refused outright. If any address of a host is refused, the whole fetch is. The connection is made to one of the checked addresses, through the handler's connect callback, never to a fresh resolution of the name, so a name whose answer changes between the check and the connection (DNS rebinding) gets the checked address all the same. TLS still validates the certificate against the host name. No proxy is used, and no cookies. Redirects are followed by hand, at most three, each hop checked like the first URL. Only text/html and application/xhtml+xml responses are read, at most 512 KB of them and no further than the end of the <head>, within one five-second budget for the whole fetch, redirects included. No Accept-Encoding is sent, so the cap counts the bytes the page sends. LinkPreviewExtractor reads the head, with comments, scripts and styles taken out, for the Open Graph tags first, the Twitter card tags next, and the plain <title> and <meta name="description"> last. Entities are decoded, whitespace collapsed, the title cut to 256 characters and the description to 512, and a relative image URL made absolute against the page; an image that is not an http or https URL is dropped. A page with no title, description or image gives no preview. A failure that may pass (a timeout, a connection or DNS failure, a 429 or 5xx answer) is retried: three attempts in all, five seconds before the second and ten before the third. A refusal, a 4xx answer, a page that is not HTML or one redirect too many is final. Either way, a failed fetch shows up only as the link keeping preview: null, plus one Debug log line naming the packet and the reason; nothing is stored or announced about it. The reason can name the linked host, which is why it is not logged at Information. For the same reason the fetches are left out of the traces, and outgoing HTTP metrics carry no host name; see Logs and telemetry. When something was found, the worker attaches it through PacketStoreService with a Marten update rather than a store: a store is an upsert and would bring back a link deleted between the fetch and the save, whereas Marten refuses to update a document that is gone, and the preview is dropped with it. The commit is followed by a NOTIFY with the change Updated, which the listener loads like a create and the streams send as packet-updated, carrying the link in the PacketResponse shape with its preview set. The limits, the retry policy and the concurrency come from the LinkPreviews configuration section; the address rules do not. See Configuration. The integration tests fetch from a Kestrel server of their own on the loopback (TestPageServer), reached by the name pages.test, which the test factory's stand-in resolver points at the loopback while it resolves every other name to a private address. So the suite never reaches the internet, and the address rules stay in force for everything but that one name. Device registry The device endpoints (Endpoints/DeviceEndpoints/) keep a list of each user's devices: what the push sender (roadmap 2.B1) will deliver to, what first-party sessions (1.B1) will belong to, and what "send to a device" will target later. Nothing sends pushes yet, and no client registers yet (2.D3 and 2.E2). Each device is one Device document (Domain/Device.cs) in the mt_doc_device table: Id, UserId, the client's InstallationId, Name, Platform (Android, Extension or Web), CreatedAt, LastSeenAt, and the push token (Push, a union of Fcm and WebPush stamped with UpdatedAt) with its PushKey. DeviceStoreService writes them, and DeviceEndpoints.DeviceResponse.From is the one mapping to the wire. The id is the API's. A version 7 Guid, encoded like a packet id. It is what anything else refers to a device by, so a session can be revoked with its device (1.B1). It is never reused: a removed installation that registers again gets a new one. Registering is idempotent. The client generates its installation id once and sends it every time; a unique index on UserId and InstallationId (mt_doc_device_uidx_user_id_installation_id) makes a second registration of the same installation find the first device, even when several arrive at once: the losers of the insert get a unique violation, read again, and answer with the winner's device without writing it. In the same way, registrations of a known installation that lose the race to move LastSeenAt find it moved by the winner and answer with that, so any number of racing registrations settle in two attempts. A known installation keeps its name, so a rename made in settings survives the next start, and only LastSeenAt moves. The same installation under another account is another account's device. The index's leading member also serves the device list and the count for the cap. A push token belongs to one device. PushKey is the SHA-256 (lower-case hex) of the kind and the FCM token or Web Push endpoint, and a unique index covers it (mt_doc_device_uidx_push_key); devices without a token leave it null, which the index allows any number of times. Hashing keeps the index entries small however long a token is, and a unique-violation message names a hash rather than the token. Setting a token first takes it off any other device that holds it, of any user, in the same commit: a token identifies an installation or a browser profile, not an account, so after a sign-out and a sign-in as someone else it arrives from the second account's device, and the first account must stop pushing to it. The move is logged at Information with the two device ids. A token's kind follows the platform. Fcm on Android, WebPush (endpoint, p256dh, auth) in the extension and the web app; the store refuses the other kind. A Web Push endpoint must be https, on a host name and the default port, because the sender will make requests to it. That does not make it safe to call: 2.B1 has to check the addresses the name resolves to, as the link preview fetcher does. Tokens stay in. The wire shape has pushUpdatedAt and nothing else of the token. Nothing logs a token, the token records override ToString so that printing a device or a request never shows one, and validation messages never repeat it. Marten logs a failed command with the document as binary, so a race leaves no token in the logs either. Changes never undo each other. Every change is a Marten update of the whole document, with optimistic concurrency on the device type. An update of a device that is gone (NonExistentDocumentException), that has changed since it was read (ConcurrencyException), or a write of a unique key another request has just written, is a lost race: the store drops its changes, reads again and decides afresh, at most three times. A rename that loses to a removal answers 404; a registration that loses to one makes a new device. A write that loses all three times (several renames or push token changes of one device at the same moment) throws DeviceWriteConflictException, which DeviceWriteConflictHandler answers with a 409 problem saying to send the request again, and logs at Warning. Lost races are logged by Marten. Marten logs a failed command at Error before the store sees the exception, so each lost insert (racing first registrations of one installation) and each lost push key (two devices given one token at the same moment) leaves a Marten.IDocumentStore error with PostgreSQL's 23505 unique violation, although the store handles it. Such races need clients sending at the same moment and are rare; an error naming mt_doc_device_uidx_user_id_installation_id or mt_doc_device_uidx_push_key with no failed request next to it is one of them. What 2.B1 needs from the document is the platform, the token and its UpdatedAt (FCM advises dropping tokens that have not been refreshed for a long time), and LastSeenAt. When a push service says a token is gone (FCM's UNREGISTERED, a Web Push 404 or 410), the sender should clear it the way ClearDevicePush does. Parcels A parcel is an uploaded file (Endpoints/ParcelEndpoints/): one Parcel document (Domain/Parcel.cs) in mt_doc_parcel, with its bytes in the parcel store: Azure Blob Storage, or a directory on a local disk for a self-hosted deployment (ADR 0004). Sending a file is two requests, an upload to POST /api/parcels and a File packet that names the parcel; see Parcels in the HTTP reference. No client uploads or shows files yet (roadmap 2.C2, 2.D2 and 2.E2). From To When (nothing) Uploading An upload starts, before its body is read Uploading Uploaded Its bytes and thumbnail are stored Uploading Deleted The upload fails, or is still unfinished after Parcels:UploadingGrace (15 minutes) Uploaded, in no packet Deleted The user discards it, or Parcels:UnattachedLifetime (an hour) passes Uploaded, in a packet Deleted Its packet is deleted, or the orphan scan finds the packet gone Deleted erased The sweep deletes the thumbnail, then the original, then the document Whether a parcel has been sent is not a status: it is AttachedPacketId. Three services change parcels: ParcelStoreService records, completes, fails and discards uploads, PacketStoreService attaches a parcel to its File packet and marks it deleted with the packet, and ParcelSweep expires and erases. Every change is a Marten update with optimistic concurrency on the parcel type. The document comes before the bytes. An upload records an Uploading parcel first, reserving its declared size against the quota, so uploads that follow at once see it. Its body is read as it arrives with MultipartReader, never bound as a form, through CountingHashStream, which counts it, hashes it with SHA-256 and stops at Parcels:MaxParcelBytes, into a temporary file that deletes itself when closed. Then it is inspected, the original and the thumbnail are put, the quota is checked again with the exact size, and the parcel becomes Uploaded with its size, type, dimensions and hash. Anything that goes wrong after the parcel is recorded marks it Deleted, so the sweep erases whatever of it was stored; if even that fails, it stays Uploading until the grace period expires it. At most Parcels:MaxConcurrentUploads (4) uploads run at once on an instance (ParcelUploadGate); the next waits five seconds and then gets 503 with Retry-After. The temporary files therefore take at most that many times the file limit of the container's disk. Blobs are named after the parcel. ParcelKeys derives the names from the id alone, {id:N} for the original and {id:N}.thumb for the thumbnail, so nothing stored can drift from the document, and blob URIs, which the Azure SDK records, name no user and no file. A put never overwrites (If-None-Match: * in Azure, a rename that refuses an existing file on disk). There is no deduplication across users, which would tell one user that another holds the same file. The type comes from the bytes. ParcelSniffer reads the first 1,024 bytes for JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP and PDF signatures; everything else is application/octet-stream, HTML, SVG, HEIC and AVIF included, and the type the client declared is never stored. Only an image that decoded, or a PDF, is served inline; anything else is an attachment, and every parcel response carries Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; default-src 'none', nosniff and no-referrer, so a file is never run as a page on the API's origin. The filter also turns response compression off for the group, which would drop the length, break ranges and weaken the strong entity tag. Images are checked before they are decoded. ParcelInspector opens the file with SkiaSharp's SKCodec, which reads the header and allocates no pixels, and goes on only when the format is JPEG, PNG, GIF or WebP and matches the sniffed type (Skia also decodes BMP, WBMP and ICO, which are refused here). An image over Parcels:MaxImagePixels (40 million) or Parcels:MaxImageDimension (16,384 on a side) is not decoded at all, so a small PNG that claims to be 100,000 pixels square costs nothing. JPEG and WebP decode at a reduced scale close to the thumbnail size; PNG and GIF can only decode at full size, which at the pixel cap is 160 MB of native memory, so decodes run one at a time on an instance. An upload waits at most Parcels:DecodeSlotTimeout (five seconds) for its turn and is otherwise stored as a plain file of its sniffed type, with no thumbnail and the failure decoder busy logged, so one slow decode delays the uploads behind it by that much at most rather than holding them all. Only a complete decode counts: a truncated image is a plain file. The first frame is resized (Mitchell), turned upright by its EXIF orientation, and encoded as lossy WebP with no colour space, so the thumbnail carries no ICC profile and Skia writes no EXIF or XMP. A file that fails any step is stored as a plain file without a thumbnail, and the step is logged at Information with the parcel id. The wait for the slot is bounded but the decode itself is not: a Skia decode is a native call that can't be cancelled, so the pixel cap is what bounds its time and memory. A progressive JPEG is the slow case left: Skia gives no cheap way to tell one from the header, and it buffers and entropy-decodes every coefficient of the image however small the scale asked for, so one near the pixel cap is far slower than a baseline JPEG of the same size; the cap and the bounded wait are the whole defence. The original is kept byte for byte, EXIF and GPS included, so the download is lossless and its SHA-256 is a strong entity tag. Only the thumbnail is stripped. The HTTP reference says so to clients. A parcel is sent once. Creating a File packet loads the parcel, stores the packet and updates the parcel's AttachedPacketId in one commit. Two sends of one parcel both update the same parcel document, so the version check alone decides between them: the loser's commit fails, writes nothing, and it answers 409. The unique index on AttachedPacketId (mt_doc_parcel_uidx_attached_packet_id) guarantees the other direction, that no packet id is on two parcels; unsent parcels leave it null, which the index allows any number of times. Deleting a packet deletes its file. PacketStoreService.Handle(DeletePacket) marks a File packet's parcel Deleted in the same commit as the packet's delete, and after the commit wakes the sweep. The request does no blob I/O. If marking the parcel loses a race (the sweep expiring it, say), the packet is deleted alone, and the orphan scan releases the parcel later. The sweep erases. ParcelSweepWorker, a hosted service, runs ParcelSweep when it is woken (a packet delete, a discard and a failed upload all wake it) and otherwise every Parcels:SweepInterval (five minutes). A run expires parcels left unsent past their lifetime and uploads stuck past their grace, each with a version check, so a send that commits first keeps its parcel; then erases Deleted parcels in batches, the thumbnail first, the original next and the document last, so a run cut short only repeats a delete that is already idempotent. A parcel whose bytes can't be deleted (storage down) stays Deleted for the next run. So a deleted file's bytes are gone within seconds, and at worst after one sweep interval while storage is reachable. The sweep sends no packet events. It logs counts at Information and parcel ids at Warning, never a user id or a file name. The orphan scan catches the rest. Every Parcels:OrphanScanInterval (a day, the first a full interval after the instance starts), the sweep also marks Deleted any sent parcel whose packet is gone, and deletes blobs older than Parcels:OrphanBlobMinimumAge (two hours) that no parcel document names. An upload always records its document before its first blob, so a blob that old without one is left over rather than in flight; a blob name that doesn't parse as a parcel's is logged and left alone. This is also what removes blobs left behind when Development's AutoCreate.All recreates the parcel table. The scan lists uncommitted blobs too, and the filesystem store the temps of uploads in progress, so what an upload staged before it was cut off (an instance stopping mid-upload) is found like any other name. Every step is idempotent or version-checked, so instances sweeping at the same time do no harm. Deletes are true deletes (ADR 0001). The Azure storage account has blob soft delete and versioning off, so a deleted blob is not kept; container soft delete (seven days) protects against losing the container, not a file. Turning blob soft delete on would keep every deleted file for its retention period. On disk a deleted file is unlinked; only the server's backups keep it, for as long as they are kept. Storage is not a health check. /health is the readiness probe of the only replica, and a storage outage must not take texts and links down, so the blob client's health check is off. Storage failures surface on the parcel endpoints instead: ParcelStoreUnavailableHandler answers an Azure RequestFailedException, the filesystem store's ParcelStoreFailedException (a full disk, a directory the API cannot write) or the stand-in store's exception with a 503 problem and Retry-After: 30, and logs a Warning with the status and error code, or the operation, the blob name and the type of the disk's error, never its message, which names the path. Other I/O errors are not storage failures: a client that stops sending its upload is an IOException too. A host with no store configured (the db-migrate job, which runs Program.cs without storage settings) registers UnavailableParcelStore, so it still builds and every file request answers 503; outside Development it logs a Warning at startup. Lost races are logged by Marten. As with devices, Marten logs a failed commit at Error before the service sees the exception, so two sends of one file at the same moment, and a send or a delete that collides with the sweep, each leave a Marten.IDocumentStore error with a concurrency failure on a parcel although the race was handled. An error like that with no failed request beside it is one of these. Parcels:Store picks the store when the host is built (Extensions/HostParcelExtensions.cs). Auto, the default, picks Azure when the passel-blobs connection string is set and UnavailableParcelStore otherwise, which is what the AppHost, the Azure deployment and the integration tests' shared host rely on; AzureBlob picks Azure and fails the options' validation at startup without the connection string; FileSystem picks FileSystemParcelStore, whose root, Parcels:FileSystemRoot, must be an absolute path. Neither store touches storage until it is used, so the db-migrate job builds the same host without a volume or a storage account. AzureBlobParcelStore uses the BlobServiceClient that Aspire.Azure.Storage.Blobs registers for passel-blobs (a connection string locally, the account's blob endpoint and the managed identity in Azure), and the container Parcels:ContainerName, which it creates if it is missing before its first write. A read is pinned to the blob's ETag and gives a seekable stream of known length, which is what lets Results.Stream answer ranges. appsettings.json keeps Azure.Core at Warning, because the client forwards the SDK's event log, which logs every request, blob URI included, at Information. A delete also erases an upload that never finished: a file over 4 MB goes up as staged blocks that become a blob only when committed, so when there is no blob under the name, the delete looks for uncommitted blocks and, if there are any, commits an empty block list over them (only while there is still no blob) and deletes the empty blob, which discards them; otherwise Azure would keep them for about a week. A parcel is erased only once it is Deleted, so an upload still running under that name has had its parcel failed or expired, and its own commit then fails. Azurite still lets a later commit of the discarded blocks succeed, so the tests check that the delete leaves no blob and no block list under the name, not that a later commit of those blocks fails. FileSystemParcelStore keeps each blob as the file {root}/{name}, flat, and writes an upload to {root}/.uploading/{name}.{random}.tmp first: it copies the bytes in, flushes them to disk, renames the temp into place without overwriting (an existing file fails the put as Azure's condition does), and then flushes the root directory itself on Linux (Services/PosixDirectory.cs, which calls libc's open and fsync), because the parcel is recorded as uploaded the moment the put returns and a rename that is not flushed can be lost in a power cut. A blob is therefore whole or absent. Only the two names ParcelKeys makes are accepted, so no name can lead out of the root. Reads open the file directly, sharing it for deletion, so the sweep can erase a file while it downloads. A delete removes the temps of that name, then the file: an upload still writing finds its temp gone when it renames and fails as discarded (Upload discarded, 503), as an Azure upload does whose blocks were discarded, and the temps of the original and the thumbnail are told apart although they share a prefix. The list gives the files in the root and the names of the temps, each as old as its last write, so a running upload keeps looking young to the orphan scan, and a crashed one is erased with its parcel or by the scan. Its own disk failures become ParcelStoreFailedException; a failure of the stream it copies from is thrown as it is. Files are created 0600 and the temp directory 0700 on Linux, for the API's own user. The root must be on a local disk: on a network share the rename that refuses to overwrite and the flushes are weaker than the store relies on. Thumbnails use SkiaSharp 3.119.4 (MIT), with SkiaSharp.NativeAssets.Linux.NoDependencies for Linux: the aspnet:10.0 image the API runs on has no fontconfig, and that build of libSkiaSharp.so needs only libc, libm, libdl and libpthread (no text is drawn). The Windows and macOS native assets come with SkiaSharp itself, for local development. ImageSharp was ruled out: from 3.2.0 its Release builds require a Six Labors licence key, and 3.1.12 fails restore on known advisories. Authentication Clients send a Google ID token as a bearer token. The API validates it against Google with these accepted audiences: Authentication:Google:ClientId Authentication:Google:AdditionalAudiences In development a policy scheme picks how each request is authenticated: A request whose Authorization header is Dev <user-id> uses the Dev scheme (Authentication/DevAuthenticationHandler.cs): it signs the request in as that user, with the id as both sub and display name, and no Google involved. The scheme only exists in Development; see Run without Google. A request with any other Authorization header uses bearer tokens. Any other request uses a cookie, issued by Google OpenID Connect login, when Authentication:Google:ClientId and ClientSecret are both set. Without them there is no cookie login, so such a request gets a plain 401 from the Dev scheme. In Development the Google settings are optional: the bearer handler is still registered, but with no client id its audience list is empty and every Google token is rejected. The OpenAPI document declares the Dev scheme so Scalar can send its header, and the Scalar banner says when Google login isn't configured. That cookie login is what lets Scalar call authenticated endpoints. The login cookie is Secure and SameSite=Strict. The OpenID Connect correlation and nonce cookies are Secure and SameSite=Lax, which works because Google returns the code in a top-level GET (response_mode=query), and the nonce in the ID token is validated. Production only accepts bearer tokens, and unauthenticated requests get a plain 401. See Google OAuth Clients for which client is which. Integration tests Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests runs the API as Program.cs builds it, in the Development environment, against a real PostgreSQL and a real blob store (Azurite). The suite needs Docker running and nothing else: dotnet test --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests/Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests.csproj dotnet atom TestWebApi runs it after the unit tests, and so do the Validate and Build workflows, since GitHub-hosted runners have Docker. The suite starts one postgres:18.3 container and one azurite:3.35.0 container (the images the AppHost runs) with Testcontainers and hosts the API in-process with WebApplicationFactory, pointed at them through the passel-db and passel-blobs connection strings. Azurite is started with --skipApiVersionCheck, because the storage SDK asks for a newer service version than that Azurite knows of (the AppHost's emulator passes the same flag). The extra hosts that some tests build on databases of their own (the empty database, the migration tests, storage being down) are given an in-memory blob store, or one that always fails, instead, and one is given the filesystem store over a temp directory, to take an upload, its download, its thumbnail and its erasure through the API on that store. The file limits are lowered for the run (1 MB a file, 3 MB and five unsent files a user) so the quota tests upload little, and the sweep's worker is off: the tests run the sweep themselves, passing it a time an hour or more ahead to expire files without waiting, apart from one test that turns the worker on and checks that a deleted file is erased within seconds. Requests are signed in with the Development Authorization: Dev <user> scheme, and every test acts as users of its own, so the tests share one database without seeing each other's packets. The rate limits are raised for the run, because paging alone creates 51 packets in a minute; the limits have unit tests of their own. Before the first test, the fixture creates packets until one arrives on an event stream, because the notification listener connects after the host has started and a packet created before then is announced to nobody. The tests speak HTTP only, as the clients do: they assert the JSON and the events, never tables or Marten types, apart from the privilege checks of the migration test and the file tests that run the sweep, read the blob store or write a parcel's document directly to set up a race. They cover creating and listing with ownership isolation, paging over 51 packets through the cursor, the delete semantics (a second delete and another user's packet are both 404), the event stream end to end (a create and a delete committed through the API arrive as packet-created and packet-deleted on the owner's stream, through the database notification, and on nobody else's), link previews (the page of a new link is fetched from the tests' own server, its preview listed and announced as packet-updated, a page with nothing to show and a refused host leave the link without one, and a link deleted while its page is being fetched stays deleted), CORS (a preflight from the configured web origin is answered without a token for every endpoint, and the answers to its requests carry the origin while another origin gets nothing), the device registry (ownership isolation, registering the same installation again, ten times at once as a new installation and ten times as a known one, one installation under two accounts, rename, remove, push tokens set, replaced and cleared, a token moving between devices and across accounts, the device cap and the validation problems), files (an upload's type, size, dimensions and thumbnail, a byte-for-byte download with its entity tag, ranges, 304 and headers, HTML stored as an attachment, a thumbnail with no metadata, ownership isolation, file names made safe, the size limit with and without a length, the storage quota and the unsent-file limit, the File packet listed and announced, a file sent only once, including two sends at the same moment and a send that read the file before another committed, a sent file that the sweep can no longer expire, a deleted packet's file unavailable at once and erased, an unsent file expired after an hour, the orphan scan, and storage being down answering 503 for files while texts still work), the blob store's contract (the Azure store, the filesystem store and the in-memory one behave the same), the filesystem store's own cases (the temps of cut-off uploads, a delete during an upload, keys that would leave its root, a root not created yet), a file and an image uploaded, downloaded and erased through the API on the filesystem store, the schema: a second API host on an empty database serves a create as its very first request; the production path: after db-migrate (run twice) the API serves creates, lists, events and deletes on a role that only has DML, which the test then checks can neither create nor alter a table, and without the migration, or with a column it needs dropped, it does not start; a rollback: after a newer release's migration adds a column, this build's API still starts and serves, and this build's migration leaves the column in place; and the contract files described next. A run takes under fifteen seconds once the images are local, longer the first time, while they are pulled, and removes its containers when it ends. Contracts Packets have one wire shape, PacketEndpoints.PacketResponse (Endpoints/PacketEndpoints/PacketResponse.cs): a GET /api/packets item, the POST /api/packets response and the packet-created and packet-updated event data are all this type, built from the stored Packet document by PacketResponse.From, the only mapper. The request body (PostPacketRequestBody) stays a type of its own, because a packet has no id and no creation time before it is stored, and the PacketContent union in Domain/Packet.cs is the storage shape, not the wire. Each endpoint declares its responses, so the OpenAPI document carries the shapes and the problem responses. The contracts/ folder at the repository root holds what the API puts on the wire, and the integration tests (ContractTests) keep it true: contracts/openapi.json is the document the Development host serves at /openapi/v1.json, which is why it declares the Dev scheme next to the bearer token, minus the servers entry, which names whatever address served the copy. The test fails when the committed document differs from the served one. contracts/fixtures/ holds a list page with every packet type (the link with its preview), a create response, a packet-created, a packet-updated and a packet-deleted event payload, serialized from fixed packets with the host's real JsonOptions (indented, with LF line endings, which the clients never see). One test fails when a committed fixture differs from what the API serializes now, another when an endpoint answers with properties other than its fixture's, and the extension and mobile app suites parse every fixture with their real parsers. contracts/feed-scenarios.json describes feed sequences and the list each must leave behind; both client suites run them through their feed stores, and the API tests check that every packet in the file is a valid wire packet. The device and parcel endpoints are in contracts/openapi.json but have no fixtures yet: the fixtures are for payloads the client suites parse, and no client calls them until roadmap 2.D3 and 2.E2 (devices) and 2.C2, 2.D2 and 2.E2 (files), which add the fixtures and their checks together. Both client suites fail on a fixture they have no check for. The File packet is covered all the same: the shape test uploads an image, sends it, and compares the listed File item with the one in the list-page fixture, and the upload response's property set is checked in the file tests. To regenerate the document and the fixtures after a change, run the integration tests with PASSEL_UPDATE_CONTRACTS=1 set, review the diff and commit it with the change; see Contracts in the testing guide.

docs/components/web-app.html.title: Web App | Passel
docs/components/web-app.html.summary: Web App src/web is Passel on the web: a landing page, the privacy and terms pages, and the app itself under /app/. It is a member of the npm workspace at src/ beside the extension (see The npm workspace), and its feed, API client and live connection come from @passel/core, its colours from @passel/ui. This is milestone 1 of the Web App Plan (roadmap 1.E2), apart from its preview deployment (see Hosting), and the public pages (1.E3). What it does Landing page (/): what Passel is, the three steps, and where to get the extension and the app (both "coming soon" until they are listed). Its footer, like the privacy and terms pages', links to the privacy policy, the terms and the documentation. Privacy policy and terms (/privacy/, /terms/): drafts, pending legal review; see The privacy and terms drafts. The app (/app/): sign in with Google, or as a development user in a development build; then the feed, newest at the top, read-only for now. Older items load as the end of the list scrolls into view. While the tab is visible the feed stays live: items sent from other devices appear at once, deletions disappear, and a link's preview (its page's title, description and image) arrives with the packet-updated event. Each item shows as a link (with its preview), a note (long ones collapsed behind Show more) or a file, which can't be opened here yet. The top bar shows Live, or when the feed was last synced, a refresh button, the account and Sign out. Sending, deleting with undo, the offline cache, installing as an app, and the mobile and two-pane layouts are milestone 2 (roadmap 2.E1). Stack The app is Preact components bundled by esbuild, like the extension (build.mjs). One bundler serves the whole workspace, and it already compiles the shared packages from source. Preact gives the components and hooks the plan asks for, rather than the extension's hand-written DOM code, for about 4 KB gzipped; the minified app is about 40 KB before compression. The static pages need no framework: they are plain HTML with no script. SvelteKit or Vite would add routing and prerendering, which milestone 1 doesn't need; that choice can be revisited when the app grows routes (/app/p/{id}, /app/settings). Modules File Responsibility src/app/main.tsx The entry point: loads the configuration, then makes the session, the API client and Google sign-in, hands them to the controller, follows the page's visibility, and renders the views into #app; with no valid configuration it shows ConfigErrorPage instead and starts nothing src/app/config.ts Fetches /app/config.json and checks it: the API URL and the Google client id (see Configuration at startup) src/app/flags.ts The two build flags compiled in by build.mjs: DEV_SIGN_IN and LIVE_RELOAD, both off in a production build src/app/controller.ts AppController: who is signed in, the FeedStore, the LiveConnection, and the rules between them (see Live updates). No DOM, so it is unit-tested src/app/session.ts Session: the token for this tab, checking a Google credential before accepting it, the development user, and the hint that offers One Tap src/app/google.ts Loads Google Identity Services and wraps its button and One Tap src/app/labels.ts The wording: what to call an item, the sync label, what the end of the feed says, which notes collapse src/app/views/ The Preact views: App, SignInPage, FeedPage (with the row after the oldest item), Tile, ConfigErrorPage and the icons src/app/app.css, src/site.css The app's styles and the static pages' styles; both import the tokens from @passel/ui static/ The static pages, the app's HTML shell and the icons, copied into dist/ policy.mjs The Content-Security-Policy headers the dev server sends, the same as the web image's Caddyfile From @passel/core: FeedStore, PacketsApi (the packet endpoints over fetch, with the Authorization header and the problem messages), LiveConnection (the event stream, reconnecting with jittered backoff), the packet and event parsers, and the JWT helpers. Sign-in Google sign-in uses Google Identity Services: the Sign in with Google button, and One Tap for someone who signed in on this browser before and didn't sign out. The ID token it returns is issued for the web client id, which is the API's main audience, so the API takes it as it is. Before accepting it, the session checks that it was issued by Google for that client id, carries the nonce this tab asked for, and hasn't expired; the API checks the signature. The token lives in the tab's session storage: a reload keeps it, closing the tab drops it. A Google ID token lasts an hour and can't be renewed without the user, so when it runs out, or the API refuses it, the app returns to the sign-in page saying the session expired and offers One Tap, which signs a returning user straight back in where Google allows it. First-party sessions with refresh tokens (roadmap 1.B1) will remove that hourly step. A development build with DEV_SIGN_IN=true (the AppHost's) also offers a Development user field, which signs in through the API's Development-only Dev scheme, like the extension's; see Run without Google. The name is kept in the tab's session storage, like a Google token, so each tab can be a different user and signing in or out in one tab leaves the others alone; the last name used is kept in local storage and offered again, in a new tab too. A production build never has it. Built without a Google client id, which only a DEV_SIGN_IN build allows, the page offers only the development sign-in. Live updates While the tab is signed in and visible, the controller keeps the API's event stream open through LiveConnection. A tab hidden for a minute closes it; one back in view before then carries on with the stream it had. Opening a stream counts against a per-user limit that the extension and the phone share (RateLimits:StreamsPerMinute, 10 by default), so a stream per glance at another tab would soon use it up for every device. If nothing has loaded yet, a failed first resync shows as a failed first load, with Retry. The stream counts as live from the server's first resync, and the controller then fetches the first page and merges it on top, so anything missed while the stream was closed shows up. The first resync after the stream opens is fetched at once; resyncs after a reconnect wait a random moment of up to three seconds, so tabs that all lost the stream together (a server restart) don't all fetch at once. A dropped stream reconnects after a jittered backoff from one second up to a minute. A stream refused for lack of a session signs the tab out instead. packet-created, packet-deleted and packet-updated go to the FeedStore, which applies them with the rules the extension and the mobile app share (contracts/feed-scenarios.json): a packet-updated event replaces a listed item in place and never adds one. Configuration at startup The built site holds no environment's values, so one build, and one web image, serves every environment. Before anything else the app fetches /app/config.json from its own origin, revalidating it every time: {"API_URL": "https://api.passel.link/api/packets", "GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID": "<id>.apps.googleusercontent.com"} API_URL is the packets endpoint, not the API root; the app appends /events to it. It must be an https URL, or http to localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1] only, with no credentials, query or fragment. GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID is the Google OAuth web client id and must end in .apps.googleusercontent.com; only a development build with DEV_SIGN_IN may leave it empty. A missing file, a file that is not JSON, or a value that breaks a rule stops the app before it makes a session, an API client or loads Google's script: the page says Passel can't start and why, rather than half-working against the wrong API. A JSON file rather than a script keeps the policy strict: it is data, so nothing in it can run, and the app's connect-src 'self' already allows the fetch. The web image writes it when its container starts (The web image); the dev server answers it from .env (Build). Build build.mjs bundles src/app/main.tsx, src/app/app.css and src/site.css into dist/, following the workspace packages into the bundle, and copies static/ alongside them. A production build (npm run build) needs no values at all. The dev server (npm run dev, npm run serve) needs two and takes two more; values already in the environment take precedence over a local .env (template: .env.example): Variable Value API_URL The packets endpoint (for example https://localhost:7030/api/packets), not the API root. The dev server serves it in /app/config.json and puts its origin into the app's policy. GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID The Google OAuth web client id, served in /app/config.json.
