Its Authorized JavaScript origins must include the app's origin; see Google OAuth Clients. DEV_SIGN_IN true compiles the development sign-in into a development build (npm run dev); GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID may then be left empty. A minified build never has it. The AppHost sets it. PORT The dev server's port, default 5245. The AppHost sets it. WEB_APP_OUT_DIR Where to build, instead of dist/; read from the environment only. build.test.ts uses it. The security policies are response headers, not <meta> tags, since the app's depends on the API's origin and a header can also forbid framing. Everything under /app/ gets the app's Content-Security-Policy: scripts from its own origin and Google Identity Services only, requests to its own origin, the API's origin and Google, preview images from any https site, and no plugins, <base>, form targets or framing. Every other page, the 404 page included, gets one that allows no script at all. The web image's Caddyfile sends them in production and policy.mjs in the dev server, and static-pages.test.ts checks that the two agree. The dev server stands in front of esbuild's, which can't set headers, and also sends Referrer-Policy: no-referrer-when-downgrade, which Google's sign-in needs on plain http://localhost. Run npm install once in src/, then, in src/web: Command What it does npm run dev Unminified build with source maps, rebuilt on every change and served at http://localhost:<PORT>/, reloading the page after each rebuild (the AppHost runs it) npm run build Type-check, then a minified build into dist/ npm run serve A minified build, served the same way, to look at what will ship. It signs in with Google only, never as a development user; like npm run dev it serves /app/config.json and the policies from .env, and the referrer policy Google sign-in needs on http://localhost npm run typecheck, npm test The TypeScript check, and the Vitest suite in test/ dotnet atom BuildWebApp Release build into atom-publish/WebApp, the same for every environment; it takes no parameters. See Build Targets Hosting dist/ is a static site, but not for a host that only serves files: the host must also serve the app's configuration and send the security policies as headers. The web image does all of it, and its deploy/web/Caddyfile is the reference for any other host: Path Serve / index.html /privacy/, /terms/ privacy/index.html, terms/index.html /app/ app/index.html, with app/app.js and app/styles.css /app/config.json The environment's configuration (Configuration at startup), revalidated on every load /privacy, /terms, /app A redirect to the same path with the trailing slash. The mobile app links to https://passel.link/privacy and https://passel.link/terms in this form Anything else 404.html, with status 404 File names carry no content hash, so the host should have browsers revalidate (Cache-Control: no-cache) rather than cache them for long. It sends the two Content-Security-Policy headers (Build) and HSTS. The API must list the site's origin in Cors:AllowedOrigins (Configuration), and the Google web client must list it as an Authorized JavaScript origin. The web image The self-hosted deployment (ADR 0004) serves the site from the passel-web image: Caddy, from deploy/web/Dockerfile, deploy/web/Caddyfile and deploy/web/entrypoint.sh, with the site from BuildWebApp in /srv. Every build of main builds it after the site and pushes it to ghcr.io/invex-games/passel-web (PublishImages), tagged with the version and sha- and the commit. The image holds no environment's values, so the same image runs in every environment and is promoted unchanged from one to the next. It is configured when its container starts, from two environment variables: Variable Value API_ORIGIN The API's origin, such as https://api.passel.link: https, a host name and an optional port, nothing else (http only for localhost or 127.0.0.1). One trailing slash is dropped GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID The Google OAuth web client id, <id>.apps.googleusercontent.com Compose sets them from the server's .env: API_ORIGIN is https://<API_HOST> and GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID is GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID, the same client id the API accepts (Configuration). The entrypoint checks both and writes /run/passel-web/config.json, which Caddy serves as /app/config.json, then starts Caddy with the checked origin, which the Caddyfile puts into the app's connect-src ({$API_ORIGIN}). A value that is missing or breaks a rule stops the container with a message saying which and why (exit code 64), so a misconfigured server never serves a half-working app. The checks admit no quote, backslash, space or control character, which keeps the values from breaking out of the JSON or, since Caddy substitutes an environment value into its configuration as text, out of the header. The image keeps the rules above: It listens on plain HTTP on port 8080, as user 1000, with Caddy's admin endpoint, automatic HTTPS and saved configuration off. TLS ends at the proxy in front of it. The only directory it writes to is /run/passel-web, which the image gives to user 1000, so the entrypoint needs no capability; a container with a read-only root filesystem needs a tmpfs there (--tmpfs /run/passel-web:uid=1000,gid=1000). /privacy, /terms and /app answer 308 with the trailing slash; anything that is not a file answers 404 with 404.html. Every response, the redirects and the 404 page included, carries Cache-Control: no-cache, Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, a Content-Security-Policy with frame-ancestors 'none' (the app's under /app/, the no-script one elsewhere, a 404 under /app/ included), X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and no Server header. Caddy's ETag and Last-Modified let browsers revalidate with a 304, /app/config.json included. Responses are compressed with zstd or gzip, and request bodies are capped at 1 MB. The Caddy binary has its capability to bind low ports removed, so the container runs with every capability dropped. To build and look at it locally (nothing is pushed off main), run dotnet atom SetupBuildInfo (with --skip, PublishImages uses the version that last stored), then dotnet atom BuildWebApp, then dotnet atom PublishImages --skip, and docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:18081:8080 --cap-drop ALL -e API_ORIGIN=https://api.example.test -e GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=<id>.apps.googleusercontent.com invex-games/passel-web:<version>. Locally the images are named without the registry, as invex-games/passel-webapi and invex-games/passel-web. The compose stack runs the image as web, behind the proxy, and the DeployCompose workflow deploys it with the API (Releasing and Deploying); the preview deployment in roadmap 1.E2 is still to come. The production build is checked on every pull request: build.test.ts runs build.mjs as part of npm test. Before the site goes up: docs.passel.link, which the static pages' footers link to as Documentation, must serve the DocFX site (PublishDocs pushes it to GitHub Pages). The mobile app's Privacy policy and Terms of service tiles stay disabled until the pages are hosted; turn on legalPagesPublished in settings_page.dart then. Tests npm test in src runs src/web/test with the other workspace members: controller.test.ts drives AppController against a fake API: signing in and out, the reload of a signed-in tab, live events, the first and later resyncs, the tab being hidden briefly and for longer, an expired session, a refused stream, and failed loads, including a first resync that overtakes the first refresh and fails. session.test.ts covers accepting and refusing Google credentials, expiry, the One Tap hint and development users, one per tab. views.test.tsx renders the views to HTML with preact-render-to-string: tiles with and without previews, escaping, links that aren't http(s), the feed's end row, the sign-in page in each build, and the page shown when the configuration is not valid. config.test.ts covers loading /app/config.json and every rule it is checked against: https only, http to this machine only, no credentials, query or fragment, a real client id unless the development sign-in is built in, and a missing, unreadable or non-JSON file. build.test.ts runs the production build into a temporary folder with no values set and checks its output: every page and bundle, no source maps, no configuration, no policy in the HTML and no API address or client id compiled in. It also starts the dev server on a free port and checks /app/config.json and the two policies it sends. labels.test.ts covers the wording; static-pages.test.ts checks that every link on the static pages resolves, that they carry no script and no policy of their own and use the ADR 0002 vocabulary and link to the documentation, that the web image's Caddyfile sends the same two policies as the dev server, and that the privacy and terms drafts say they are drafts, quote the limits the API's options actually default to, and don't promise a single preview request. The privacy and terms drafts The two pages describe what the code does today, and they are marked as drafts pending legal review. Facts the repository doesn't hold (the operator, contact, hosting region, retention of logs and backups, the legal clauses) are highlighted placeholders such as [CONTACT EMAIL]; static-pages.test.ts fails if one isn't marked. Before publishing, fill them all in, have the pages reviewed, and remove the draft notice and the noindex tag. When the code changes what it stores or does, update the pages; their sources: Statement Where it comes from What is stored with an item, and that a delete erases it Domain/Packet.cs, PacketStoreService, ADR 0001 Only the Google sub is kept, as the user id The endpoints read ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier; nothing stores the email or name How a preview is fetched, its limits and its User-Agent; the image is never fetched by the server LinkPreviewFetcher, LinkPreviewOptions, LinkPreviewAddressPolicy, LinkPreviewResponse.ImageUrl Rate limits and quotas RateLimitOptions, QuotaOptions (checked by the test) Logs, traces and metrics Invex.Passel.ServiceDefaults: OpenTelemetry for ASP.NET Core and HttpClient; the log messages carry internal ids, not content What each client keeps The web app's session.ts, the extension's auth.ts and cache.ts, the mobile app's auth_repository.dart and packet_cache.dart

docs/decisions/0001-packets-as-documents.title: ADR 0001: Packets are plain documents | Passel
docs/decisions/0001-packets-as-documents.summary: ADR 0001: Packets are plain documents Status: accepted, October 2026. Decides: the storage model for packets, the open question from the codebase health chapter of the evaluation. Context Packets were event-sourced: each packet was a Marten event stream (TextPacketCreated, LinkPacketCreated, FilePacketCreated, PacketDeleted) with PacketAggregate kept as an inline snapshot document, which the reads queried. Nothing read the history. The consequences, from the evaluation: A delete only removed the snapshot. The body or URL stayed in mt_events forever, in every backup and in any operator query, so "delete" never erased content (security, finding 1) and the event table grew without bound (performance, finding 6). Every create wrote the event and the snapshot, and read the snapshot back; a delete appended an event and ran the projection. Bodies were stored twice. Each future feature on a packet (previews, pins, parcels, trash) meant an event type plus projection code, and the runtime code generation and rebuild machinery that come with projections. The options were to keep event sourcing with archiving and a purge job, to store packets as plain documents, or plain documents plus a per-user change log for resumable sync. Decision Packets are plain Marten documents. One Packet document holds Id (a version 7 Guid, so id order is creation order), UserId, CreatedAt and the Content union. Creating is one upsert, deleting is one delete, and the feed is a LINQ query served by the composite index on UserId and Id. The event types, the aggregate and the inline projection are gone. CreatedAt is returned by the list and create endpoints and in the packet-created event, so clients can show times and day headers. A delete erases the packet: the document was its only record. Trash and restore, when they come (roadmap package 2.B3), will mark documents deleted and purge them later rather than bring back an event history; Marten's soft-delete support fits that, so no DeletedAt field is reserved now. The per-user change log is deferred until resumable streams or ?since= delta sync are wanted (roadmap package 2.B4). It is a small table written in the same transaction as the document, and the document model does not change for it. Consequences Deletes are true deletes, which the privacy findings asked for, and storage holds each packet once. The write path is simpler and faster: one statement per create or delete, and no projection rebuilds or generated projection code. Features become fields on the document rather than events. There is no audit trail of packet changes. Nothing used it, and the change log can provide a bounded one when sync needs it. A database created before this change keeps its event-sourcing tables (mt_doc_packetaggregate, mt_events, mt_streams). Nothing reads them and they can be dropped. Old packets are not migrated: no production data existed when the change landed. The ids, the public id encoding, the feed query and its index, the quota aggregate and the live-update flow are unchanged apart from the table they read, so the clients needed no change beyond tolerating the new createdAt field, which both already did.

docs/decisions/0002-product-decisions.ht.title: ADR 0002: Ordering, vocabulary, web app stack, parcel storage and hosting | Passel
docs/decisions/0002-product-decisions.ht.summary: ADR 0002: Ordering, vocabulary, web app stack, parcel storage and hosting Status: accepted, October 2026. Decides: roadmap package 0.F1, the product decisions the evaluation left open, plus the hosting choice that package 0.A2 needs. Context The evaluation found the clients disagreeing on the order of the feed (UX, finding 4) and leaking internal vocabulary into the screens (finding 5), compared stacks for the web app (Web App Plan) and storage backends for parcels (Feature Ideas), and noted that nothing deploys the API yet (Developer Experience, finding 1). Each of those gates later work: the share target, the landing, privacy and terms pages, parcels, the tile redesigns, the web app and the deployment pipeline. The recommendations of those chapters are adopted as they stand. Decisions Ordering: newest at the top, everywhere. The feed is a feed, not a chat. The extension already shows newest first; the mobile app flips to match, so the same item sits in the same place on every device, pull-to-refresh is the usual pull down at the top, and older items load at the bottom. The web app follows. Vocabulary: one verb, "Send"; the nouns are link, note and file. Screens, notifications and store listings use those words; "item" or "items" where the type is not known. "Packet" and "parcel" stay as code and API terms, and the API contract does not change. Web app: a TypeScript progressive web app sharing a core package with the extension. The extension's chrome-free modules (feed state, parsing, server-sent events, types) become that package first (roadmap package 1.E1), the web app consumes it (1.E2), and the extension becomes another consumer. Flutter Web and Blazor were compared and set aside: the web platform's own strengths (selection, search engines, share target, push, installability) matter for this app, and the shared code with the extension is the larger saving. Parcels: Azure Blob Storage behind an IParcelStore interface, with Azurite running locally under the AppHost. The interface (put, get as a stream, delete, later a signed URL) keeps an S3-compatible implementation to about a day's work if hosting ever moves. Hosting: Azure. The build already uses Azure (Key Vault), the parcel store is Azure Blob, and Aspire's Azure integrations cover the local run. Package 0.A2 chooses the concrete compute and database services and documents the secrets. Superseded by ADR 0004: Passel moves to Docker Compose on the owner's server, with the files on its disk. Consequences The mobile feed changes direction, which also changes the pull-to-refresh gesture; the hint text and the app bar behaviour follow. Visible strings in both clients change; later packages keep to the vocabulary, and the privacy and terms pages and the store listings (1.E3, 2.A1) use it from the start. The web app work can start with the core extraction; nothing in the extension's behaviour changes until it consumes the package. Parcels and the deployment pipeline can be designed against Azure services without a further decision. Should hosting leave Azure, the parcel store swaps behind its interface and the deployment target changes; nothing in the clients depends on either.

docs/decisions/0003-hosting-on-azure.htm.title: ADR 0003: Hosting the API on Azure | Passel
docs/decisions/0003-hosting-on-azure.htm.summary: ADR 0003: Hosting the API on Azure Status: superseded by ADR 0004, November 2026: Passel runs on Docker Compose on the owner's server instead, and the Azure code and the Deploy workflow stay in place unused. Before that it was proposed, November 2026. The owner still has to confirm the subscription, the region and the services below, then do the one-off setup at the end; until then the Deploy workflow has nothing to run against. Decides: roadmap packages 0.A2 (deploying the API) and 0.A3 (the production schema and startup), within the Azure choice of ADR 0002. Context Nothing deployed the API (Developer Experience, finding 1): no image, no infrastructure, no documented source for the production settings, and Marten created and changed the schema at startup with the API's own credentials, racing across replicas (Security, finding 5). ADR 0002 chose Azure and left the compute and database services to 0.A2. The local loop had to stay as it was: aspire run with a PostgreSQL container, and tests that need nothing but Docker. Options Compute For Against Azure Container Apps, consumption plan Aspire's main Azure target, so aspire deploy provisions and deploys it from the AppHost; revisions that only take traffic once their readiness probe passes; jobs for one-off work such as a migration; managed identity and Key Vault references; an idle rate when nothing is happening A replica kept running costs more than a basic App Service plan; the HTTP scaler counts every open event stream as load, so scaling has to be set by hand Azure App Service (Linux, containers) Simple, always on, B1 is cheap Nothing like a Container Apps job for one-off work such as a database migration; staging slots need the Standard tier AKS Full control A cluster to run and pay for, for one small API A VM with Docker Compose Cheapest Patching, TLS, backups and deployment all by hand Database For Against Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server Managed PostgreSQL 18 (what the AppHost and the tests run), automatic backups with point-in-time restore, Microsoft Entra authentication so no password exists, LISTEN and NOTIFY work The smallest server is still a fixed monthly cost PostgreSQL in a container app Cheap No backups or restore, and Container Apps storage is not meant for a database Decision Compute: Azure Container Apps on the consumption plan, one environment (passel-env) with its own Azure Container Registry and a Log Analytics workspace. The API runs as one container app with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB, and exactly one replica (minimum and maximum): the rate limits and the event-stream caps are counted per instance, and the HTTP scale rule would treat every open event stream as load. Scaling out comes with shared rate limiting. Readiness is /health (every check, the database included) and liveness is /alive, both sent with Host: localhost, which the API's AllowedHosts includes so host filtering doesn't refuse the probes. The environment's own Aspire dashboard is turned off; telemetry goes to Application Insights instead. Database: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, Burstable B1ms, PostgreSQL 18, 32 GB with storage auto-grow, high availability off. Backups are kept for 14 days, set explicitly rather than left to Aspire's default of 7, and any point in that window can be restored to a new server. Geo-redundant backup is off. It can only be chosen when the server is created, so turning it on later means restoring to a new server; the owner should decide before the first deployment. Password authentication is disabled: everything signs in with Microsoft Entra tokens for its managed identity. The server is on a public endpoint whose firewall only admits Azure services (Aspire's default rule). A private endpoint is the next step when the cost is justified. Secrets: Key Vault, holding the API's one production secret, the Sqids alphabet (Encoding:Alphabet), which the container app reads as a Key Vault reference through its identity. Nothing else needs a secret: the database has no password, the Google client ids are public, and the Google client secret is only used by the development-only Scalar login, so it is not deployed at all. The Application Insights connection string is an ingestion endpoint and key rather than a credential, and is set as a plain environment variable, as Aspire does. Telemetry: Application Insights, workspace-based on the same Log Analytics workspace. ServiceDefaults sends logs, traces and metrics with the Azure Monitor OpenTelemetry distro whenever APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING is set, and to the OTLP endpoint otherwise, as before. Npgsql's per-command logs are kept to warnings in Production (appsettings.Production.json), so the workspace doesn't receive every SQL statement. Telemetry must not hold what users send, because it outlives a delete: the workspace keeps it for its default of 30 days. Requests are traced by route and status with the query redacted, and SQL is traced as statements without parameter values. The link preview fetcher is the one component that requests a URL a user sent, so its requests are left out of the traces (ExcludeFromTelemetry), outgoing HTTP and DNS metrics drop the host and address dimensions, and the reason a link got no preview, which can name the host, is logged at Debug, below what Production keeps. Identities. Every resource signs in as a user-assigned managed identity. The API has its own (passel-api-identity), which can read the Key Vault secret and log in to PostgreSQL as an ordinary role. The migration job has another, which Aspire makes a Microsoft Entra administrator of the server. The environment's identity pulls images from the registry. Infrastructure as code: generated by Aspire. The Azure resources are modelled in the AppHost (AzureHosting.cs) with the Aspire Azure hosting integrations, and only when it is published or deployed. Locally, AddAzurePostgresFlexibleServer(...).RunAsContainer(...) gives the same passel-pg container as before, and the Azure-only resources are never added, so aspire run and the tests need nothing from Azure. No Bicep is written by hand or committed. aspire publish writes it from the model, every pull request runs that through PublishAzureInfrastructure and attaches the files to the run for review, and aspire deploy provisions it. Images: the .NET SDK's container support. aspire deploy builds the API's image with dotnet publish (PublishContainer), tags it with GitVersion's version for the commit, pushes it to the environment's registry and points the container app at it. Pipeline: a manual Deploy workflow. DeployWebApi runs only on workflow_dispatch, in the production GitHub environment, and signs in with azure/login through a federated credential (OIDC): no Azure secret is stored in GitHub. Deployments queue rather than cancel each other. Merging this changes nothing until the owner has done the setup below. Schema: applied by the deployment, never by the API. Outside Development the store uses AutoCreate.None. The API never changes the schema, and its role can't: the migration job grants it DML only. A migration job (passel-migrate, the same image started as db-migrate) applies the schema as the Entra administrator, creates the DML-only role passel_app, and makes the API's identity a member of it. aspire deploy runs the job between updating it to the new image and updating the API's container app, through a step added to Aspire's deployment pipeline, so a migration that fails stops the deployment with the running revision untouched. The job runs inside the Container Apps environment, so neither the runner nor the deployment identity ever needs access to the database. ApplyAllDatabaseChangesOnStartup. The roadmap listed it for production, so replicas don't race the schema check. With the migration in the pipeline, production has nothing to apply, so Development keeps it, which keeps the local loop and the tests unchanged. Production checks the schema at startup instead (DatabaseSchemaCheck): a replica that finds a table, column or function it needs missing fails to start, never becomes ready and never takes traffic. The race is gone too, because nothing applies the schema concurrently. Marten's AssertDatabaseMatchesConfigurationOnStartup was the first choice, but it refuses any difference, a newer release's extra index included. The migration runs before the new revision starts, so if the deployment failed after it, the previous revision would fail at its next restart and, with one replica, the API would be down until someone fixed it. The check accepts what it doesn't need and logs it. Migrations are add-only. Plain CreateOrUpdate drops every column, index and foreign key the configuration no longer declares. Rolling back to an older release would then delete the columns a newer release added, and their data: soft-delete flags, for example, once the trash exists. db-migrate marks every table add-only (Weasel's AddOnlyMigrations) and logs what it leaves in place. Removing a column for good is a deliberate statement run by hand, which db-patch writes. Static code generation: not needed. The evaluation asked for TypeLoadMode.Static and codegen write because Marten used to generate and compile code with Roslyn on first use. Marten 9, which the API runs on, removed runtime code generation entirely: document storage is fixed code, codegen write finds nothing to generate, and TypeLoadMode no longer exists on StoreOptions. Nothing is committed and nothing needs regenerating after a merge, a new document type included. A unit test fails if a package ever registers code that would need generating ahead of time (Wolverine, for example), at which point the build needs that step and a check for stale output. Cost A ballpark in US dollars at East US list prices, before tax; the region chosen and the pricing calculator give the real figure. Resource Monthly Container Apps: one 0.5 vCPU / 1 GiB replica, always running, after the monthly free grant About 10 when mostly idle, up to about 35 when busy all month PostgreSQL flexible server: B1ms, 32 GB, backups up to the storage size included About 16 Container Registry: Basic About 5 Log Analytics and Application Insights: the first 5 GB a month free 0 to a few Key Vault and managed identities Cents Total About 30 to 60 Geo-redundant backup roughly doubles the backup storage, and high availability doubles the database compute. Consequences The API now signs in to PostgreSQL through Aspire.Azure.Npgsql. A connection string with a password (the AppHost, the tests) is used as it is; one without uses an Entra token for the managed identity. Program.cs runs JasperFx commands when the first argument names one (db-migrate, db-assert, db-patch), and the API otherwise. A schema change is applied by the next deployment's migration job before the new revision starts, while the old revision is still serving. Changes must therefore be backwards compatible with the running code: add first, remove in a later release. The Deploy workflow only deploys main, so a rollback is a revert merged to main and deployed. Its migration puts back the older Marten functions and leaves what the newer release added, which the older code ignores. Until then, the container app can be pointed at an earlier image by hand, because the older code starts on the newer schema (Rolling back). Columns and indexes nothing uses any more stay until someone drops them by hand. The AppHost uses two experimental Aspire APIs, the deployment pipeline step and the image push options (ASPIREPIPELINES001, ASPIREPIPELINES003). An Aspire upgrade may change them. The migration step finds the two provisioning steps it sits between by their container apps and their provision-infra tag, and fails the pipeline if it can't, so an upgrade that moves them breaks aspire publish on its pull request rather than deploying the API without its migration. Nothing here has been provisioned. The Bicep, the images, the migration and the API's startup against a DML-only role are verified locally (see Deploying); the Entra mapping of the API's role and the first aspire deploy can only be checked in Azure. One-off setup by the owner Commands use the Azure CLI. <sub>, <rg>, <region> and the names are placeholders, and the repository is Invex-Games/passel. Deploying explains each step. [ ] Choose the subscription and region, confirm the services and cost above, decide on geo-redundant backup, and change this ADR's status to accepted. [ ] Register the resource providers once in the subscription: Microsoft.App, Microsoft.ContainerRegistry, Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL, Microsoft.Insights, Microsoft.KeyVault, Microsoft.ManagedIdentity, Microsoft.OperationalInsights (az provider register --namespace <name>). [ ] Create the resource group the API lives in: az group create --name <rg> --location <region>. The deployment never creates one. [ ] Create the deployment identity in a separate resource group, so it can't change its own credentials: az identity create --name passel-github-deploy --resource-group <ops-rg>. [ ] Give it a federated credential for the environment: az identity federated-credential create --name github-production --identity-name passel-github-deploy --resource-group <ops-rg> --issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com --subject repo:Invex-Games/passel:environment:production --audiences api://AzureADTokenExchange. [ ] Assign it roles on <rg> only: Contributor, and Role Based Access Control Administrator limited to the two roles Aspire assigns (AcrPull and Key Vault Secrets User); the condition is in Deploying. [ ] In GitHub, create the production environment, with required reviewers and deployments limited to main. [ ] Add the variables (to the environment or the repository): AZURE_CLIENT_ID (the identity's client id), AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP, AZURE_LOCATION, GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID, and CHROME_EXTENSION_CLIENT_ID if it isn't set already. [ ] Generate the Sqids alphabet once and add it as the environment secret ENCODING_ALPHABET. It must never change once ids are in use. [ ] Run the Deploy workflow, then check /health on the URL in the run's summary. [ ] When the domain is ready: add its DNS records, set API_DOMAIN, deploy, create the managed certificate, set API_CERTIFICATE_NAME and deploy again (Custom domain).

docs/decisions/0004-hosting-on-docker-co.title: ADR 0004: Hosting on Docker Compose on the owner's server | Passel
docs/decisions/0004-hosting-on-docker-co.summary: ADR 0004: Hosting on Docker Compose on the owner's server Status: accepted, November 2026. Supersedes ADR 0003. The filesystem parcel store, the images, the compose stack and the DeployCompose workflow are all built; the deploying guide describes the server setup the owner does once before the first deploy. Decides: where the API and the web app run, how they are built, deployed and rolled back, and where uploaded files are kept outside Azure. Context ADR 0003 put the API on Azure Container Apps with a managed PostgreSQL server, Key Vault and Application Insights. The owner has an Ubuntu x64 server of their own, and for one small API with one replica the Azure services cost more each month than the server does in a year. ADR 0003 weighed a VM with Docker Compose and set it aside because patching, TLS, backups and deployment would all be by hand; this decision answers each of those below. ADR 0002 anticipated the move: should hosting leave Azure, the parcel store swaps behind its interface, and nothing in the clients depends on either. Options Option For Against Azure Container Apps (ADR 0003) Managed revisions, jobs, identities and TLS; nothing to patch The running cost for one replica and a database server; Azure-only pieces in the AppHost Docker Compose on the owner's server One server already paid for; the same containers as anywhere else; a stack small enough to read in one file One machine: no failover, and the owner patches and backs it up k3s on the same server Rolling deploys and probes as in Kubernetes A cluster to run for two containers and a database, with nothing it does that Compose and a deploy script can't for one replica A platform as a service (Fly.io, Render, Railway) TLS, deploys and logs managed Another bill and another vendor, managed PostgreSQL priced like Azure's, and nowhere obvious for the files Decision The API, the web app and PostgreSQL run as one Docker Compose project on the owner's server, deployed from GitHub Actions over SSH. Azure stays in the code but is no longer where Passel runs. Versions and images. The build takes its version and build id from GitVersion, which IBuild uses as its provider. The version is GitVersion's SemVer (the same as its FullSemVer under ContinuousDelivery), which on main ends in the number of commits since the last version, as in 0.2.0-rc.12, so every commit on main has a version of its own. Every image gets two tags: the version, with + and / replaced by -, which is immutable and is what gets deployed and rolled back to, and sha- with the first seven characters of the commit, for tracing an image to its source and as a backstop should two builds ever produce the same version, as two branches with the same name at different times could. There is no latest. The images live in GitHub Container Registry under ghcr.io/invex-games/: passel-webapi, the API, which also runs the db-migrate command; passel-web, Caddy serving the static web app; and passel-deploy, an image built from scratch that holds the compose files and scripts of the release under the same tag. Images are pushed only by builds of main; other builds build them without pushing. A version tag that exists already is never overwritten: before a push the build looks the tag up, skips the push when it is there with the same org.opencontainers.image.revision, and fails when it is there with another. The job that publishes depends on the API's tests, because the merge commit is what ships, whatever its pull request showed. Environment values. Neither image holds an environment's values, so the image that ran in one environment is promoted unchanged to the next. The web app reads the API's address and the Google web client id from /app/config.json when it starts, and the web image writes that file when its container starts, from the server's .env (https://<API_HOST> and GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID), refusing to start when either is missing or not valid. Its content security policies are response headers, the app's built from the same origin. An earlier version of this decision compiled both values into the site from repository variables, which meant one web image per environment and a rebuild to move the API; the build no longer reads those variables. The API image is built by the .NET SDK's container support; its registry, repository and tags are passed by the publishing target only, so the Azure path's image naming does not change. The web image. Caddy serves the output of the one web app build, with the security headers in a snippet that both the site and its 404 page import, the app's policy over them under /app/, its admin endpoint and automatic HTTPS off, and running as an unprivileged user. An entrypoint checks the two values and writes the app's configuration to a directory the image gives that user before Caddy starts; a value that could break out of the JSON or the Caddyfile is refused, not escaped. The base image's capability to bind low ports is removed from the Caddy binary, since it listens on 8080 and a binary with a file capability will not start in a container that drops every capability. TLS ends in front of it. Files. A new FileSystemParcelStore keeps the bytes of uploaded files in a directory on a local disk, chosen with Parcels:Store=FileSystem and Parcels:FileSystemRoot. The default, Auto, keeps the old behaviour: Azure when the passel-blobs connection string is set, no store otherwise. Naming AzureBlob without that connection string stops the API at startup rather than quietly leaving it with no store. The store writes each upload to a temp file, flushes it, renames it into place without overwriting and then flushes the directory, so a parcel recorded as uploaded has its bytes on disk even after a power cut; its own disk failures are answered with 503 like a storage outage, and are kept apart from other I/O errors such as a client that stops sending. It works on a local disk only: a network share weakens the rename and the flushes it relies on. See Parcels. The database and its roles. PostgreSQL 18 runs in the stack with a data volume. A script run on every deploy, as the superuser the container creates, makes sure two logins exist with the passwords in the server's .env: passel_owner, which owns the database and may create roles but is not a superuser, and passel_api. The db-migrate command always runs as passel_owner; the default privileges it grants apply only to tables later created by the same login, so it must be the same login every time. Should passel_owner turn out to lack a privilege the migration needs, the migration runs as the superuser instead, under the same rule. The API connects as passel_api, which the migration makes a member of passel_app and which therefore has only DML. The proxy. Neither the API nor the web app publishes a port. By default a bundled Caddy (the edge profile) takes ports 80 and 443, gets certificates with ACME, and is the only address the API trusts forwarded headers from: it has a fixed address on the stack's edge network, outside the range the other containers get theirs from, and the API sets ForwardedHeaders:Enabled with that address as its one known network, never ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED. A server that already runs a proxy uses an override file instead: one joins the proxy's own Docker network, another binds the API and the web app to the loopback for a proxy on the host. The server's .env names the files and profiles, so every compose command sees the same stack. Compose 2.24 or later is required. Deploying. A manual workflow, DeployCompose, deploys to one of two stacks, pre-prod or production, chosen by its required target input; it runs in the GitHub environment of that name, which holds that stack's server, user, host keys and deploy key, with a concurrency group per stack, deploy-compose-<target>, beside the Azure workflow's deploy-webapi. The two stacks can share a server: each has its own directory, project name, subnets, proxy aliases and gate, and each key is forced to its own stack's gate, which deploys only the directory it is installed in. It checks that all three images exist at the tag, then connects over SSH with a key whose authorized_keys entry forces one command, a gate script that accepts only deploy <tag> and optionally --no-migrate, checks the tag against ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,127}$, reads a registry token from standard input into a temporary Docker configuration that it removes afterwards, pulls the deploy image, copies its files to releases/<tag>/ and runs that release's deploy script. The tag is checked in the build, in the gate and in the script. The script runs the one-off services in order (the roles, the parcels directory, the migration unless told not to), then starts the API and the web app and waits for them to be healthy, then checks /health through the proxy. Passel's own images are pulled only when the server lacks them, since their tags never move, the other images are pulled on every deploy, which brings their patches in, except on a rollback (--no-migrate), which uses the images the server has and so needs no registry at all; a deploy whose other registries are unreachable goes on with the images the server has. The gate and the script hold one lock, so one deploy runs at a time. Only after the check does it record the release; a failed deploy prints the API's and the web app's logs (the migration's output is already in the run's log) and leaves the record as it was. The server keeps the current and previous release and an append-only log of releases. Rolling back. A rollback is the same workflow with an older tag and the migration off, which brings back that release's images together with that release's compose files. That only works if the previous release runs against the newer schema, so a release may add columns only when they are nullable or have a default; the migration never drops one. Settings. The API and the migration get an explicit environment in the compose file, never an env_file, with ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT and DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT both Production. The Azure settings stay unset: APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING, every AZURE_* variable, Database:ApiRoleObjectId, Authentication:Google:ClientSecret and ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED. Passwords are generated as hex, which needs no quoting in a connection string or in compose; the Sqids alphabet is quoted in .env, and must equal the one any earlier deployment used. Health and hardening. The API's container is checked with a plain HTTP request to /health from inside it, with localhost as the host, which AllowedHosts lists, made with the image's bash, since it has no curl or wget. The web app's is a wget of its root. The API and the web app run without new privileges and with every capability dropped. Every service's logs rotate at 10 MB, five files. Backups. A script run by cron on the server dumps the database first, in PostgreSQL's custom format, with its roles alongside, and then archives the parcels volume. Shipping the backups off the server is the owner's choice of tool. Azure. The Azure code stays where it is: the AppHost's Azure hosting, the Azure blob store, the Deploy workflow and its concurrency group. Nothing removes it in this change. Answers to "all by hand" TLS: the bundled Caddy gets and renews certificates by itself, or the server's existing proxy keeps doing it. Patching: unattended-upgrades patches the server. Dependabot updates the dependencies, and every build of main rebuilds the images from fresh base images, so a deploy picks up patched images too. PostgreSQL minor versions arrive with the image; a major version is a dump and a restore. Backups: the backup script and the restore drill in the deploying guide; the database and the parcels volume are consistent only as a pair. Deployment: the manual workflow, with GitHub's run history as the audit trail and the production environment's protection rules in front of it. Consequences One machine is a single point of failure. That is accepted: the API already ran one replica, because its rate limits, stream caps and upload gates count per instance. The owner runs the server: its updates, its disk, its backups and its restore drills. The web app is built once for every environment and its image promoted unchanged; the server's .env holds the API's address and the web client id, and the web container refuses to start without them. The parcels volume and the database must be backed up and restored together. New columns must be nullable or have a default, so a rollback keeps working. The deploy key can run Docker, which is as good as root on the server. The forced command is what limits it to deploying a validated tag. Follow-ups Removing the Azure path once the server has run for a while. An S3-compatible parcel store, should the files outgrow one disk. How a staging environment would be named and built, given one web image per environment.

docs/evaluation/codebase-health.html.title: Codebase Health | Passel
docs/evaluation/codebase-health.html.summary: Codebase Health Scope: structure, duplication, test coverage, error handling, configuration, dependencies, dead code and the deployment story across the API, the extension, the mobile app and the Atom build. Method: every component was read in full, every build and test command was run (results in Developer Experience), and package freshness and vulnerability scans were taken. Size for reference: API 1,638 lines of C# plus 511 of tests; Atom build 1,049; extension 1,971 lines of TypeScript plus 389 of tests; mobile 3,743 lines of Dart plus 2,810 of tests. Largest files: popup.ts 710, packets_provider.dart 552, theme.dart 386, packet_list.dart 360. Verdict This is a small, strict and readable codebase with zero warning debt, fast green test suites, and the hard concurrency cases reasoned about in comments and tests. Its weaknesses are structural rather than local: the API's real behaviour (HTTP, auth, Marten, SQL, LISTEN/NOTIFY, SSE) has no automated coverage at all; the packet wire shape is declared four times in C# and hand-parsed twice in the clients with nothing detecting drift; the trickiest logic in the repository, the feed state machine, exists twice with only the author's memory keeping them in step; and there is no CI, no automated dependency updates and no deployment path. All of these are cheap while the codebase is this size. Score: 3 / 5. Strengths Concurrency and failure modes are written down and tested: NOTIFY only after commit, with the reason it can't be queued in the session; bounded subscriber channels that complete instead of dropping; the hub subscribes before the first resync; heartbeat and idle timeouts aligned across server and both clients. Security-aware details throughout (404 for foreign ids, canonical-only id decoding, http(s)-only links on both sides, nonce and state checks, single-flight token refresh). Both clients tolerate unknown packet types and malformed events instead of failing the page. Strictness everywhere: TreatWarningsAsErrors, nullable, C# 14 extension members used tastefully, TypeScript strict and isolatedModules, Dart strict modes. Zero warnings in every suite. The tests that exist are behaviour tests with hand-written fakes and good names, and the whole loop runs in under ten seconds warm. Non-obvious code carries explanatory comments (feed.ts, packets_provider.dart, build.mjs). Pinned and locked dependencies (package-lock.json honoured with npm ci, pubspec.lock tracked, exact NuGet versions), and nothing vulnerable in any .NET project including transitives. Findings Ordered by importance. The API's real behaviour has no automated coverage (High). The 42 tests cover Validate, Paginate, StreamPacketEvents, the hub, notification parsing and id encoding, all pure helpers; the test project references only xunit.v3. Untested: PacketStoreService (Marten FetchForWriting, the inline snapshot, ShouldDelete), the cursor query over UUIDv7 ids, NOTIFY after commit through LISTEN to the hub to SSE, JSON polymorphism with out-of-order metadata, the development policy scheme, the request size limit. The testing guide admits it: "check those by running the AppHost". A Marten or Npgsql upgrade or a mapping change can break production silently, and the resync guarantee both clients rely on is unproven. Fix: an integration test project with Testcontainers.PostgreSql and WebApplicationFactory<Program> (InternalsVisibleTo is already declared), a test authentication scheme that reads the user id from a header, and tests for create-then-list and ownership isolation, paging over 51 packets with the returned cursor, delete semantics (204, then 404, other user 404), SSE end to end (open the stream with ResponseHeadersRead, create, assert resync then packet-created, which exercises pg_notify and the listener for real), and schema creation from an empty database. Aspire.Hosting.Testing is closest to production but starts the extension build and the tunnel too; keep it for one optional smoke test. Wire the new project into atom TestWebApi. The packet wire model is declared four times and hand-parsed twice, with nothing detecting drift (High). The domain union Packet in PacketAggregate.cs, PostPacketRequestBody and PostPacketResponseBody in PostPacket.cs, and GetPacketsResponseBody.Packet in GetPackets.cs; the last two are field-for-field identical and mapped twice. Each client re-encodes the $type, name|title|fileName and url|body|parcelId mapping on its own (packets.ts, packet.dart). OpenAPI exists only at runtime in Development and is never exported. Adding CreatedAt today means four C# edits, two client edits and three test suites, and no test fails if one is missed. Options: Shared contracts with generated clients (Kiota for TypeScript and Dart, or openapi-generator): best typing, but the $type union maps to oneOf plus discriminator, where Dart generators are weakest, and it adds a code-generation step to two toolchains for five endpoints. Hand-written clients plus contract fixtures: cheap, and catches drift in all three suites. Committed OpenAPI as documentation only: no enforcement. Recommendation: the fixtures now, generation if the API grows past a handful of endpoints. Collapse the C# declarations to one response DTO used by create, list and SSE with one mapper; export the OpenAPI document at build (Microsoft.Extensions.ApiDescription.Server) and commit it under docs/reference/ with a test that fails when it is stale; write contracts/fixtures/ (one JSON file per $type, a page, the three SSE payloads) from a C# test using the real JsonOptions, and make packets.test.ts and packet_test.dart parse those files. The feed state machine is implemented twice with identical invariants and nothing enforcing parity (High). FeedStore in feed.ts and PacketsNotifier in packets_provider.dart share generation, fetch sequence, arrivals, deleted ids, hidden map, the reconcile step and the syncLatest overlap rule; the Dart one adds an auth epoch and loading-state branches. The tests mirror by name (18 TypeScript cases, 37 Dart). A bug fixed in one is not necessarily fixed in the other, and this is the code most likely to regress under a small change. Sharing code across TypeScript and Dart is not sane. Fix: make parity executable with a language-neutral scenario file (contracts/feed-scenarios.json: a list of operations such as showCached, refresh:start, refresh:resolve, applyCreated, applyDeleted, hide, unhide, loadMore:resolve, each with the expected id list afterwards) and a 60-line interpreter in each suite; both suites already use a hand-resolved fake source and an in-memory cache. Separately, if the SSE stream carried event ids or the list endpoint took ?since=, clients could replay instead of reconciling in-flight fetches, which shrinks both machines; consider it with the storage-model decision below. Document the invariants once (Developer Experience, finding 9). Error handling is consistent on the server and lost on the mobile client (Medium). The API uses ProblemDetails and field-keyed validation problems; the extension's readError turns title, detail and errors into one sentence and maps network failures to a friendly message, with three remaining raw Error: … sites in popup.ts. The mobile validateResponse never reads the body (throw Exception('$context failed with HTTP …')), so a 400 the server carefully composed is discarded, and the UI shows 'Push failed: $e', 'Refresh failed: $e', 'Couldn't delete packet: $e', asyncState.error.toString(), e.toString() and 'Auth error: …'. Fix: parse application/problem+json into an ApiException with status, title, detail and field errors (mirroring api.ts), wrap socket and timeout errors into a NetworkException, map both to copy in one describeError used by every snackbar, and add Dart tests mirroring the extension's readError cases. Dead and speculative code (Medium). Domain/Commands/CreateFilePacket.cs has no references. The File packet exists in six C# declarations and both clients while the API rejects creating one, which the docs then have to explain as "returned only". EndpointBuilderExtensions.cs defines thirteen helpers of which only AcceptsJson is used. IFlutterHelper.cs contains two unexplained Task.Delay(2000) calls. Fix: delete the unused command and helpers; since no production data can contain a File packet, remove it end to end and reintroduce it with parcels; replace the sleeps with the condition they wait for. Google client ids live in six places under four naming schemes (Medium). AppHost parameters (google-client-id, google-client-secret, google-extension-client-id) in user secrets; the extension's .env (GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID); the mobile .env (SERVER_CLIENT_ID, APP_CLIENT_ID); _atom/appsettings.json (server-client-id, mobile-app-client-id, with Key Vault secret names as placeholder values); a git-ignored _atom/appsettings.Development.json; and the API's git-ignored appsettings.Development.json. The web client id alone has four names. The local extension .env on this machine has already drifted (it carries variables build.mjs never reads). Fix: make the AppHost user secrets the single development source, add a sync step to SetupDevEnvironment that writes both .env files from them (plus the stable tunnel URL), use one vocabulary everywhere (GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_SECRET, GOOGLE_EXTENSION_CLIENT_ID, GOOGLE_ANDROID_CLIENT_ID), rename the Atom parameters to match, and drop the placeholder strings so "not configured" is explicit. Dependency hygiene: well pinned, not automated, build tooling drifting (Medium). No Directory.Packages.props (OpenTelemetry and JetBrains versions repeated across projects), no SDK pin in global.json, no Node pin, no Renovate or Dependabot, no CI. _atom is on Invex.Atom 3.7.0 while the global tool is 4.2.0 and 5.0.0 is current. Pending majors: TypeScript 7, vitest 5 (which also clears the four dev-only advisories), flutter_riverpod 3, share_plus 13, dynamic_color 2; Aspire 13.6.3 is a patch away. Atom can generate the missing automation: the Invex.Atom.Module.GithubWorkflows package (present in the NuGet cache, not referenced) exposes workflow and Dependabot definitions, and Invex.RepoUtils has a DocFX publish step; exact usage unverified. Fix: central package management, global.json with rollForward: latestFeature, engines in package.json, the workflows module with Test on pull requests and Build* plus docs publish on main, a Dependabot definition for NuGet, npm, pub and actions, npm audit fix and vitest 5 now, and the Riverpod 3 migration as its own change (an automated migration exists). Structure and naming: mostly clean, with a mislabelled layer, one oversized module and three verbs for one action (Low). PacketStoreService lives in Domain/ while doing Marten and Npgsql I/O; Domain/Commands are endpoint-to-service DTOs. popup.ts mixes DOM wiring, feed rendering, delete and undo, the copy menu, toasts and an icon atlas, with module-level getElementById calls that make it impossible to import under test. packets_provider.dart hosts two notifiers. The API says Create, the extension says send, the mobile app says push, and the title-ish field is name, title or fileName on the wire. The mobile app sends ?api-version=1 on every call and the extension sends none. Fix: "send" for user-facing verbs and Create for API names; split popup.ts into feed view, composer and toast modules behind a controller that receives its document and messaging so it can run under jsdom; move the store service to an application folder; pick one API-version convention. Client test gaps (Low). Extension: auth.ts (URL building, prompt modes, state, nonce, audience and expiry checks), api.ts (the 401-refresh-retry-sign-out path, readError, the idle timeout), live.ts (port lifecycle, backoff), background.ts (delete scheduling and cancel, context-menu mapping), cache.ts and popup.ts have no tests. Mobile: 12 of 170 tests are widget tests; PacketFeedPage, PacketList (load-more trigger, error row, signed-out prompts), the send sheet, the tiles and packet_helpers.dart have none. No coverage is collected anywhere. Fix: vitest with jsdom and a stubbed chrome global for the popup modules, fetch stubs for the 401 matrix and problem parsing, fake timers for backoff and delete scheduling; Flutter widget tests with ProviderScope overrides reusing test/fakes.dart; coverage flags on all three Atom test targets. Deployment story is undefined (High for shipping, noted here for completeness). BuildWebApi publishes to a folder; there is no container image, no infrastructure definition, no documented production configuration source, Marten runs DDL at startup, the extension version is a hard-coded "1.0.0" while .NET versions come from GitVersion, and there are no Web Store or Play publishing steps. Details and the fix are in Developer Experience, finding 1. Nits. [PublicAPI] on 54 declarations where [UsedImplicitly] or nothing says what is meant; npm clean and package scripts shell out to PowerShell; pubspec.yaml keeps about seventy lines of flutter create comments and cupertino_icons; src/mobile_app/.flutter-plugins is tracked although it says not to be, is stale and contains machine-specific paths; ios/ carries sixty tracked scaffold files the docs call unconfigured; avoid_print: false disables a lint no code triggers; Directory.Build.props carries packaging properties no project packs; IFlutterHelper locates Flutter by string-matching PATH entries; 46 files start with a BOM and the worktree is 42 percent CRLF against an LF index (see Developer Experience, finding 4). Decision: storage model for packets Three reports converge on the same question. Packets are event-sourced (two or three events per stream, an inline snapshot), and nothing reads the history. The consequences: deletes never erase content (Security, finding 1), the event table grows forever and bodies are stored twice (Performance, finding 6), creates and deletes cost extra round trips (finding 7 there), and every future feature (previews, pins, parcels) adds events and projection code. Option Pros Cons Keep event sourcing, archive and purge: ArchiveStream on delete, partitioned archive, a purge job after N days, hard delete for account deletion Smallest change; keeps the door open for per-user event replay Content lingers until the purge; bodies still stored twice; rebuild and codegen complexity stays; every feature is an event plus projection work Plain Marten documents: one Packet document with Id, UserId, CreatedAt, DeletedAt and the content union; Store, Delete, LINQ with the composite index True deletes, half the writes, fewer round trips, simpler service and tests, features become fields; trash and restore is a DeletedAt field plus a purge Rewrites PacketStoreService, the projection and their tests (about a day); loses an audit trail nothing uses Documents plus a per-user change log: the above, plus a small changes table (user, sequence, packet id, change) written in the same transaction Enables resumable SSE (Last-Event-ID) and ?since= delta sync, which shrinks both client state machines (finding 3) Slightly more code than plain documents Recommendation: plain documents, with the change log added when resumable sync is wanted (it is the natural companion of the device registry and push work). Record the decision as an ADR before parcels and previews add more events. If the team prefers to keep event sourcing, do the archive-and-purge option in Phase 0 regardless. Steps forward Integration tests for the API (M). Finding 1; everything else in the API is safer with this net. Storage-model ADR and implementation (M). The decision above; before parcels and previews. One wire DTO, committed OpenAPI, contract fixtures (M). Finding 2. Feed scenario file (S to M). Finding 3. Mobile error mapping (S). Finding 4. Delete dead code, the File branch and the placeholder config (S). Findings 5 and 6. Central package management, pins, workflows and Dependabot through Atom, vitest 5 (M). Finding 7; lands with the CI work. Vocabulary and structure cleanups (S to M). Finding 8, after the product decision in UX. Client tests and coverage (M). Finding 9. Nits in one sweep (S). Finding 11.

docs/evaluation/developer-experience.htm.title: Developer Experience | Passel
docs/evaluation/developer-experience.htm.summary: Developer Experience Scope: what it takes to go from clone to a running system, to a passing test run, and to a release, on the machine a developer actually has. Method: every documented command was run from the repository root with warm caches, the onboarding docs were checked claim by claim against the repository, and the Atom build, the ignore rules and line endings were inspected. The AppHost itself and the atom Build* targets were read rather than run. Verdict The inner loop is excellent: one build, three test suites, zero warnings, all green in seconds, with docs that are structured, honest and precise, an AppHost that provisions the database, the extension's watch build and a phone-reachable tunnel, and a ConfigErrorPage that tells a mobile developer exactly which value is missing. The outer loop is missing: there is no CI, no deployment path, no release automation and no contribution conventions. And the first ten minutes for a stranger end at a Google Cloud console, because nothing in the system can authenticate without three real OAuth clients. Score: 4 / 5 for the inner loop, 1 / 5 for the outer loop. The developer loop as measured Command Result Time (warm) Notes dotnet build Invex.Passel.slnx -c Debug 5 projects, 0 warnings, 0 errors 7.2 s TreatWarningsAsErrors holds dotnet test --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi.Tests/… 42 passed 4.0 s Needs --project under Microsoft.Testing.Platform; docs say so npm run typecheck (extension) clean 0.85 s npm test (extension) 39 passed 1.0 s flutter analyze no issues 22.4 s The slowest step flutter test 170 passed 4.2 s dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive (5 projects) none vulnerable 1 to 9 s each npm audit 4 advisories, all dev-only (vitest 3 chain, esbuild) 2 s vitest@5 and npm audit fix clear them flutter pub outdated 7 direct outdated, 3 majors (flutter_riverpod 3, share_plus 13, dynamic_color 2) 1.8 s google_sign_in current atom -h (as the README says) prints the global tool wrapper's own usage, not the targets dotnet run --project _atom -- --help lists all ten targets dotnet run --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi (API alone) fails: ConnectionString is missing Clear message; there is no way to run the API without PostgreSQL and Google settings Tool versions on this machine: .NET SDK 10.0.401, Node 24, Flutter 3.41.0, Docker 29, Aspire CLI 13.6.2, Dev Tunnels 1.0, Invex.Atom.Tool 4.2.0 globally against Invex.Atom.Build 3.7.0 in _atom (5.0.0 is current). Strengths Documentation far above the solo-project norm: getting started, components, guides and reference; honest about limits; precise about ports, precedence and SSE semantics; already a searchable DocFX site. Every port, endpoint, limit and precedence rule the docs state was checked and is correct. The AppHost removes most setup pain: PostgreSQL with pgweb, the extension's watch build with injected configuration, a stable tunnel for phones, parameter prompting persisted to user secrets, telemetry to the dashboard. SetupDevEnvironment is idempotent and prints an install hint for each missing tool; ConfigErrorPage names the missing dart-define and the exact command to run. Fast, green, warning-free verification, so a newcomer's first change is judged by the same bar as the existing code. .env.example files with real comments for both clients. Findings There is no deployment or release path (High). _atom/appsettings.json names https://api.passel.link, but BuildWebApi only publishes to a folder; there is no container image, compose file, Bicep, Terraform or azd definition; Marten applies schema at startup with the application's credentials; the production values for the connection string, the Google settings, the Sqids alphabet and the telemetry endpoint have no documented source; the extension's version is a hard-coded "1.0.0" while .NET versions come from GitVersion; BuildChromeExtension makes a zip with no Web Store step; BuildMobileAppAndroid makes a bundle with no Play step. Fix, the minimum repeatable path: dotnet publish /t:PublishContainer with tags from GitVersion pushed to a registry; one host (a container app or a small VM with compose) with managed PostgreSQL; AutoCreate.None in production and schema applied at deploy with the JasperFx command line or a one-shot job; secrets from the host's store as environment variables with the keys documented; a DeployWebApi Atom target and workflow; version stamped into dist/manifest.json from GitVersion and published with chrome-webstore-upload-cli; Gradle Play Publisher or fastlane supply for the bundle and mapping.txt. No CI, no contribution conventions, no governance files (High). No .github/, no pull-request or issue templates, no CODEOWNERS, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG or LICENSE (nothing says whether the code may be used at all), yet GitVersion.yml encodes conventional-commit bump rules and feat/, fix/, chore/ branch names that the history already follows. Fix: generate the workflows with Atom's GitHub workflows module (Test on pull requests, Build* and docs publish on main, a Dependabot definition), add CONTRIBUTING.md (branch and commit conventions and their version effect, atom Test before a pull request, how the .env files work), a LICENSE, a one-line CODEOWNERS, a pull-request template, and a CHANGELOG generated from conventional commits. The first ten minutes end at a Google Cloud console (High). Every packet endpoint requires a Google ID token, the AppHost prompts for three OAuth values, Scalar's login needs the web client secret, and there is no development scheme, seeded user or fake issuer. A contributor without access to the maintainer's Cloud project must create a project and three clients (web with secret, extension, Android with their debug SHA-1) before a single request succeeds. Fix: a Development-only authentication scheme selected by the existing policy scheme (Authorization: Dev <user-id>, or tokens from dotnet user-jwts) so Scalar, curl and the integration tests work with the Google parameters empty; make the three AppHost parameters optional in Development; add a "run without Google" section to the running-locally page and keep the OAuth page for real sign-in. Line endings, BOMs and no .gitattributes (Medium). The index is 100 percent LF, the worktree is 42 percent CRLF because core.autocrlf=true, .editorconfig demands CRLF for every file, one file has mixed endings, 46 tracked files start with a BOM and the rest don't, and git warns on every status and diff. Fix with zero churn: .gitattributes with * text=auto eol=lf plus binary rules for *.png and *.psd, .editorconfig end_of_line = lf, git add --renormalize . (a no-op for the index), and let the IDE strip the BOMs. The documented target discovery doesn't work, and tool versions float (Medium). atom -h with the installed 4.2.0 global tool prints the wrapper's usage; atom -- -h errors; the tool is not resolvable from Git Bash at all because the shim is atom.cmd. _atom is on 3.7.0, the global tool is 4.2.0, 5.0.0 is current, and there is no tool manifest. Fix: a dotnet-tools.json manifest so dotnet tool restore and dotnet atom <Target> give everyone the same version in every shell; fix the README and the build-targets page; upgrade _atom to the current Atom in its own change. Google OAuth setup is incomplete for a stranger (Medium). The OAuth page has no consent-screen or test-users step, no keytool command for the debug SHA-1, doesn't say that each developer's debug keystore SHA-1 must be added to the one Android client, names no one to "ask for the existing ids", and doesn't explain why APP_CLIENT_ID is optional when the Android client must still exist. Fix: a numbered from-zero walkthrough with the keytool command, the consent screen, the per-developer SHA-1 note, and a short "if sign-in fails with X, check Y" table (redirect URI mismatch for the extension id, missing SHA-1 giving DEVELOPER_ERROR on Android, audience not in AdditionalAudiences giving 401). Cross-platform friction (Medium). atom.cmd is invisible to bash; the npm clean and package scripts require PowerShell; the uncommitted launch configuration uses a backslash path; Atom helpers branch on Windows with where/which and PATH-string heuristics; the loop has never been recorded on macOS or Linux. Fix: the tool manifest (finding 5), Node-only npm scripts, a note about the .cmd shim in prerequisites, and one run of the loop on macOS or Linux written into the docs. SetupDevEnvironment under-checks and under-automates (Low). It probes five tools, Docker running and the dev certificate, but not the .NET SDK version, Node version, JDK or Android SDK, git, or whether devtunnel is logged in; it creates src/mobile_app/.env from the example and leaves every value to be typed by hand. Fix: version checks, a devtunnel user show hint, the configuration sync from Codebase Health finding 6, and a printed next-steps checklist. Documentation gaps (Low, specific). No architecture diagram (one Mermaid sequence diagram for create, pg_notify, LISTEN, hub, SSE, client reconcile would do; the modern DocFX template renders Mermaid), no page on how the feed state machine works (its invariants exist only as comments in feed.ts and packets_provider.dart), no ADRs (event sourcing for a two-event aggregate, Sqids ids, the implicit id_token flow, LISTEN/NOTIFY over SignalR or Redis, tunnel over emulator), no troubleshooting page (Docker not running, dev certificate untrusted, devtunnel not logged in, extension id and redirect mismatch, port 7030 busy, atom not found in bash), no release or deploy page, and the HTTP API page restates what a committed OpenAPI document could carry. A debug build through Atom appears to need Key Vault secrets (Low, unverified by execution). BuildMobileAppAndroid declares the keystore alias and password as required parameters although they are only used for the production flavor, so a development APK through Atom needs Key Vault access while the docs say the secrets are for production. Fix: require them only when the flavor is production, and document flutter run --flavor development --dart-define-from-file=.env as the day-to-day path. Repository noise and sharing (Low). A real signing keystore sits in the repository root (ignored, never committed, still one git add -f from history; Key Vault already holds it); devtools_options.yaml is untracked and un-ignored; the generated .flutter-plugins is tracked, stale and machine-specific; the 14 KB .gitignore concatenates the Visual Studio, JetBrains and Flutter-SDK templates (so version and *.lock are ignored everywhere and pubspec.lock survives only through a nested re-include); .idea/ is fully ignored so Rider run configurations can't be shared; .vscode/launch.json has a personal device id pending. Fix: move the keystore out, commit devtools_options.yaml, untrack .flutter-plugins, trim the ignore file to what the repo needs, add shared launchers (tasks.json for atom Test and aspire run, allow the Rider run-configuration folder through the ignore rules), and don't commit the device id. Version pinning is partial (Low). Flutter 3.41.0 is pinned for release builds only and the build may switch a developer's own SDK; TestMobileApp uses whatever Flutter is on PATH; no SDK pin in global.json; no Node pin. Fix: global.json with rollForward: latestFeature, engines in package.json, FVM or a warning when the PATH Flutter differs from the pinned version. A small tool that fell out of this review The extension popup was reviewed by running the real popup.js bundle in a plain browser tab with a 60-line stub of the chrome.* APIs (runtime.sendMessage and connect, storage, tabs) returning canned packets. It renders every state (signed out, empty, feed, copy menu, undo toast, dark mode) without loading the extension or signing in, reloads instantly, and would make a fine npm run harness for popup work and for screenshot tests. It lives in this session's scratch folder; it is worth adding to src/chrome-extension/harness/. Steps forward CI through Atom's workflow generator, with Dependabot and the governance files (M). Findings 2 and 12. Deploy the API repeatably and stamp versions into every artifact (L). Finding 1. Development auth scheme and optional AppHost parameters (S). Finding 3; also what the integration tests need. Tool manifest, .gitattributes, LF, no BOMs, fix the README (S). Findings 4, 5, 7. OAuth walkthrough, troubleshooting page, architecture diagram, feed state-machine page, ADRs (M). Findings 6 and 9. SetupDevEnvironment version checks and config sync; keystore out of the tree; ignore-file trim (S to M). Findings 8, 10, 11. Popup harness in the repo (S). Useful for the redesign work in UI Design.

docs/evaluation/features.html.title: Feature Ideas | Passel
docs/evaluation/features.html.summary: Feature Ideas A brainstorm of what Passel could do next, starting with the one the codebase is already half-built for: parcels. Each idea has a rough value and effort so the Roadmap can sequence them. Sizes: S under a day, M a few days, L a week or more, XL several weeks. Summary # Feature Value Effort Touches Depends on 1 Parcels: files and images High XL API, storage, all clients Storage choice 2 Device registry and push notifications High L API, all clients Nothing (registry first) 3 Android share target and process-text High S to M Mobile Nothing 4 Timestamps, day headers, relative time High S API, all clients Nothing 5 Link previews (title, description, image, favicon) High M API, all clients SSRF safeguards 6 Search and filters Medium M API, all clients Nothing 7 First-party sessions (token exchange, refresh tokens) High for web L API, all clients Nothing 8 Send to a specific device Medium M API, all clients 2 9 Pin, archive, labels Medium M API, all clients Nothing 10 Retention and auto-expiry Medium S to M API, settings UI Nothing 11 Trash and restore Medium S API, clients Nothing (event-sourced already) 12 Extension: side panel, commands, omnibox, send all tabs, drag and drop High M Extension Nothing (parcels for files) 13 Mobile: widget, quick-settings tile, app shortcuts, deep links Medium M Mobile 7 for deep links to work signed-in 14 Account: delete, export, usage High for store listing M API, mobile, web Nothing 15 Public API, API keys, CLI, webhooks Medium L API, new CLI 7 16 Offline send queue Medium M Clients Nothing 17 Read and opened state Low M API, clients Nothing 18 Collections (send several items as one) Low L All 1 19 Markdown and code notes Low M Clients Nothing 20 Desktop app (global hotkey, clipboard) Medium XL New client 7 21 iOS app and share extension High for reach XL Mobile Apple sign-in, 7 22 End-to-end encryption (opt-in) Low now XL All Design decisions 1. Parcels: bring back files and images Where it stands The first commit had the whole feature on the client side: PARCELS_URL in the extension build, uploadParcel in api.ts, a context-menu image upload in background.ts, ParcelService and parcel_cache_manager.dart (on flutter_cache_manager) in the app, an image FileTile with tap-to-fullscreen, and image copy and share sheets. It was removed in the hardening commits (31c9b70, f0ec238, 20e13a1) because the server had nowhere to put the bytes. The domain model kept the shape: FilePacketCreated carries ParcelId, ContentType, IsImage and FileName, PacketAggregate projects it, and GET /api/packets already returns File items with parcelId and isImage. The clients still parse them and render a placeholder. So what's missing is storage, two endpoints, the File branch of POST /api/packets, and the client features coming back. Storage Option Pros Cons Azure Blob Storage The build already uses Azure (Key Vault invex-passel); SAS URLs for direct downloads later; lifecycle rules; Aspire has a first-party integration with Azurite for local runs Ties hosting to Azure S3-compatible (Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, MinIO) R2 has no egress fees; portable API; MinIO container locally Another vendor; the Aspire integration comes from the community toolkit PostgreSQL (bytea) No new infrastructure; transactional with the packet; trivial local dev Database and backup bloat; poor for files over a few MB; the API always proxies bytes Local disk Trivial Not durable, single instance only Recommendation: put an IParcelStore interface in front of it from day one (put, get stream, delete, maybe signed URL) and implement Azure Blob first, with the Aspire Azure Storage integration running Azurite locally. If hosting ends up elsewhere, an S3 implementation is a day's work behind the same interface. Keep Postgres as a fallback for tests only. API POST /api/parcels: multipart or raw body with Content-Type, file name in a header or form field. Limits: 25 MB by default (configurable), per-user quota (for example 500 MB total, enforced with a 413 and surfaced in settings), a rate limit. Images are sniffed and decoded, dimensions recorded, and a thumbnail generated at upload (ImageSharp or SkiaSharp, 512 px WebP) which also strips metadata. Returns { parcelId, contentType, size, isImage, width, height }. POST /api/packets with $type: File and parcelId: the parcel must belong to the caller and not already be attached. Parcels not attached within an hour are swept. GET /api/parcels/{id} and GET /api/parcels/{id}/thumbnail: owner check, streamed, Range support, ETag, Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable (parcels never change). Non-image, non-PDF types are served with Content-Disposition: attachment and the whole endpoint sends Content-Security-Policy: sandbox so an uploaded HTML file can never run against the API origin. Deletion: when PacketDeleted is applied, the parcel is marked for deletion and a background sweep removes blobs and thumbnails (a Marten async projection or a small hosted service; a nightly orphan sweep catches the rest). Model: parcels are plain Marten documents (Parcel { Id, UserId, ContentType, Size, FileName, IsImage, Width, Height, StorageKey, Sha256, CreatedAt, AttachedPacketId }), not event streams. Only packets need history. Later: pre-signed direct-to-storage uploads so the API doesn't proxy bytes. Start with proxying: it enforces limits in one place and keeps a single origin. Extension Paste an image into the popup or side panel (ClipboardEvent.clipboardData.files), show a preview, upload, send. Drag and drop files onto the panel. "Send image" from the context menu needs the image bytes. The manifest deliberately limits host_permissions to the API origin, so the service worker can't fetch arbitrary image URLs.
