Options: optional_host_permissions: ["<all_urls>"] requested on first use (the context-menu click is a user gesture, so chrome.permissions.request works there), or let the server fetch the URL (works for the web app too, but is a server-side request forgery risk that needs scheme and private-address blocking, size and time limits). Do the first; add the second only with those safeguards. Display: thumbnails in tiles, a viewer, download, copy image to clipboard (PNG only in Chrome), open in a tab. Mobile Share target for image/* and */*, the image picker and the camera. Loading parcels needs a bearer token, so either bring back the authenticated flutter_cache_manager from the first commit, or have the API hand out short-lived signed URLs so standard image widgets can load them. The cache manager is less moving parts. Viewer with pinch zoom, share as a file, save to gallery. Rollout API, storage and tests (L). Extension paste and drop (M). Mobile share, picker and viewer (M). Web app drag, drop and paste (M, with the web app). 2. Device registry and push notifications Each client registers itself once: POST /api/devices { name, platform, pushToken? }, keyed by a client-generated id and the user. The API stores it as a Marten document and the clients let you rename or remove devices in settings. When PacketStoreService commits a packet it already notifies Postgres; add a second consumer that sends a push to the user's other devices: Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android, Web Push (VAPID) for the extension (MV3 service workers can receive push events) and the web app. Notifications carry the packet id and type so the tap opens the item; links get an "Open" action, notes a "Copy" action. The registry is also what makes feature 8 possible. 3. Android share target See UX finding 1. ACTION_SEND for text and images, PROCESS_TEXT for selected text in any app, a share handler plugin, and a pre-filled sheet or an immediate send with undo. 4. Timestamps CreatedAt into PacketAggregate and the responses, relative times on tiles, day headers in the feed. Small and unlocks most of the tile redesign. 5. Link previews At link creation, queue a fetch of the page: og:title, og:description, og:image, the favicon. Store the result as a LinkPreviewFetched event on the packet stream so the aggregate gains a Preview, and emit a packet-updated SSE event so clients refresh the tile. Fetch asynchronously (a Marten async projection or a channel-fed hosted service), with hard safeguards because the API is fetching user-supplied URLs: http/https only, resolve DNS and refuse private and link-local ranges, follow at most three redirects re-checking each hop, 5-second timeout, 1 MB body cap, decode only the <head>. Preview images go through the parcel thumbnail pipeline so clients never load third-party images directly. 6. Search and filters Client-side first: filter the loaded pages by text and type in both clients. Then GET /api/packets?q=: Marten's full-text index on the snapshot document (Schema.For<PacketAggregate>().FullTextIndex(...)) over title, body, URL and preview text, scoped to the user, same cursor paging. 7. First-party sessions Today every client sends a Google ID token (one-hour lifetime) and refreshes it silently through Google. That works, but the web app can't refresh silently without One Tap prompts, there is no revocation or "sign out everywhere", and API keys for a CLI are impossible. Option Pros Cons Keep Google ID tokens as the API credential Stateless, no secrets, already done One-hour lifetime, silent refresh depends on the Google session, no revocation, no API keys, awkward on the web Exchange the Google ID token for Passel tokens (POST /api/auth/google returns a short access token and a rotating refresh token, stored hashed, revocable per device) Long sessions on every client, revocation, device-bound sessions, API keys fall out of the same table, Google stays the identity provider Signing keys to manage, refresh storage, more code and tests Cookie session for the web app only Simplest for a same-site web app, browser handles storage Different auth model per client, CSRF handling, nothing for the extension or mobile Recommendation: the exchange. Access tokens of 15 minutes signed with a key in Key Vault, refresh tokens of 30 days rotated on use, a devices link so a session can be revoked from settings. The clients keep their existing Google flows for the initial sign-in and send the Passel access token afterwards. The API accepts both Google ID tokens and Passel tokens during the migration. 8. Send to a specific device With the registry in place, packets gain an optional targetDeviceId. Clients show "Send to phone" or "Send to laptop" as chips, the feed can filter by target, and push goes only to the target. Default stays "all devices". 9. Pin, archive, labels Three more events on the packet stream (PacketPinned, PacketArchived, PacketLabelled), a projection change, and feed filters. Pinned items float to the top; archived items leave the default feed. Labels can wait until there is demand. 10. Retention and auto-expiry A per-user setting ("delete items after 30 days", off by default) plus a per-packet override ("keep"). A nightly job appends PacketDeleted to expired streams, which already removes the snapshot and notifies clients. Keeps the feed and storage small without the user doing anything. 11. Trash and restore Event sourcing makes this nearly free: PacketDeleted already exists, so add PacketRestored, keep the snapshot for deleted packets with a DeletedAt instead of removing it, show a Trash view, and purge for real after 30 days. This also gives the undo window a server-side backstop. 12. Extension additions Side panel hosting the same bundle, so the feed stays open beside the page. commands for "send current page" and opening the panel; an omnibox keyword. "Send all tabs in this window" as a collection or as several links. Drag and drop links, text and files onto the panel. Badge count of unread items since the panel was last open; desktop notifications once push exists. 13. Mobile additions A home-screen widget showing the latest few items with copy and open actions. A Quick Settings tile that sends the clipboard. App shortcuts ("Send clipboard", "New note"). Android App Links for passel.link/p/{id} so a shared or pushed link opens the item in the app. 14. Account Settings screen with the signed-in account, devices, theme override, retention, storage usage, data export (a zip of JSON plus parcels, produced by a job and downloaded from a signed URL) and account deletion (a UserDeleted event, purge job, and confirmation). Account deletion is required by Google Play for apps with sign-in. 15. Public API, keys, CLI, webhooks Once sessions exist, API keys are a session type without expiry, shown once in settings. A small passel CLI (passel send "text", passel send --file photo.jpg, passel list) in .NET or Go, and outgoing webhooks per user ("POST this URL when a packet arrives") for Zapier and home automation. Publish the OpenAPI document that already exists in development. 16. Offline send queue Both clients fail outright without a network. Queue sends locally and flush on reconnect: workmanager on Android, chrome.alarms plus storage in the extension, Background Sync in the web app. 17. Read and opened state A PacketOpened event when an item is opened on any device, shown as a subtle marker, which makes "unread on this device" possible for badges and widgets. 18. Collections Send several items as one bundle (all tabs, a set of photos). A Collection packet type holding child packet ids, or a collectionId on packets with grouping in the feed. Wait for parcels. 19. Markdown and code notes Detect code and fenced blocks, render Markdown in notes, syntax highlight in the detail view, copy as plain text. Client-only. 20. Desktop app A Flutter desktop or Tauri app with a global hotkey to send the clipboard or the current selection, a tray icon with the latest items, and clipboard sync between desktops. Big, and overlaps with the extension and web app; only worth it if clipboard sync becomes the product. 21. iOS The ios/ scaffolding exists but is unconfigured. An iOS app needs Sign in with Apple alongside Google (App Store rule when third-party sign-in is offered), a share extension for the share sheet, and an Apple developer account. Large but it doubles the reachable audience. 22. End-to-end encryption Opt-in client-side encryption with a passphrase-derived key means the server never sees content. It breaks server-side search, previews and thumbnails and complicates recovery, so it should be a deliberate product decision, not a checkbox. Note it as a possible differentiator, design the storage so content fields could be opaque later, and leave it there for now.

How it was done: every source file was read; three independent review passes (security, performance, codebase health with developer experience) each produced evidence-backed findings and ran the real tooling (builds, all three test suites, dependency and vulnerability scans, the extension's production build); the extension popup was rendered from its real bundle against a stubbed chrome.* API in every state and screenshotted; the mobile app was reviewed from source. Numbers that could not be measured without a running database are marked as estimates in the chapters. docs/evaluation/performance.html.title: Performance | Passel
docs/evaluation/performance.html.summary: Performance Scope: the API and its database access, the live-update path, the extension popup and service worker, and the mobile app. Method: static review of every hot path against Marten, Npgsql, Chrome and Flutter behaviour, plus measurements where they could be taken without a running database (extension bundle sizes and test timings). Database numbers are estimates until an EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a seeded table confirms them; they are marked as such. Verdict Nothing is slow today, and the design choices that matter at scale are mostly right: UUIDv7 ids make the feed an append-only index, cursor paging never uses OFFSET, the inline snapshot means reads never replay events, the NOTIFY payload carries only ids, the fan-out channels are bounded, and the extension bundles are tiny. The problems are the ones that only show up with volume: both clients persist their entire loaded feed on every change, the mobile app re-parses that cache on every event, the list query has no index that matches it, and the event store grows forever. All are cheap to fix now and expensive to fix after there is data. Score: 3 / 5 today, trending to 2 / 5 at a few thousand packets per user without the fixes below. Measurements Item Value Extension production build (node build.mjs, minified) background.js 10.1 KB (4.1 KB gzip), popup.js 14.6 KB (5.3 KB gzip), popup.css 20.7 KB, built in 0.10 s Extension dev build background.js 18.1 KB plus 51.8 KB map, popup.js 27.6 KB plus 67.6 KB map Extension tests (vitest run) 3 files, 39 tests, all pass in 347 ms (1.47 s wall with npx start-up) NOTIFY payload About 100 bytes, bounded, covered by a test against the 8000-byte limit Popup start-up I/O One storage.local read before the cached feed renders, then one message to the worker, one port, one list fetch and one SSE stream Source size Dart 3,743 lines (packets_provider.dart 552), extension 1,971 lines (popup.ts 710), API tests 511 lines Not measured: query plans, Marten DDL, cold-start code generation, mobile frame times. The next step for the database findings is a seeded table and EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). Findings Ordered by impact. "When it bites" gives the data volume or concurrency at which the problem becomes visible. Mobile re-serialises and re-parses the whole feed on every change (High). _persist in packets_provider.dart runs after every state change (nine call sites: build, refresh, load more, push, live create, live delete, hide, unhide, sync) and does two things: PacketCache.save encodes every loaded packet, all pages ever loaded, into one shared_preferences string, then ref.invalidate(hasCachedPacketsProvider) re-reads and fully re-parses that string only to answer isNotEmpty. All of it runs on the UI isolate, and on Android the platform rewrites the whole preferences XML file per commit, with every quote escaped. One local delete is two full cycles (hide, then the echoed delete event). When it bites: fine at one page; roughly 10 to 30 ms of jank per event at 1,000 packets; 100 ms and ANR risk on pause with 64 KB bodies. Fix: cache only the first page and its cursor (the cache exists to show something instantly; older pages are refetched by load-more anyway), replace the invalidation with an in-memory flag, and debounce writes by about 300 ms so bursts write once. Isolate.run for the encode would hide the jank but not the file churn; a database would be right only if large bodies had to be cached. The extension cache is unbounded and the popup rebuilds, animates and layout-thrashes every cached tile on every open (High). FeedStore.commit in feed.ts saves the full list to chrome.storage.local on every commit and loadMore keeps appending, so the cache grows by 50 per scroll-to-end and is never trimmed. On every open renderFeed builds a tile for every cached packet, .packet has a slide-in animation so all of them animate at once, and measureClampedTiles interleaves a layout read (scrollHeight) with a write (classList.remove, body.after) per text tile, forcing one synchronous layout per tile. Without unlimitedStorage the cache hits the 10 MB quota at about 30,000 average packets or 160 maximum-size ones, after which every save fails silently and the stale cache is shown forever. When it bites: one page is a few milliseconds; 1,000 cached packets is 10,000 DOM nodes, 1,000 forced layouts and 1,000 simultaneous animations, hundreds of milliseconds to seconds on every open. Fix: cap the cache at the first page; split measureClampedTiles into a read loop then a write loop; animate only packets that arrive live; consider content-visibility: auto on .packet. No index serves the list query (High). Program.cs declares .Index(p => p.UserId), which Marten creates as an expression index on (data ->> 'UserId'), and GetPackets.cs runs where data ->> 'UserId' = $1 and id < $2 order by id desc limit 51. PostgreSQL has two single-column paths and no composite one: scan the user's expression index and sort every one of their rows per page, or walk the primary key backwards filtering every user's rows until 51 of this user's turn up. The planner chooses by statistics, so a heavy user pays a full scan of their rows on every page and a misestimate with many users visits roughly 51 times the user count. When it bites: below about 5,000 packets per user both plans are a few milliseconds; a user with 100,000 packets pays 100 to 300 ms warm per page. Fix: one composite computed index, .Index([p => p.UserId, p => p.Id]), which turns the query into a bounded backward range scan of 51 entries regardless of table size. Verify the DDL Marten emits uses the id column for the identity member; if it emits (data ->> 'Id') instead, use .Duplicate(p => p.UserId) and a Weasel index over user_id, id. The single-column index becomes redundant. Live-update dispatch is serial, one query per notification (Medium). PacketNotificationListener.DispatchAsync opens a query session and loads one aggregate per Created notification, sequentially, so every queued notification waits for the ones before it and a slow query stalls live updates for everyone on the instance. When it bites: throughput caps at one database round trip per notification per instance (hundreds per second), far above human send rates, so in practice it is latency under bursts. Fix: per wake-up, collect the ids whose users have subscribers and load them with one LoadManyAsync, then publish per user in arrival order. Reconnect and resync storms (Medium). Both clients use base × (0.75 + random × 0.25) backoff, so after a server restart (every stream ends on ApplicationStopping) all clients reconnect within a 250 ms window, and every connection's first resync triggers an immediate GET /api/packets. When the LISTEN connection drops, PublishToAll(Resync) makes every open stream on the instance refetch at once, against the database that just recovered. When it bites: around 1,000 concurrent streams per instance, that is 1,000 list queries, JWT validations and TLS handshakes inside one second. Fix in both clients: full jitter (random × base) and a random 0 to 3 s delay before the resync fetch. Optionally send an SSE retry: value and spread PublishToAll over a few seconds. The event store grows forever (Medium). Deleting appends PacketDeleted and the inline projection removes the snapshot, but mt_events keeps both events and mt_streams keeps the stream; nothing archives, and UseArchivedStreamPartitioning is off. A 64 KB text body is stored twice while live and once forever after deletion. Rebuilding the snapshot replays every event ever written, deleted packets included. When it bites: 10,000 users sending 10 a day is about 36 million events and 20 to 40 GB a year plus indexes, vacuum and backups; at hundreds of users it is a non-issue for years. Fix: ArchiveStream in the delete handler in the same save, turn on archived-stream partitioning so queries and rebuilds skip them, and purge the archived partition after some days. The larger alternative is that packets don't need event sourcing at all (one document store and delete), which halves write volume; that is an architecture decision rather than a tuning fix and is discussed in Codebase Health. Four to six round trips per create and delete, and runtime code generation on first use (Medium). Create does FetchForWriting on a brand-new id (a batched select that can't find anything), SaveChangesAsync (begin, batch, commit), a pg_notify on a second connection, then FetchLatest to re-read an aggregate whose content the code already knows. Delete is LoadAsync, then a save in which the inline projection has to look up the stream itself, then notify. When it bites: latency only, 2 to 3 ms at 1 ms database round trip, 10 to 30 ms with a managed database in another zone. Fix: StartStream<PacketAggregate>(id, event) for create and return the aggregate built from the event; FetchForWriting plus AppendOne for delete, which also gives optimistic concurrency. Separately, Marten generates storage and projection code with Roslyn on first use after every start, typically one to three seconds of first-request latency per deploy and replica; mitigate with OptimizeArtifactWorkflow(TypeLoadMode.Static) and codegen write in the pipeline, and ApplyAllDatabaseChangesOnStartup() so replicas don't race the schema check. Mobile cold start waits for Google before showing the cached feed, and parses the cache twice (Medium). StartupRouter in app.dart shows a spinner until both the auth provider (Google Sign-In initialise plus a silent sign-in round trip) and the cache check complete, even though the feed page already handles "signed out with cache". The cache is parsed once by hasCachedPacketsProvider and again by PacketsNotifier.build. When it bites: every cold start, by seconds on a slow network. Fix: route to the feed as soon as the cache check completes and treat auth-pending as signed out; expose one cached-state provider that both the router and the notifier read. The SSE loop throws a TimeoutException per heartbeat per stream (Low). GetPacketEvents.WaitAsync ends each 20-second idle wait with a thrown and caught exception. At 10,000 idle streams that is 500 exceptions a second, one to three percent of a core. Fix: Task.WhenAny(waitToRead, Task.Delay(interval, ct)). Also exclude /api/packets/events from tracing in ServiceDefaults/Extensions.cs next to the health endpoints, since each stream otherwise keeps an Activity alive until it disconnects. Mobile list details (Low). packet_list.dart keys children by packet id but passes no findChildIndexCallback, so every insert at the top of the reversed list discards and rebuilds every visible tile's state (controllers, Dismissible, cards); about a millisecond per event today. AutomaticKeepAliveClientMixin on PacketList does nothing because the list sits in a Column, not a lazy viewport. The 60-second setState in PacketFeedPage only rebuilds the app bar because PacketList is const. Fix: add the callback over a per-build id-to-index map and delete the mixin. Mobile SSE and HTTP: no problems found. The 45-second idle timeout against a 20-second heartbeat, the cancel path with AbortableRequest, the shared http.Client, the de-duplicated token refresh and the backoff reset on resync all check out. Extension service-worker lifetime: assumptions hold (Low). The popup's 20-second port pings keep the worker inside Chrome's 30-second idle limit while the popup is open; the streaming fetch body does not keep the worker alive by itself, so if Chrome ever kills it the popup's onDisconnect reconnects after a second and the resync refetches the first page. Scheduled deletes are 4-second timers, inside the idle window. Document these assumptions in the extension doc so a future change doesn't break them silently. Already good UUIDv7 stream ids and Id < cursor paging with Take(51): O(page) per request once finding 3 is fixed. Lightweight sessions, inline snapshots, request limits (256 KB body, 64 KB text, 2 KB URL). NOTIFY carries ids only, HasSubscribers is checked before loading, one LISTEN connection per instance with a keep-alive, bounded per-subscriber channels that complete on overflow so the client resyncs instead of the server buffering, locks held only for dictionary operations, streams closed on shutdown. SSE transport: heartbeat under the client timeouts, X-Accel-Buffering: no, and response compression leaves text/event-stream alone. Extension: bundles under 15 KB, tiles cached by id and only re-inserted when the order changed, the stream exists only while a popup is open, deletes survive the popup closing. Mobile: lazy ListView, one http.Client, de-duplicated silent refresh, a StreamTransformer SSE decoder so cancelling closes the socket immediately. Steps forward Bound both caches to the first page, debounce the mobile write, drop the cache re-parse (S, mobile and extension). Fixes 1 and 2 and removes the quota cliff. Composite index and the round-trip fixes (S, API). Fixes 3 and 7; verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a seeded table and keep the explain output in the repo as a test fixture or doc. Archive deleted streams and partition (S, API). Fixes 6 before there is data to migrate. Batch dispatch, full jitter, resync delay (S, API and clients). Fixes 4 and 5. Static code generation and startup schema application (S, API and pipeline). Part of 7; belongs with the deploy work. Mobile start-up routing and the list callback (S, mobile). Fixes 8 and 10. A load test (M): a k6 or NBomber script that signs in a few hundred synthetic users, holds streams open, and sends packets, run against a staging deployment before the first public release; it will confirm or correct every estimate above.

Critical paths Ship: 0.X, 0.A1, 0.A2, 0.A3, with 0.B1 and 0.B2 landing before the first public deployment. Parcels: 0.B2, 1.B3, then 2.C2, 2.D2 and 2.E2 in parallel. Design: 0.F1, 0.B2, 1.F1, then 2.C1, 2.D1 and 2.E1 in parallel. Web app: 0.C1, 1.E1, 1.E2, 2.E1; public launch also wants 1.B1 (so the web session doesn't expire hourly) and 2.A1. Notifications: 1.B2, 2.B1, then 2.D3 and 2.E2. Store listings: 0.F1, 1.E3, 1.D2, 2.B3, 2.D4, 2.A1. If one person does it all Quick wins first, then ship, then the thing users notice most, then the web app, then parcels: 0.X, 0.F1, 0.D1, 0.C1, then 0.B1, 0.B2, 0.B3, 0.B4, then 0.A1, 0.A2, 0.A3, 0.A4, then 1.D1, then 1.A1, 1.E1, 1.E2, 1.E3, then 1.B3 followed by 2.C1, 2.C2, 2.D1, 2.D2, then 1.B2, 2.B1, 2.D3, then 1.B1, 2.C3, 2.D4, then 2.E1, 2.B3, 2.A1, and the rest as demand dictates.

docs/evaluation/security.html.title: Security | Passel
docs/evaluation/security.html.summary: Security Scope: the API (authentication, authorization, input handling, live updates, database trust), the AppHost and local development setup, the Chrome extension, the mobile app, the Atom build and git hygiene. Method: an adversarial read of every component with evidence per finding, npm audit on the extension, a search of tracked files and git history for secrets, and a check of what the .gitignore rules actually cover. No server was run, so dev-tunnel behaviour and one Atom internal are marked unverified. Verdict No critical or high findings. The authentication core is correct and fails closed: Google ID tokens are validated against Google's keys with explicit issuers and audiences, every handler re-checks the user id, every query is owner-scoped, foreign ids look like missing ids, the clients keep tokens out of persistent storage, and nothing secret is in the repository or its history. The material issues are about abuse and privacy rather than break-ins: anyone with a Google account can fill the database without limit, "delete" never erases content, there is no account deletion (a Play Store policy blocker), the dev tunnel publishes a Development-mode API to the internet, and event streams have no caps. Score: 4 / 5 for exposure to attackers, 2 / 5 for abuse resistance and privacy obligations. Verified controls These are right and worth protecting from regression. Token validation (HostWebExtensions.cs): Authority is https://accounts.google.com with HTTPS metadata required, signing keys come from Google's JWKS, signed tokens are required (so alg: none and key-confusion don't apply), ValidIssuers lists both Google issuer forms and ValidAudiences is the web client id plus the configured extras, so a token minted for any other Google app is rejected. Lifetime is checked with the default five-minute skew. If the client id is missing in production the audience list is empty and every token fails. Identity and scoping: sub becomes ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier and every handler returns 401 when it is absent. Reads filter by UserId, deletes check ownership and return 404 for missing and foreign ids alike, the SSE hub is keyed by user, and the notification listener re-verifies ownership before fanning out created packets. Email and email_verified are never used for authorization. Development-only auth paths: the cookie and Google OIDC login, the policy scheme and Scalar exist only under IsDevelopment(); production's default scheme is the bearer handler and unauthenticated requests get a plain 401. Input limits: URLs must be absolute http or https and at most 2,048 characters, names and titles 256, bodies non-blank and at most 64 K characters, File packets rejected, request bodies capped at 256 KB through endpoint metadata, JSON depth at the framework default of 64. Ids are checked for canonical encoding so aliases are impossible and malformed ids become 404s, never exceptions. Live updates: NOTIFY payloads carry ids only, never content, and are sent after commit; subscriber channels are bounded and close rather than drop; the heartbeat and client timeouts line up. Errors and telemetry: ProblemDetails and the exception handler give generic 500s outside Development; LoggerMessage calls log packet ids only; no request logging middleware; OpenTelemetry instrumentation captures no bodies. Extension: fresh nonce and state per sign-in, both checked along with aud and exp; the token lives in chrome.storage.session; message and port handlers reject other senders; no content scripts, no externally_connectable, minimal permissions, host_permissions derived from the API origin, the key pins the extension id so the OAuth redirect cannot drift. All rendering uses textContent and createElement; the only innerHTML is static SVG; only http(s) URLs become anchors, with rel="noopener noreferrer". The cache is cleared on sign-out and account change. Mobile: token in memory only; a rejected token is never re-sent; redirects are not followed and HTML bodies are rejected; only http(s) links are tappable and they open externally; allowBackup=false with data-extraction rules excluding everything; only INTERNET requested; only the launcher activity exported; cleartext blocked by default; R8 plus Dart obfuscation on release; production builds refuse to build without release signing. Secrets and git: no client id, secret or key in any tracked file or in history (only placeholders); every local secret-bearing file is ignored (*.Development.json, both .env files, *.keystore, local.properties, key.properties); AppHost parameters go to user secrets and build secrets come from Azure Key Vault. Findings Ordered by severity. "Delete" never erases content (Medium, privacy and compliance). PacketStoreService.Handle(DeletePacket) appends PacketDeleted, and PacketAggregate.ShouldDelete removes only the inline snapshot. The TextPacketCreated body and LinkPacketCreated URL stay in mt_events forever; nothing calls ArchiveStream or deletes the stream, and archiving would retain the data anyway. There is no endpoint that deletes a user's data as a whole, no export and no retention job. Scenario: a user sends a password or a 2FA code to their phone and deletes it; it remains in every backup, in pgweb, and in any operator or attacker query. Someone who wants to leave can't. Google Play requires an account-deletion path for apps that sign users in, and GDPR erasure can't be satisfied without manual SQL. Options: Keep event sourcing and hard-delete the stream in the same transaction (QueueSqlCommand against mt_events and mt_streams): minimal change, bends the event-store invariants. Store packets as plain Marten documents and Delete them: true deletes, simpler, drops an audit trail nothing reads. Discussed as the storage-model decision in Codebase Health. A retention policy that expires packets after N days, regardless of the above: bounds storage and blast radius; a product decision. Recommendation: plain documents plus retention, and in any case DELETE /api/me (everything where UserId == sub, then the user's open streams), a web page that performs the same deletion for the Play policy, and GET /api/me/export once the per-user query exists. No quotas or rate limiting (Medium, abuse and cost). Program.cs and HostWebExtensions.cs register no rate limiter and no per-user caps beyond the 256 KB request limit; each create is an event, a snapshot and a NOTIFY. Token minting is open to the world by design: the extension's client id is public, the implicit-flow URL in auth.ts works from any browser, so anyone with a Google account can script the API. Scenario: a loop of 64 KB text packets from a throwaway account writes tens of gigabytes that finding 1 then can't reclaim; cheaper variants hammer the list endpoint or open thousands of streams. Fix: AddRateLimiter partitioned by sub (for example 30 creates a minute, 120 reads a minute, 429 on rejection) plus an application quota (maximum packets and bytes per user, checked with an indexed count before create). Proxy-level limits by IP are a weak third layer. The dev tunnel publishes the Development-mode API anonymously on a stable URL (Medium, developer exposure). AppHost.cs adds the tunnel with WithAnonymousAccess(), the API runs as Development (Scalar, OpenAPI, the cookie and OIDC endpoints, AutoCreate.All, the developer exception page with stack traces), and the tunnel URL is compiled into every development APK and documented as stable. Scenario: anyone who sees a dev build, a screenshot or the dashboard has a persistent URL to the developer's workstation and, with a self-issued token, can read the OpenAPI document, fill the dev database and provoke stack traces. Whether the cookie login can complete through the tunnel depends on how the tunnel rewrites Host and is unverified; Google should reject the redirect URI, but nonce validation is off (finding 7) so don't lean on it. Fix: document adb reverse tcp:7030 tcp:7030 as the default for USB-attached phones (and 10.0.2.2 for emulators); when a remote device is really needed, drop anonymous access and send the tunnel token from a dart-define; at minimum add WithExplicitStart() so the tunnel only runs when started from the dashboard, and consider RequireHost("localhost") on the dev endpoints. Event streams have no caps and outlive the token (Medium to Low, denial of service). PacketEventHub.Subscribe appends channels per user without limit and Publish copies the list per event; GetPacketEvents ties a stream to RequestAborted and ApplicationStopping only, never to the token's exp; and after every LISTEN reconnect PublishToAll(Resync) makes every client refetch at once. Scenario: one account opens 20,000 streams, each holding a connection, a channel and an iterator; separately, a stolen token keeps delivering the victim's new packets for as long as the connection lives, hours past expiry. Fix: cap streams per user (five, completing the oldest so its client reconnects cleanly) and per instance (429 or 503 beyond it); CancelAfter(exp - now + skew) on the stream's token source so it ends when the identity would no longer authenticate, which the clients already handle by reconnecting with a fresh token; jitter the resync as described in Performance; and set KestrelServerLimits.MaxConcurrentConnections as a last line. Schema changes run under the API's role, and the NOTIFY channel trusts any writer (Low, trust boundary). AutoCreate.CreateOrUpdate outside Development means the API's database role needs DDL rights and migrates at startup, racing across replicas. PacketNotificationListener parses any payload on the channel; created events are verified by loading the packet, but deleted events are forwarded unverified, so anything with database access can make clients hide a packet until restart, or trigger a load per notification. Database access is already game over, so the impact is low; the point is least privilege. Fix: AutoCreate.None in production, schema applied by the pipeline, a DML-only role for the API. Optionally store the user id as stream metadata so deleted notifications can be verified too. Open HTTP hygiene (Low). CORS is AllowAnyOrigin, there is no HSTS, no HTTPS redirection, AllowedHosts is *, and there is no forwarded-headers handling. CORS creates no CSRF here because bearer tokens aren't ambient and AllowAnyOrigin forbids credentialed requests, and neither current client needs CORS at all (the extension's host_permissions bypass it, the app is not a browser). Fix: remove CORS until the web app needs it, then allow only its origin; add UseHsts outside Development or terminate TLS at the edge; set AllowedHosts to the API host; add UseForwardedHeaders if a proxy fronts the API. Development auth shortcuts (Low, dev only). ProtocolValidator.RequireNonce = false disables replay protection on the OIDC response; the cookie scheme uses default secure-policy and same-site settings; and the AppHost launch profiles set DOTNET_DASHBOARD_UNSECURED_ALLOW_ANONYMOUS, so the Aspire dashboard on localhost shows the client secret and database password without its login token to any local process or DNS-rebinding page. Fix: delete the nonce line and fix the cause (usually the correlation cookie being dropped on the /scalar redirect; SameSite=Lax and SecurePolicy=Always on the correlation and nonce cookies), set the cookie to Secure and Strict, and remove the dashboard variable so Aspire prints a token. Release signing material handling (Low). A real PKCS#12 keystore (invex.keystore) sits in the repository working tree; it is ignored and was never committed, but an ignore rule is not a secrets control: the folder gets zipped, synced, indexed and opened by IDEs. The build writes the Key Vault keystore to a fixed temp name and passes both passwords through environment variables to the Gradle daemon, deleting the file in a finally that a killed process skips. Fix: delete the working-tree copy (Key Vault holds it), write the temporary keystore under the OS temp directory with a random name and restrictive permissions, run release Gradle with --no-daemon so the signing environment doesn't linger, and confirm the process runner never logs environment variables (unverified in Atom's internals). Extension dev dependencies have known vulnerabilities (Low, supply chain). npm audit reports four: vitest 3.2.7 with tinypool and @vitest/mocker (two critical, one moderate: prototype-pollution gadgets and mock-registration file read and code injection, all in the test runner) and esbuild 0.28.0 (low, dev-server file read on Windows; the project never uses serve). Nothing ships to users: the bundle has zero runtime dependencies. Fix: vitest@^5 and esbuild@^0.28.1, rerun the tests. Informational. Public ids are reversible Sqids over UUIDv7, so a holder of an id can read its creation timestamp; with 74 random bits and owner scoping everywhere, enumeration is infeasible and the leak is only to the owner. Revisit if ids become shareable links. A stolen ID token is usable for up to about 65 minutes with no revocation; inherent to ID-tokens-as-bearer and mitigated by TLS and the clients' storage choices. First-party sessions (Features, item 7) add revocation. Response compression over HTTPS is not a BREACH risk today because responses contain only the caller's own data and no reflected secret; re-evaluate if a share token ever appears in a response. /health is unauthenticated and includes the database check but returns only the aggregate status; restrict it to the internal network if the platform allows. "Send Current Page" sends tab.title and tab.url untruncated, so pages with titles over 256 characters or URLs over 2,048 fail; truncate the name client-side. The extension's SSE parser buffer is unbounded; only the pinned API can abuse it, but cap it at a megabyte and reconnect. The undo window lives in the service worker's memory, so a worker termination inside the four seconds loses the delete. Functional only. The Flutter SDK is cloned by tag rather than commit, and the build runs git clean and checkout --force on a developer's own SDK; pin a commit for reproducible builds. Aspire.AppHost.Sdk 13.3.1 and Aspire.Hosting.* 13.6.2 are out of step; align them. The uncommitted .vscode/launch.json change adds a personal device serial; keep it out of the commit. Steps forward Rate limiter and per-user quotas (S, API). Finding 2. Stream caps, expiry-bound streams, resync jitter, Kestrel limits (S, API). Finding 4. Storage-model decision, then account deletion, export and retention (M, API and clients). Finding 1; the deletion page is needed before the Play listing. Dev tunnel: explicit start now, adb reverse as the documented default, tunnel token when remote (S, AppHost and docs). Finding 3. Production schema via the pipeline and a DML-only role (S, API and deploy). Finding 5; belongs with the deploy work. HTTP hygiene (S, API). Finding 6. Dev auth cleanup and the dashboard token (S). Finding 7. Delete the stray keystore, harden the build's keystore handling (S). Finding 8. Bump vitest and esbuild (S). Finding 9. Add a vulnerability scan to CI (dotnet list package --vulnerable, npm audit, flutter pub outdated) so findings 9 and the dependency notes recur as alerts rather than reviews.

docs/evaluation/ui-design.html.title: UI Design | Passel
docs/evaluation/ui-design.html.summary: UI Design Scope: how the clients look, as opposed to how they work (User Experience). The extension popup was rendered from the real bundle with sample data; the screenshots below are in images/. The mobile app was reviewed from its widgets and theme, not from a device, so its findings are about structure and colour rather than pixel polish. Feed (light) Feed (dark) Signed out Scrolled feed Copy menu After sending Verdict Clean, consistent and clearly Material 3: both clients use the same seed colour and token set, dark mode is correct, and the mobile app picks up Material You dynamic colour. What holds it back is the tile. Every item is drawn as a small window with a saturated title bar and three always-visible buttons, so the feed is heavy, repetitive and low on information: a link looks like a note looks like a file, there is no time or source, and link bodies are raw URLs. The composer also takes a quarter of the popup permanently. The fix is a lighter list item with better metadata, not a new design language. Score: 3 / 5. Strengths One palette, two platforms: popup.css carries the full MD3 token set (light and dark) generated from the same seed as theme.dart, so the extension and the app feel related. Dark mode is a first-class citizen (prefers-color-scheme in the popup, darkTheme plus dynamic colour on Android) and reads well. MD3 components are reproduced faithfully by hand in the popup: filled and tonal buttons, outlined text field with a floating label, menu, snackbar, icon buttons with state layers. Motion is restrained and purposeful: tiles slide in, the app bar collapses on scroll, the refresh indicator has a proper armed state, and the mobile list staggers entrance animations. Loading and feedback states exist for every action (button spinners, "Sending…", undo snackbars, "Live" indicator). Findings Tile anatomy is heavy (Medium). Each tile has a 48 px primary-container header strip holding an icon, the title and two or three icon buttons, over a pale body (popup.css .packet-header, tile_header.dart). Three and a half tiles fit in the popup. The strips are the most saturated thing on screen, so the eye lands on chrome rather than content, and a list of twenty items is twenty identical blue bars. Types are not differentiated (Low). The only difference between a link, a note and a file is an 18 px glyph. Colour, shape and layout are identical. Link bodies are raw URLs (Medium). A long URL wraps over four lines and dominates the tile (images/extension-feed-light.jpg). There is no favicon, host or preview image. No metadata line (Medium). Nothing shows when an item was sent or from where. This is an API gap first (UX finding 3) but it also leaves the tile with nothing to put in a secondary line. "Packet" placeholder titles (Low). Every untitled item gets a bold title that says "Packet". The composer is always expanded (Low). "Send Current Page", a two-row text area and a send button occupy about 150 px of the 600 px popup before the first item. Two feedback styles and a layout shift (Low). The status bar is in normal flow and pushes everything down when it appears (images/extension-send-status.jpg); the toast overlays. One snackbar should do both jobs. Bare signed-out and empty states (Low). A single button over a greyed-out composer, and a single sentence of text. Thin branding (Low). The paper-plane icon appears in the popup header and store icons, but the mobile login page uses Icons.send_rounded (login_page.dart) rather than the logo, there is no wordmark, and the docs site uses the icon with default theming. A small brand kit (logo, wordmark, colour, icon style, tone of voice) would tie the clients and the coming web app together. Icon sets differ (Low). The popup draws its own line icons as inline SVG paths (popup.ts ICONS), the app uses Material Icons. The link and delete glyphs differ between clients. MD2-style app bar on mobile (Low). packet_feed_page.dart colours the app bar with inversePrimary, a light blue band. MD3 top bars sit on surface colours and tint on scroll; the band dates the screen and competes with the tiles. Popup type is small (Info). Body text is 13 px and titles 14 px; MD3 body-medium is 14 px and title-medium 16 px. Fine for a dense popup, but the web app should not inherit it. Direction Keep the tokens, drop the window chrome. The proposed list item for all three clients: [favicon or type glyph] Title or host 2h learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/... (links) First line of the note… (notes) IMG_20261021.jpg · 1.2 MB · thumbnail (files) Leading: the site favicon for links (fetched server-side once with the link preview, or from a favicon service as a stopgap), a tonal circle with a glyph for notes and files, a square thumbnail for images. Title line: the real title, else the host for links or nothing for notes. Never a placeholder word. Secondary line: host or snippet, truncated to one line; relative time right-aligned; day headers ("Today", "Yesterday", "14 October") between groups. Actions: on desktop, revealed on hover and in an overflow menu; on mobile, swipe and long-press, with the open action on tap. Delete stays reachable by keyboard. Surfaces: items on surface-container-low over a surface background, no header strip. Reserve primary for the send button and FAB. Use tertiary-container for file items and secondary-container for notes if type colour is wanted; keep it subtle. Tap: opens the link, or expands the note in place (desktop) or opens a detail page (mobile) with full text, selectable, with copy and share. Density: aim for six to eight items per popup screen. Composer: make "Send current page" the one prominent button and collapse the note field to a single row that grows when focused. Put the account in an avatar menu instead of spelling out the email in the header. States: the signed-out popup gets the logo, one sentence, the sign-in button and a link to the phone app; the empty feed gets three tips. Both get a simple illustration from the brand kit. Options for building it Option Pros Cons Keep the hand-rolled MD3 CSS in the extension and share it with the web app as a small CSS and component package Already works, tiny, matches theme.dart exactly, no framework lock-in Every component is bespoke; menus, dialogs and sheets need writing and testing by hand Google's @material/web components Official MD3 look, accessible, framework-agnostic web components Google put the project in maintenance mode in 2025; limited components (no list item, no navigation rail), uncertain future A framework kit (MUI for React, Vuetify for Vue, Beer CSS for plain HTML) Complete component sets, themable from the same tokens, active maintenance Pulls a framework into the extension or diverges the extension from the web app Recommendation: keep the hand-rolled tokens and grow them into a shared @passel/ui package consumed by both the extension and the web app, adding only the components the design above needs (list item, day header, snackbar, sheet, menu, avatar menu). The mobile app keeps Flutter's Material components with the same tokens. Revisit a framework kit only if the web app grows well past the feed. Steps forward Decide the vocabulary and ordering (UX findings 4 and 5) so the redesign uses them. Add CreatedAt to the API (needed for the metadata line). Redesign the list item in the extension first (smallest surface, fastest to iterate), using the harness approach from this review to preview it without loading the extension. Port the item, day headers and states to the mobile app; replace the inversePrimary app bar with a surface-coloured one. Produce a small brand kit (logo, wordmark, icon style, illustrations for empty states) and apply it to the login page, the signed-out popup and the docs site. Use the same tokens and components in the web app from day one.

docs/evaluation/ux.html.title: User Experience | Passel
docs/evaluation/ux.html.summary: User Experience Scope: the two shipped clients (the Chrome extension popup and the Android app) and the API where it limits what the clients can do. Evidence: the real popup.js bundle was run in a browser against a stubbed chrome.* API with sample data (screenshots in images/), the mobile app was reviewed from source, and both were checked against the HTTP API. Verdict The core loop works and the hard parts are handled with unusual care: live updates, an offline cache, undoable deletes, silent token refresh and session expiry all behave sensibly. The gaps are in the moments around the loop: getting content into Passel from the phone (no share sheet), knowing that something arrived (no notifications), and finding things later (no timestamps, search or metadata). The two clients also disagree on ordering and vocabulary, so the product feels like two apps rather than one. Score: 3 / 5 for simple tasks, 2 / 5 for anything beyond them. What works well Three ways to send from the desktop: the popup's "Send Current Page", typed or pasted text (links are detected automatically, Enter sends), and context menus for links, selections and images. The feed appears instantly from cache, then refreshes; a "Live" label and a "Synced X ago" label say how fresh it is. Deletes are optimistic with a 4-second undo on both clients, and the extension still commits the delete if the popup closes. Session expiry is graceful: the mobile app keeps the cached feed browsable and asks you to sign in from a bottom sheet instead of a dead end; the extension signs out and says why. Switching Google accounts clears the previous account's cached packets on both clients. Copy and share menus let you pick title, content or both. Keyboard: Enter sends, Shift+Enter adds a line, Escape closes menus, icon buttons have aria-labels and the copy menu uses role="menu" with focus moved to the first item. Task walkthroughs Task Extension Mobile Friction Send the page I'm on to my phone Open popup, one click n/a Popup only: no keyboard shortcut, no omnibox, no "send all tabs". Send a link from my phone to my desktop n/a Open app, FAB, paste, Push No Android share sheet entry: you have to copy the URL, switch apps and paste. This is the single biggest gap. Notice that something arrived Only while the popup is open (SSE in the worker, live.ts) Only while the app is in the foreground (packetLiveUpdatesProvider) No notifications, no badge count. You must go and look. Open a link I was sent Click title button or the URL; opens a new tab, which closes the popup Tap the URL; opens externally Fine, but the popup closing after every open is tiring. A side panel fixes it. Copy a phone number I was sent Copy button Copy button Fine. Untitled items copy directly; titled ones show a menu. Send a photo from my phone n/a Not possible File packets are rejected by the API (PostPacket.cs, the File branch returns 400). Send an image from a web page Context menu sends the image URL as a link n/a Misleading: it arrives as a link, and data: or blob: images can't be sent at all (background.ts, packetFromContext). Find the link I sent last Tuesday Scroll Scroll No timestamps, no search, no filter. Read a long note Clamped to 6 lines, "Show more" Entire body rendered (standard_tile.dart) A 64 KB note becomes a screen-long tile on mobile. Use two Google accounts Account picker on sign-in; cache cleared on switch Same Fine. Use it offline Cached feed shown; sends fail with a clear message Cached feed shown; sends fail No outgoing queue. Findings Severity: High blocks or seriously hurts the core job, Medium is noticeable friction, Low is polish. No share-sheet entry on Android (High). android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml has no ACTION_SEND intent filter and pubspec.yaml has no share-receiving plugin, so the only way in is open app, FAB, paste. On a phone, "Share" is how people send things. Fix: add ACTION_SEND filters for text/plain (and image/* once parcels exist), handle them with receive_sharing_intent or share_handler, and either send immediately with an undo snackbar or open the push sheet pre-filled. Also register as a PROCESS_TEXT target so selected text in any app can be sent. Nothing tells you a packet arrived (High). Both clients only receive while open and visible, by design of the SSE stream. For an app whose whole job is "it shows up on the other device", this is the expectation gap users will hit first. Options: Push notifications (Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android, Web Push for the extension and the future web app): the right answer. Needs a device registry (device id, platform, push token) and a sender in the API, triggered where PacketStoreService already sends pg_notify. Larger piece of work, see Features. Extension polling with chrome.alarms every minute plus a badge count: cheap and server-free, but delayed and wakes the service worker constantly. Recommendation: build push with the device registry; use the badge count from the popup's own feed state in the meantime. No timestamps anywhere (High). The events carry CreatedAt (Domain/Events/TextPacketCreated.cs) but PacketAggregate drops it and neither GetPacketsResponseBody.Packet nor the SSE payload includes it, so clients can't show "2 hours ago" or group by day. Fix: add CreatedAt to the aggregate and the response records (an additive change, no API version bump), then show relative time on every tile and day headers in the feed. The clients disagree on ordering (Medium). The mobile list is reversed, newest at the bottom like a chat (packet_list.dart, reverse: true), with pull-to-refresh at the bottom and "You've gone back to the beginning!" at the top; the extension shows newest at the top. The same packet is in a different place on each device. Pick one. Newest-at-top is the convention for feeds and matches the extension and the web app to come; if the chat layout is deliberate on mobile, make it a setting. Internal vocabulary leaks into the UI (Medium). Mobile says "Push packet", "Push a packet", "Packet deleted", "No packets yet"; the extension says "Send Current Page", "Text sent!", "Packet deleted". Users think in links, notes and files, not packets. Decide on one verb ("Send") and one set of nouns for the UI (link, note, file, or just "item"), keep "packet" and "parcel" as code and API terms, and apply the decision to the store listings too. Untitled items are labelled "Packet" (Medium). popup.ts packetTitle() and tile_header.dart fall back to "Packet", which says nothing. Show the host for links (and its favicon), nothing or the first line for notes, and only draw a title row when there is a real title. Links are shown as raw URLs (Medium). The body of a link tile is the full URL; a Microsoft Learn URL wraps over four lines (see images/extension-feed-light.jpg). Show host and title, keep the URL to one truncated line, and fetch link previews server-side later (see Features). No search or filtering (Medium). Infinite scroll is the only navigation. Start with a client-side filter over the loaded pages (both clients already hold them in memory), then add ?q= to GET /api/packets backed by a Marten full-text index on the snapshot document. Mobile renders whole text bodies (Medium). standard_tile.dart draws Text(packet.payload) with no maxLines, while the API accepts bodies up to 65,536 characters. Clamp to a few lines with an expand action, or open a detail page on tap, as the extension already does with "Show more". Raw exceptions reach users on mobile (Medium). 'Push failed: $e' (push_packet_sheet.dart), 'Refresh failed: $e' (packet_list.dart), 'Couldn't delete packet: $e' (delete_packet.dart) and 'Auth error: ${authState.error}' (app.dart) show strings like Exception: Push packet failed with HTTP 500. Map failures to short messages the way the extension's api.ts does (OFFLINE_MESSAGE, ProblemDetails titles). Desktop is popup-only (Medium). The popup is 380 by 600 pixels and closes whenever focus leaves it, including when you open a link from it. Chrome's side panel API (sidePanel permission, chrome.sidePanel.setPanelBehavior) can host the same popup.html bundle persistently beside the page. Keep the popup for quick sends. No keyboard shortcut or omnibox (Medium). static/manifest.json declares no commands. Add a send-current-page command with a suggested key and _execute_action to open the popup; an omnibox keyword (passel <text>) is a cheap extra. "Send image link" is a stand-in for sending the image (Low). Resolves with parcels. Until then, rename the menu item so it doesn't promise an image. Two feedback mechanisms in the popup (Low). Send and sign-in results use an in-flow status bar that pushes the whole layout down (images/extension-send-status.jpg); copy and delete use an overlay toast. Use one overlay snackbar and never shift the layout. The signed-out popup shows a disabled composer (Low). images/extension-signed-out.jpg: a greyed "Send Current Page" and text field sit under the sign-in button. Hide them and use the space for one line on what Passel does and a link to the phone app. Empty states are a single sentence (Low). "No packets yet. Send one above, or from another device." and "No packets yet. Pull down to refresh." Replace with three concrete tips (right-click a link, share from your phone, the keyboard shortcut) and an illustration. Titles exist in the model but can't be typed (Low). Neither composer has a title field; titles only come from the tab title or a selection. Either add an optional title to both composers or stop showing a title row for notes. No settings or account surface on mobile (Low). No version, no account switch, no theme override, no account deletion or data export. Google Play's account deletion policy requires an in-app deletion path for apps with sign-in, so this becomes a blocker for a store listing. Offline sends fail outright (Low). Queue them and send on reconnect (mobile: workmanager; extension: retry from the worker with chrome.alarms). Accessibility gaps (Low). The popup's .md-btn and .md-btn-icon have hover styles but no :focus-visible style in popup.css, so keyboard focus is only as visible as the browser default. The mobile theme defines medium and high contrast schemes in theme.dart but app.dart never selects them (MediaQuery.highContrast is not consulted). Swipe-to-delete has a button alternative, which is right. Steps forward In rough value-for-effort order. Sizes: S under a day, M a few days, L a week or more. Add CreatedAt to the API responses and show relative time and day headers (S, API plus both clients). Unlocks 3 and improves 7 and 8. Android share target and PROCESS_TEXT (S to M, mobile). Fixes 1, the largest gap. One ordering, one vocabulary (S, both clients). Fixes 4 and 5; decide before the web app copies either. Tile redesign per UI Design: host and favicon for links, clamp on mobile, no "Packet" placeholders (M, both clients). Fixes 6, 7, 9. Extension side panel and commands (S to M). Fixes 11 and 12. Error copy, empty states, signed-out state, single snackbar (S, both clients). Fixes 10, 14, 15, 16. Client-side filter, then server search (M). Fixes 8. Device registry and push notifications (L, API plus clients). Fixes 2. The registry is also the base for "send to a specific device". Settings and account page with deletion and export (M, mobile and web). Fixes 18 and is required for the Play Store. Parcels end to end (L). Fixes 13 and the photo scenario; see Features.

docs/evaluation/web-app.html.title: Web App Plan | Passel
docs/evaluation/web-app.html.summary: Web App Plan Goal: a first-class client at passel.link that matches the mobile app rather than the extension popup: the full feed, sending, live updates, undo, offline cache and settings, in a layout that works on a phone's browser and scales to a desktop screen. Plus a public landing page, since passel.link is also where people will look first. What "a closer match to the mobile app" means The popup is a 380 by 600 pixel window that closes when you look away; the mobile app is a full screen with a collapsing app bar, a feed, a floating send button that opens a sheet, swipe to delete with undo, pull to refresh and a sign-in sheet when the session lapses. The web app should reproduce that screen one to one below 600 px wide, and above 840 px widen into a two-pane layout: navigation rail, feed list, detail pane. Everything the mobile app can do, the web app can do; everything a browser can do better (keyboard, drag and drop, a wide screen) it adds. Information architecture URL Page passel.link Landing: what it is, get the extension, get the app, sign in passel.link/app The feed with the composer (signed in), or the sign-in page passel.link/app/p/{id} Item detail: full text, link preview, parcel viewer, copy, share, delete passel.link/app/settings Account, devices, theme, retention, storage, export, delete account passel.link/privacy, /terms Required for the Chrome Web Store and Google Play listings api.passel.link The existing API docs.passel.link The DocFX site Serving the app under /app on the same host as the landing page keeps one origin for cookies and share-target registration; app.passel.link is the alternative if the landing page is hosted elsewhere. Stack options TypeScript PWA (shared core with the extension) Flutter Web (the mobile app compiled for the browser) Blazor WebAssembly Fidelity to the mobile app Rebuilt from the same design; close, not identical Identical widgets and behaviour Rebuilt; MD3 fidelity weakest Code sharing feed.ts, packets.ts, sse.ts, types.ts from the extension are already free of chrome.* and move as-is; the extension becomes another consumer All of lib/ except sign-in and SSE transport DTOs with the API via a contracts project; nothing with the clients Initial download About 100 to 200 KB 1.5 to 3 MB (CanvasKit or WASM renderer), slow first paint 2 MB plus with trimming Web platform Native: text selection, find in page, SEO for the landing page, accessibility, Web Share Target, Web Push, Background Sync, installable PWA Weak: canvas rendering, no SEO, selection and accessibility via workarounds, share target and push need JS interop Partial: needs JS interop for Google sign-in, push and share target Google sign-in Google Identity Services button and One Tap; ID token has the web client id as audience, which the API already accepts google_sign_in_web renders the GIS button; authenticate() is unsupported on web so the sign-in UI changes anyway GIS through JS interop Live updates fetch plus the existing SSE parser The default http client on web is XHR-based and doesn't stream; needs fetch_client or similar HttpClient streaming works in WASM Team fit TypeScript already in the repo Dart already in the repo C# already in the repo Verdict Recommended Good for a quick internal preview; not the public site Only if the front end must be C# Within the TypeScript option Framework: SvelteKit is the lighter fit (small bundles, built-in routing, static adapter for CDN hosting, prerendering for the landing page). React with Vite is the safer pick if contributors know React. Both consume the same plain-TypeScript core. Avoid rebuilding the extension's hand-written DOM code for a multi-page app; it was right for a popup, it won't scale to routes, lists and sheets. Monorepo: an npm workspace at src/ with packages/core (feed store, packet parsing, SSE, API client, auth helpers, tests), packages/ui (the MD3 tokens and the handful of components from UI Design), apps/extension (the current extension, consuming both packages) and apps/web. The AppHost already runs the extension's watch build with AddJavaScriptApp; it runs the web app the same way. State and cache: the FeedStore from feed.ts with an IndexedDB cache (idb-keyval) instead of chrome.storage, so the feed shows instantly and offline. PWA: vite-plugin-pwa or Workbox for the app shell, a web manifest with share_target (so an installed PWA appears in Android's share sheet, which covers phones without the store app), display: standalone, icons from the brand kit, Web Push subscription stored in the device registry, Background Sync for queued sends. Layout: below 600 px the mobile screen (top bar, feed, FAB and bottom sheet composer, swipe to delete via pointer gestures or an explicit delete); 600 to 840 px a single column with a docked composer; above 840 px a navigation rail, the feed list and a detail pane, keyboard shortcuts (n new note, / search, j/k move, Enter open, Delete delete with undo). Hosting: static files on a CDN (Azure Static Web Apps or Cloudflare Pages) with the API on its own host; CORS on the API limited to https://passel.link. Serving the static files from the API itself is the fallback if a second host is unwanted. Authentication on the web The simplest path that works today: Google Identity Services issues an ID token for the web client id, which is already the API's main audience, so the web app can call the API with no API changes. The catch is the one-hour lifetime: a browser tab can't silently mint a new ID token without a One Tap prompt, so users would see a prompt roughly hourly. That is the strongest reason for first-party sessions (Features, item 7): exchange the Google token once for a Passel access token and a rotating refresh token, keep the access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie scoped to api.passel.link/auth, and the web session lasts for weeks. Build the web app against Google tokens first so it ships, and switch when sessions land; the API should accept both during the overlap. For local development the web app should also offer the API's Development-only Dev scheme behind a build flag, as the extension (DEV_SIGN_IN) and the mobile app (DEV_USER) do: a development build then runs without a Google client and can switch between named users, which is how per-user behaviour gets tested (Running Locally). A production build never has the flag. Milestones Milestone Scope Size M1 Skeleton Workspace set up; packages/core extracted from the extension with its tests; web app with Google sign-in, read-only feed, live updates, deployed to a preview URL; the AppHost runs it locally M M2 Parity Send text and links, delete with undo, offline cache, PWA install, the mobile layout below 600 px and the two-pane layout above 840 px, settings page, timestamps and day headers (needs the API change), the agreed vocabulary and ordering L M3 Beyond Parcels with drag, drop, paste and a viewer; share target; Web Push; search; device targeting; export and account deletion L to XL, tracks the API features Landing page Prerendered pages: hero, three steps, extension and app buttons, privacy, terms, docs link S M1 and the landing page can start now in parallel with the API work; M2 needs the timestamp change and the vocabulary decision; M3 follows the Roadmap feature tracks. Risks Two feed implementations become three. The feed state machine already exists in TypeScript and Dart. Extracting the TypeScript one into packages/core is the fix, not a third copy. Hourly sign-in prompts until first-party sessions exist. Acceptable for a preview, not for launch. Chrome Web Store and Play Store policies need the privacy page and account deletion before public listing; the landing page should carry them from the start. Flutter Web temptation. It is a few commands away from "working" and will look right in a demo; its first-load cost and web-platform gaps make it the wrong public site. Use it for a stakeholder preview only if that's useful.

docs/getting-started/google-oauth.html.title: Google OAuth Clients | Passel
docs/getting-started/google-oauth.html.summary: Google OAuth Clients Every Passel client signs in with Google and sends the resulting ID token to the API as a bearer token. The API accepts a token only if its audience (aud) is one it knows about. That makes the client ids the one piece of configuration all three apps share. The clients Create these in a Google Cloud project, under APIs & Services → Credentials. If you're joining the team, ask for the existing ids instead of creating new ones. Client Google client type Setup Used by Web client Web application Authorized redirect URI https://localhost:7030/signin-oidc, used by the development-only Scalar login; Authorized JavaScript origins http://localhost and http://localhost:5245, for the web app's sign-in button and One Tap (add the deployed site's origin, such as https://passel.link, when it is hosted) The API (its main audience), the web app's GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, the mobile app's SERVER_CLIENT_ID Extension client Web application Authorized redirect URI https://aikjdmilnbdacmaeahelifppjjgppemj.chromiumapp.org/ The extension's GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID; the API accepts it as an additional audience Android client Android Package com.invex.passel.mobileapp.dev (development flavor) and the SHA-1 of your signing certificate (the debug keystore for local builds) The mobile app's APP_CLIENT_ID The extension id aikjdmilnbdacmaeahelifppjjgppemj comes from the key field in src/chrome-extension/static/manifest.json. Don't change that key: the id, and with it the redirect URI, would change. The mobile app asks Google for a token for the web client (serverClientId), and the web app signs in with that client directly, which is why neither needs an audience of its own. Giving the values to the AppHost The AppHost declares three parameters: Parameter Value google-client-id The web client id google-client-secret The web client secret (secret parameter) google-extension-client-id The extension client id The AppHost reads them from its user secrets. In Development they're optional, so the dashboard doesn't ask for them: without them the API runs with the Dev scheme described in Run without Google. Set the ones you have with: dotnet user-secrets --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.AppHost set Parameters:google-client-id <web client id> dotnet user-secrets --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.AppHost set Parameters:google-client-secret <web client secret> dotnet user-secrets --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.AppHost set Parameters:google-extension-client-id <extension client id> The AppHost passes these values to the API, the extension's watch build and the web app's dev server, so none of them needs a local config file. The mobile app is built separately, so its ids still go in src/mobile_app/.env; see Running Locally.
