docs/getting-started/running-locally.htm.title: Running Locally | Passel
docs/getting-started/running-locally.htm.summary: Running Locally Start the AppHost aspire run Or, without the Aspire CLI: dotnet run --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.AppHost The Aspire dashboard opens at https://localhost:17106. It asks for a login token, because it shows the Google client secret and the database password: the console prints a link that carries the token (https://localhost:17106/login?t=<token>), and aspire run opens that link for you. The AppHost starts these resources: Resource What it is passel-pg PostgreSQL in Docker, with pgweb for browsing data. The container is persistent, so data survives AppHost restarts. passel-storage Azurite in Docker, the Azure Storage emulator, holding uploaded files in its parcels blob container (passel-blobs and passel-parcels are its blob service and that container). Persistent too, with a data volume, so files survive AppHost restarts as their records in the database do. invex-passel-webapi The API at https://localhost:7030. It waits for the database and the parcels container. chrome-extension The extension's watch build. It rebuilds src/chrome-extension/dist on every change. web-app The web app's dev server at http://localhost:5245, rebuilt on every change. See Web app. passel-api-tunnel A dev tunnel giving the API a public HTTPS URL, for a phone that is not on USB. It doesn't start with the AppHost: start it from the dashboard when you need it, see the dev tunnel. The Google client values are optional in Development. Without them, use the Dev scheme described in Run without Google; to sign in with Google, set them in the AppHost's user secrets, see Google OAuth Clients. Web API Scalar API reference: https://localhost:7030/scalar. Use the Login with Google banner, or the Dev security scheme, to call authenticated endpoints from the browser. Health checks: /health (every check, including the database; file storage is deliberately not one, so the API stays ready while Azurite is down and only the file endpoints answer 503) and /alive (liveness only). Logs, traces and metrics: the dashboard. Warning In development, Marten recreates any table whose schema doesn't match the code (AutoCreate.All). Expect local data to be dropped when you change the document model. When the parcel table is recreated, the files it described stay in Azurite until the orphan scan removes them, which first runs a day after the API starts (Parcels:OrphanScanInterval) and only takes files more than two hours old. An API restarted more often than that never gets there; lower the interval in appsettings.Development.json, or remove the passel-storage container and its volume to start with no files. To run the API on its own, outside the AppHost, use its https launch profile. You then need to supply a passel-db connection string, a passel-blobs one if you want file uploads to work (without it they answer 503), and any Authentication:Google:* settings you want, in src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi/appsettings.Development.json (git-ignored). See Configuration. For files without Azurite, set Parcels:Store to FileSystem and Parcels:FileSystemRoot to an absolute path, a directory of your own such as C:\passel\parcels or /tmp/passel-parcels, which the API creates on the first upload; this is the store a self-hosted deployment uses. Run without Google In Development the three Google values are optional, so a fresh clone runs without a Google Cloud project. Leave them unset and the API accepts a development scheme in place of Google tokens: Authorization: Dev <user-id> signs the request in as that user. An id is one to 255 letters, digits or -._@+, and different ids are different users, each with their own packets. curl -H "Authorization: Dev alice" https://localhost:7030/api/packets Scalar opens with the Dev scheme selected and filled in with Dev alice, so its requests go out as alice straight away; open Auth (or the lock on a request) to change the user. With Google login configured the document also declares a GoogleLogin scheme, which stands for the login cookie: once you log in with Google from the banner, the page selects it, the browser sends the cookie by itself, and requests go as your Google account with nothing to enter. Pick the Dev scheme again to act as a development user while logged in: a Dev header wins over the cookie. The banner at the top says who you are logged in as, and when Google login isn't configured. The clients can use the scheme too, in their development builds only: Chrome extension: the AppHost builds it with DEV_SIGN_IN=true (for a standalone build, set it in src/chrome-extension/.env), and the popup then has a Development user field under the Google button. Type a name and sign in; the name is offered again next time. Built without a GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, the popup offers only the development sign-in. npm run build never compiles the field in. Web app: the AppHost builds it with DEV_SIGN_IN=true (for a standalone build, set it in src/web/.env), and the sign-in page then has a Development user field under the Google button. The name is offered again next time. Built without a GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID, the page offers only the development sign-in. npm run build never compiles the field in. Mobile app: set DEV_USER=<name> in src/mobile_app/.env (or pass --dart-define=DEV_USER=<name>), and the development flavor signs in as that user without Google, so SERVER_CLIENT_ID isn't needed. The login page has a Development user field, prefilled with that name, for signing in as someone else, and the app comes back as whoever signed in last. The production flavor refuses to start with DEV_USER set. Signing in as a different user is an account change: the client drops its cached packets, so each user sees only their own. That is how per-user behaviour gets tested from one browser or one phone: sign in as alice, send a packet, sign out, sign in as bob and the feed is empty. The same id reaches the same account from every client, so Dev alice in curl, the extension and the app share one feed. The scheme only exists while the API runs as Development; outside it, only Google tokens are accepted, and a client signed in as a development user is signed out as soon as the API refuses it. Google sign-in needs the real clients from Google OAuth Clients. Setting those parameters later and restarting the AppHost turns Google sign-in on without affecting the Dev scheme. Chrome extension Open chrome://extensions and turn on Developer mode. Select Load unpacked and choose src/chrome-extension/dist. After the watch build rebuilds, select the reload icon on the extension card. Popup changes appear the next time you open the popup. The AppHost builds the extension against https://localhost:7030/api/packets. The API always runs on that port, so an extension you've loaded keeps working across runs. Web app Open http://localhost:5245/ for the landing page, or http://localhost:5245/app/ for the app. The dev server rebuilds src/web/dist on every change and reloads the page. The AppHost builds the app against https://localhost:7030/api/packets with the web client id, and gives the API http://localhost:5245 as its one CORS origin. The port is fixed, because Google signs in only from the origins registered on the web client: add http://localhost and http://localhost:5245 to its Authorized JavaScript origins (Google OAuth Clients), or use the development user. To run the web app without the AppHost, copy src/web/.env.example to src/web/.env, fill it in, and run npm run dev in src/web. The API then needs Cors:AllowedOrigins set to the web app's origin; see Configuration. Mobile app The app has the API's URL compiled in, as the device will reach it. By default that is your machine over the USB cable; the dev tunnel is only for a phone that is not on USB. A phone on USB, or an emulator Fill in src/mobile_app/.env (SetupDevEnvironment creates it from .env.example): keep API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:5218, and set SERVER_CLIENT_ID (the web client id) and APP_CLIENT_ID (the Android client id), or set DEV_USER instead to skip Google altogether (Run without Google). Plug the phone in with USB debugging on, and make its port 5218 reach your machine: adb reverse tcp:5218 tcp:5218 The forward lasts until the phone is unplugged or restarted, so run it again after that. With more than one device attached, add -s <serial> (adb devices lists them). An emulator needs no forward: set API_BASE_URL=http://10.0.2.2:5218, the address an emulator reaches its host by. Run the Mobile app (development) launch configuration in VS Code, or run: cd src/mobile_app flutter run --flavor development --dart-define-from-file=.env This works because the API also listens for plain HTTP on port 5218 (the https launch profile, see Properties/launchSettings.json), and the development flavor of the app allows plain HTTP to localhost, 127.0.0.1 and 10.0.2.2 only (android/app/src/development/res/xml/network_security_config.xml). The app checks the URL at start-up: the development flavor rejects an http:// URL to any other host, and the production flavor rejects every http:// URL, so a store build can never talk to the API in the clear. Nothing leaves your machine; the phone reaches the API through the cable. The development flavor installs as Passel Dev (com.invex.passel.mobileapp.dev), alongside the production app. If a required value is missing, or a value can't be used in that flavor, the app opens on a configuration page that says which. A phone that is not on USB: the dev tunnel The passel-api-tunnel resource gives the API a public HTTPS URL. It doesn't start with the AppHost: start it from the dashboard when you need it (the resource's Start action), and stop it when you are done. The first time, sign in to Dev Tunnels: devtunnel user login. The dashboard also prompts you if you aren't signed in. Copy the tunnel URL from the dashboard into API_BASE_URL in src/mobile_app/.env. The URL stays the same between runs. Run the app as above. The URL is compiled in, so rebuild when you switch between the USB URL and the tunnel URL. Warning While the tunnel runs, anyone with its URL can reach your API, and it is the Development configuration they reach: every packet endpoint, with a Google ID token anyone can mint for their own account; the Development exception page with stack traces; the Dev <user> scheme, which signs in as any user without a password; and a database that Marten recreates freely. Scalar, the OpenAPI document and the browser login only answer on localhost, so they are not served through the tunnel. The URL is stable, so treat it like a credential: keep it out of screenshots and commits, and stop the tunnel when the phone is back on USB. Requiring a token To make the tunnel refuse anyone without a token, turn off anonymous access and give the app a token: Set DevTunnel:AllowAnonymous to false for the AppHost: in its user secrets (dotnet user-secrets set DevTunnel:AllowAnonymous false --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.AppHost), in its git-ignored appsettings.Development.json, or as the DevTunnel__AllowAnonymous environment variable. Restart the AppHost and start the tunnel. Issue a token for the tunnel: devtunnel token <tunnel-id> --scopes connect. The tunnel id is the resource name followed by a short hash (passel-api-tunnel-xxxxxxxx); devtunnel list shows it, and it is also the start of the tunnel URL. Put the token in TUNNEL_ACCESS_TOKEN in .env and rebuild the app. It sends X-Tunnel-Authorization: tunnel <token> with every request, and the tunnel checks it before forwarding. Tokens expire, so repeat the last two steps when the app starts reporting that the session has expired (the tunnel's 401 looks like one to the app). The production flavor refuses to start with a tunnel token, since it is a development credential that would otherwise be compiled into a store build.

docs/guides/ci.html.title: Continuous Integration | Passel
docs/guides/ci.html.summary: Continuous Integration The workflows under .github/workflows/ and the Dependabot configuration in .github/dependabot.yml are generated from _atom/IBuild.cs by the Atom GitHub workflows module. Don't edit the YAML by hand: change the definitions and run dotnet atom Gen. Running any target locally in interactive mode regenerates the files too, and a headless run (CI) fails early if the committed files are out of date. On Windows the generator writes CRLF line endings, so after an interactive run git lists the files under .github/ as modified although only the line endings differ. git checkout -- .github puts them back, and a headless run never rewrites them. Workflows Workflow Runs on Jobs Validate Pull requests into main, manual dispatch TestWebApi, TestChromeExtension and TestMobileApp (their coverage reports attached to the run as ChromeExtensionCoverage and MobileAppCoverage), PublishAzureInfrastructure (the Azure deployment's Bicep attached as AzureInfrastructure, nothing signed in to), ValidateCompose (the compose files and deploy scripts checked, nothing run) and BuildDocs, in parallel; nothing is published Build Pushes to main, manual dispatch SetupBuildInfo (the GitVersion version), the three test suites (the extension's and the mobile app's coverage reports attached to the run), BuildWebApi, BuildChromeExtension and BuildWebApp (artifacts attached to the run), PublishImages and PublishDeployBundle (the API, web and deploy bundle images, pushed to GHCR from main only once TestWebApi has passed), BuildDocs and PublishDocs (the site force-pushed to the gh-pages branch) DeployCompose Manual dispatch only, with the inputs target (preprod or production, required), image-tag (blank for the run's own commit) and migrate SetupBuildInfo, then DeployCompose in the GitHub environment named by target: deploys a tag to that self-hosted stack over SSH, or rolls back to an older one; see Releasing and Deploying. One run at a time per stack (deploy-compose-preprod, deploy-compose-production); a second to the same stack waits instead of cancelling the first Deploy Manual dispatch only SetupBuildInfo, then DeployWebApi in the production environment: signs in to Azure with OIDC and deploys the API; see Releasing and Deploying. One run at a time; a second waits instead of cancelling the first Dependabot Weekly, Monday 06:00 Brisbane time One grouped pull request each for NuGet, npm, pub and GitHub Actions, with build(...) commit prefixes so versions don't bump A newer run of Validate or Build on the same branch cancels the one still in progress; DeployCompose and Deploy runs queue instead. Every job checks the repository out and sets up the .NET 10 SDK; Node and Docker come with the runner (TestWebApi starts PostgreSQL and Azurite in containers for the integration tests), and TestMobileApp installs the Flutter version pinned in _atom/appsettings.json into .flutter/ because runners don't have one. The mobile app's release build (BuildMobileAppAndroid) is not in a workflow yet: it needs the Android keystore and client ids from Azure Key Vault, so the repository first needs an Azure identity with access to the vault. What the repository needs Setting Where Used by CHROME_EXTENSION_CLIENT_ID Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, Variables BuildChromeExtension, which otherwise has no Google client id outside a developer's .env, and DeployWebApi, which gives it to the API as an accepted audience GITHUB_TOKEN Provided by GitHub Actions PublishDocs, which needs contents: write on the job; PublishImages and PublishDeployBundle, which need packages: write to push to GHCR; DeployCompose, which needs packages: read and hands the token to the server for the one deploy. All are declared on the jobs AZURE_VAULT_ADDRESS, AZURE_VAULT_TENANT_ID, AZURE_VAULT_APP_ID (variables) and AZURE_VAULT_APP_SECRET (secret) Same pages Only targets that read Key Vault secrets; the current workflows don't, so these can stay unset until the mobile release build is added production and preprod environments, each with its own DEPLOY_HOST, DEPLOY_USER and DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS (variables) and DEPLOY_SSH_KEY (secret) Settings, Environments DeployCompose, in the environment its target names; see Server setup and Pre-prod and production on one server GHCR packages passel-webapi, passel-web and passel-deploy Each package's settings, once the first build of main has pushed it Private. Under Manage Actions access, this repository keeps the Admin role the first push gave it (or at least Write), or the package inherits access from the repository: PublishImages and PublishDeployBundle push to the packages, so a Read role breaks them, while DeployCompose only reads production environment, with AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID, AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP, AZURE_LOCATION, GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID, API_DOMAIN and API_CERTIFICATE_NAME (variables) and ENCODING_ALPHABET (secret) Settings, Environments DeployWebApi (legacy). The Azure side (the identity and its federated credential) is set up once as Releasing and Deploying describes; until then the workflow has nothing to deploy to GitHub Pages source Settings, Pages: deploy from the gh-pages branch Serving the published docs site Branch protection on main Settings, Branches Require the Validate jobs to pass and at least one review before merging The Build workflow no longer reads the repository variables GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID and API_BASE_URL: the web app is built without them, and the web image takes the API's origin and the client id from the server's .env when it starts (The web image). Once nothing else of yours uses them they can be deleted. The production environment's own GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID is a different variable, which the legacy DeployWebApi still reads. Running a workflow's target locally Each job runs one target in headless mode, for example: dotnet atom TestWebApi --headless --headless makes the build fail instead of prompting for anything, which is also a quick way to find a target that would hang in CI.

docs/guides/deploying.html.summary: Releasing and Deploying Passel runs on the owner's Ubuntu server as one Docker Compose project per stack: PostgreSQL, the API and the web app, with an optional Caddy in front for TLS (ADR 0004). There are two stacks, pre-prod and production, which can share one server (Pre-prod and production on one server). Every build of main pushes the images to GitHub Container Registry, and a manual workflow deploys a tag to the stack it is told to over SSH. Nothing deploys on a merge. The Azure deployment of ADR 0003 is still in the code and is described at the end, under Azure (legacy, ADR 0003). The extension and the mobile app are not deployed from here yet; their release builds are described in Build Targets. Self-hosted (Docker Compose) Versions and tags Versions come from GitVersion and the conventional commit prefixes described in CONTRIBUTING.md; on main every commit has its own, such as 0.2.0-rc.12. The Build workflow tests every push to main, then builds three images and pushes them to ghcr.io/invex-games/, each tagged with the version (+ and / become -) and with sha- and the first seven characters of the commit: Image What it is passel-webapi The API, from the .NET SDK's container support. The same image runs db-migrate passel-web Caddy serving the web app's static site (Web App) passel-deploy No program at all: the release's compose files and scripts from deploy/compose, which the server copies out of it The version tag is the one deployed and rolled back to. It never moves: a build that finds the tag in the registry for another commit fails rather than push over it. There is no latest. Builds of other branches build the images without pushing them. What gets deployed deploy/compose/compose.yaml describes the stack. Its project is named passel, so its volumes are passel_pgdata and so on; a stack whose .env sets COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, such as passel-preprod, has passel-preprod_pgdata and its own containers and networks. Service Image Runs Purpose postgres postgres:18 Always The database, in the pgdata volume. Only on the internal backend network db-roles postgres:18 Once per deploy db/roles.sh as the superuser: creates or updates the passel_owner and passel_api logins with the passwords in .env, and makes passel_owner the database's owner parcels-init busybox Once per deploy Creates the parcels directory in the parcels volume, owned by the API's user (1654) and readable by it alone db-migrate passel-webapi Once per deploy, unless skipped db-migrate as passel_owner: applies the schema and grants passel_api the API's DML-only privileges (Schema in production) api passel-webapi Always The API as passel_api, keeping uploaded files in the parcels volume (Parcels:Store=FileSystem). Healthy when /health, which checks the database too, answers 200 web passel-web Always The web app edge caddy:2.10-alpine With the edge profile TLS for both hosts on ports 80 and 443, with certificates from Let's Encrypt dashboard aspire-dashboard With the telemetry profile A telemetry viewer on the server's loopback api and web publish no port: a proxy reaches them on the edge network as passel-api:8080 and passel-web:8080 (PASSEL_API_ALIAS and PASSEL_WEB_ALIAS rename them). Both run with every capability dropped and no-new-privileges, and so does edge but for NET_BIND_SERVICE, which it needs to bind 80 and 443. Every service's logs rotate at 10 MB, five files. The server's .env supplies every setting; Configuration maps each one to the API's. Server requirements Ubuntu on x64 (the images are linux/amd64), with ports 80 and 443 free for the bundled edge. Docker Engine with the Compose plugin 2.24 or later (docker compose version); deploy.sh refuses an older one. curl, and openssl for generating passwords. Both come with Ubuntu. Disk for the images (about 1 GB a release), the database and the uploaded files, at most 500 MB per user by default. Server setup Once, as an administrator on the server, then on GitHub. These steps set up production in /opt/passel; a pre-prod stack beside it follows the same steps with its own directory, key and settings, as described in Pre-prod and production on one server. Updates. sudo apt install unattended-upgrades and keep it on, so security updates install themselves. The deploy user. It runs Docker, and a member of the docker group can do anything root can, so it gets no password and no other use: sudo adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" deploy sudo usermod -aG docker deploy The directory. Everything lives in /opt/passel, owned by the deploy user: sudo install -d -o deploy -g deploy -m 750 /opt/passel Deploys add releases/<tag>/ (each release's compose files), current (a link to the running release), release.env and release.env.previous (the running tag and the one before), releases.log (one line per successful deploy, appended to) and, with the default, backups/. The deploy key and the gate. Install the gate from the repository, owned by root so the deploy user cannot edit it, and make a key for the workflow on your own machine: sudo install -o root -g root -m 755 deploy/compose/deploy-gate.sh /opt/passel/deploy-gate.sh ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C passel-deploy -f passel-deploy Add the public key to ~deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys (mode 600, the directory 700) behind a forced command, on one line: command="/opt/passel/deploy-gate.sh",restrict ssh-ed25519 AAAA... passel-deploy Whatever a client asks for, SSH runs the gate, which accepts only deploy <tag> and deploy <tag> --no-migrate and refuses anything else before running a thing; restrict turns off forwarding, terminals and agent use. The gate deploys the stack in the directory it is installed in, /opt/passel here, and takes that from its own location only: no variable, from the key's line or from the client, can point it at another directory. The private key goes to GitHub in step 7; delete both files from your machine afterwards. The settings. Copy deploy/compose/.env.example to /opt/passel/.env, readable by the deploy user only (chmod 600), and fill it in. Generate each password with openssl rand -hex 32: hex needs no quoting in a connection string or in the file. ENCODING_ALPHABET is the Sqids alphabet for public ids, single-quoted. Generate it once and never change it; if the Azure deployment ever held data, use its ENCODING_ALPHABET secret instead, or every id a client holds stops working. Keep a copy of the finished .env off the server, in a password manager for instance: the backups don't include it, and without the same alphabet a restored database's ids and shared links no longer decode. POSTGRES_PASSWORD only takes effect when the database is first created (see Troubleshooting). DNS and the proxy. Point API_HOST and WEB_HOST at the server, then pick how requests reach the stack, with COMPOSE_FILE and COMPOSE_PROFILES in .env: Setup COMPOSE_FILE COMPOSE_PROFILES PROXY_TRUSTED_CIDR The bundled edge: Caddy on 80 and 443 with Let's Encrypt (the default) compose.yaml edge Unset: the edge's fixed address, PASSEL_EDGE_ADDRESS (172.30.0.2) as a /32 A proxy already running in a Docker network of its own compose.yaml:compose.external-proxy.yaml, and PROXY_NETWORK naming the network empty The proxy container's address as a /32, or the network's CIDR (Behind your own Caddy container) A proxy running on the host, such as nginx compose.yaml:compose.ports.yaml (the API on 127.0.0.1:18080, the web app on 127.0.0.1:18081, or API_PORT and WEB_PORT) empty Not used: Docker's port forwarding connects from the host's address on one of the API's two networks, which one depending on the Docker version, so the override trusts both gateways, PASSEL_EDGE_GATEWAY and PASSEL_BACKEND_GATEWAY (172.30.0.1 and 172.30.1.1) The API believes X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto from PROXY_TRUSTED_CIDR only. The stack's two networks have fixed subnets, 172.30.0.0/24 (edge) and 172.30.1.0/24 (backend) unless .env sets others (PASSEL_EDGE_SUBNET, PASSEL_BACKEND_SUBNET and their gateways), so no other Docker network on the server may use them. An .env from before these settings existed needs no change: every default is the old fixed value. If it still has PROXY_TRUSTED_CIDR=172.30.0.2/32 from the old template, that is the same as leaving it unset. For the bundled edge, open 80/tcp, 443/tcp and 443/udp. Another proxy must pass the client address and scheme in those two headers, stream the event stream at /api/packets/events without buffering, keep it open for up to an hour and accept 25 MB uploads; It must also pass the client's original Host header (API_HOST for the API), since the API answers 400 Invalid Hostname to any other. For nginx that is proxy_set_header Host $host, which nginx doesn't do by default (it sends the proxy_pass address, such as 127.0.0.1:18080), then proxy_buffering off, proxy_read_timeout 1h and client_max_body_size 32m, besides the usual proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for and X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme. Caddy does all of it by default. IPv6 and the bundled edge. The edge network is IPv4 only. On a server with an IPv6 address, Docker still publishes 80 and 443 on IPv6 too, and its userland proxy (docker-proxy) carries each IPv6 connection to the edge over IPv4, from the network's gateway, 172.30.0.1. Caddy then sees every IPv6 client as that one address and passes it on in X-Forwarded-For, so the API logs it for all of them and counts all their unauthenticated requests against one rate limit. IPv6 is not turned on by default, since it needs settings that depend on the server. Pick one of these, in a file of your own such as /opt/passel/compose.edge.yaml, added to COMPOSE_FILE by its full path (compose.yaml:/opt/passel/compose.edge.yaml), since the release's files are replaced on every deploy. Both use !override, which needs Compose 2.24.4 or later: IPv4 only. Publish the edge's ports on IPv4 alone, and give API_HOST and WEB_HOST no AAAA record, so no client tries IPv6: services: edge: ports: !override - "0.0.0.0:80:80" - "0.0.0.0:443:443" - "0.0.0.0:443:443/udp" IPv6 on the edge network. Give the network an IPv6 subnet of its own, a unique local (ULA) one such as fdc4:9a3e:7b10::/64 or another fd prefix no other network on the server uses, and Docker forwards IPv6 clients to the edge with their own addresses. The edge needs a fixed IPv6 address like its IPv4 one, with dynamic addresses kept in the upper half, and the API must trust that address as well, since Caddy may reach passel-api over either: networks: edge: enable_ipv6: true ipam: config: !override - subnet: 172.30.0.0/24 gateway: 172.30.0.1 ip_range: 172.30.0.128/25 - subnet: fdc4:9a3e:7b10::/64 gateway: fdc4:9a3e:7b10::1 ip_range: fdc4:9a3e:7b10:0:8000::/65 services: edge: networks: edge: ipv4_address: 172.30.0.2 ipv6_address: fdc4:9a3e:7b10::2 api: environment: ForwardedHeaders__KnownNetworks__1: fdc4:9a3e:7b10::2/128 This is for the bundled edge only: compose.ports.yaml sets ForwardedHeaders__KnownNetworks__1 itself. It needs Docker Engine 27 or later, where IPv6 port forwarding (ip6tables) is on by default; an older Engine needs "ip6tables": true in /etc/docker/daemon.json. The server's firewall must let IPv6 through to 80 and 443 as well. Changing the network's settings means recreating it, so dc down (the volumes stay) before the next deploy (Troubleshooting). The production environment on GitHub (Settings, Environments): required reviewers, and deployment branches limited to main. A pre-prod stack gets a preprod environment of its own with the same four entries (Pre-prod and production on one server). Add these to it, as environment variables and an environment secret, not repository ones, so each stack's run gets its own: Name Kind Value DEPLOY_HOST Variable The server's host name or address DEPLOY_USER Variable deploy DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS Variable The server's host key as a known_hosts line, from ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 <host>. Compare its fingerprint (ssh-keygen -lf on the line) with ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub run on the server, so the workflow never trusts a key it has only seen over the network DEPLOY_SSH_KEY Secret The private key from step 4 The web image needs no repository variables: it is the same image in every environment, and takes the API's origin (https://<API_HOST>) and the Google web client id (GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID) from the server's .env when it starts. The repository variables GOOGLE_WEB_CLIENT_ID and API_BASE_URL that earlier builds compiled into it are no longer read (Continuous Integration). The packages. After the first build of main has pushed them, make passel-webapi, passel-web and passel-deploy private (the package's settings on GitHub). Leave this repository's role under Manage Actions access as the first push set it, Admin, or at least Write, or leave the package inheriting access from the repository: the Build workflow pushes every later release to the same packages with its own token, and a Read role makes those pushes fail. The deploy job only reads them, with its own token, and the server signs in with that token for the one deploy only. Google. Add https://<WEB_HOST> to the Google web client's Authorized JavaScript origins (Google OAuth Clients). The first deploy. Run the DeployCompose workflow from main with target set to production and the tag left blank. Then https://<API_HOST>/health should answer Healthy, and signing in at https://<WEB_HOST>/app/ should show an empty feed. Pre-prod and production on one server Pre-prod is a second, complete stack: its own directory, settings, database, files, Google origins and deploy key. It can run on its own server, set up exactly as above, or beside production on the same one, which needs the differences below. Only a separate server keeps what is deployed to pre-prod away from production's data: a deploy runs the release's deploy.sh as the deploy user, with the whole Docker daemon and so root on the server, and on a shared server that reaches production's volumes, containers and .env as well. So on one server a pre-prod deploy needs the same review as a production one (GitHub, below), and a pre-prod meant for unreviewed builds needs a server of its own. The same images serve both; only the server's .env tells them apart. Layout. Production stays in /opt/passel, and an .env from before pre-prod existed needs no change. Pre-prod lives in /opt/passel-preprod, created like step 3, with its own copy of the gate: sudo install -d -o deploy -g deploy -m 750 /opt/passel-preprod sudo install -o root -g root -m 755 deploy/compose/deploy-gate.sh /opt/passel-preprod/deploy-gate.sh Each gate deploys the directory it is installed in, takes its own lock there, and keeps its own releases/, current, release.env and releases.log, so the two stacks deploy, roll back and fail independently, even at the same time. The deploy user and keys. One deploy user with two keys is enough: make a second key (ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -C passel-deploy-preprod -f passel-deploy-preprod) and give each key its own line in ~deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys, forced to its own stack's gate: command="/opt/passel/deploy-gate.sh",restrict ssh-ed25519 AAAA... passel-deploy command="/opt/passel-preprod/deploy-gate.sh",restrict ssh-ed25519 AAAA... passel-deploy-preprod The pre-prod key then can't ask for a production deploy, whatever it sends. That keeps mistakes apart, not people: the release it deploys runs with the whole Docker daemon, so it can reach production anyway. A separate user per stack (deploy-preprod, also in the docker group) is no stronger, since membership of docker gives either one the whole daemon. The settings. /opt/passel-preprod/.env is a copy of .env.example filled in as in step 5, with new passwords, a new ENCODING_ALPHABET (pre-prod's ids need not match production's) and pre-prod's hosts, plus the keys that would otherwise clash with production's (Configuration): COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=passel-preprod PASSEL_BACKEND_SUBNET=172.30.3.0/24 PASSEL_BACKEND_GATEWAY=172.30.3.1 PASSEL_EDGE_SUBNET=172.30.2.0/24 PASSEL_EDGE_GATEWAY=172.30.2.1 PASSEL_EDGE_IP_RANGE=172.30.2.128/25 PASSEL_EDGE_ADDRESS=172.30.2.2 PASSEL_API_ALIAS=passel-preprod-api PASSEL_WEB_ALIAS=passel-preprod-web PASSEL_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT=preprod # With compose.ports.yaml, and with the telemetry profile API_PORT=18082 WEB_PORT=18083 DASHBOARD_PORT=18890 The project name keeps the containers, networks and volumes apart (passel-preprod_pgdata beside passel_pgdata); the subnets must not overlap production's or any other Docker network's (docker network inspect $(docker network ls -q) --format '{{.Name}} {{range .IPAM.Config}}{{.Subnet}} {{end}}' lists them). Add pre-prod's web origin to a Google web client too; a separate client for pre-prod keeps its sign-ins apart. The proxy. Only one stack can have the bundled edge, since it binds the server's 80 and 443. With two stacks, put both behind one proxy: your own Caddy container, below, or a proxy on the host with compose.ports.yaml, pre-prod on its own ports. GitHub. Create a preprod environment beside production, with its own DEPLOY_HOST, DEPLOY_USER and DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS variables and the pre-prod private key as its DEPLOY_SSH_KEY secret. On one server the first three are the same values as production's; the key is not. Give it the same protection as production: required reviewers, and deployment branches limited to main. Without them, anyone with write access to the repository could deploy to pre-prod, and so run code as root beside production, with no review: a dispatched run uses the workflow and build code of its own branch, and an environment open to any branch hands that branch its key. The registry doesn't stop it either. Only the Build workflow on main pushes images, but the packages role from step 8 lets a workflow on any branch push a passel-deploy of its own under a new tag, and the deploy checks only that the tag's three images exist. A pre-prod that should take other branches' builds without review needs its own server, where all it can reach is itself. Then deploy with target set to preprod. The oldest release pre-prod can run. Releases from before stacks could share a server fix production's aliases, subnets and edge address in their compose files. Pre-prod running one would join a shared proxy network as passel-api and passel-web and take some of production's traffic, or clash with its own networks. Never deploy or roll back a second stack below the first release whose compose.yaml reads PASSEL_API_ALIAS and PASSEL_BACKEND_SUBNET. The gate enforces it: in a stack whose COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME is not passel, it refuses such a release before running anything from it. Production, as passel, can still roll back to any of them. Backups. Each stack backs up its own volumes with its own backup.sh, into its own directory: 15 3 * * * /opt/passel/current/backup.sh /var/backups/passel >>/var/log/passel/backup.log 2>&1 45 3 * * * /opt/passel-preprod/current/backup.sh /var/backups/passel-preprod >>/var/log/passel/backup-preprod.log 2>&1 Behind your own Caddy container When the server already runs Caddy in a container on a Docker network of its own (proxy here), both stacks use compose.external-proxy.yaml and join that network, and Caddy reaches each stack's API and web app by its aliases. Each stack's .env has: COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.external-proxy.yaml COMPOSE_PROFILES= PROXY_NETWORK=proxy PROXY_TRUSTED_CIDR=<the Caddy container's address>/32 and pre-prod's has its own aliases as well (PASSEL_API_ALIAS=passel-preprod-api, PASSEL_WEB_ALIAS=passel-preprod-web). The aliases must differ: Docker answers a name two containers share on one network with either of them, so pre-prod's API could answer production's traffic. For the same reason, never point Caddy at the service names api and web, which both stacks' containers answer to on that network. The PASSEL_EDGE_* settings are not used in this setup, but PASSEL_BACKEND_* still must differ. Add a site for each host to your Caddyfile, and reload Caddy (docker exec <caddy> caddy reload --config /etc/caddy/Caddyfile): api.passel.link { # The API accepts 25 MB files; the rest is the multipart framing request_body { max_size 32MB } reverse_proxy passel-api:8080 { # The event stream at /api/packets/events goes out as each event comes flush_interval -1 # No read_timeout: Caddy counts it from the start of the request, upload included, so it would cut off # a slow 25 MB upload. The default has none, like the bundled edge transport http { dial_timeout 10s } } } passel.link { reverse_proxy passel-web:8080 } api.preprod.passel.link { request_body { max_size 32MB } reverse_proxy passel-preprod-api:8080 { flush_interval -1 transport http { dial_timeout 10s } } } preprod.passel.link { reverse_proxy passel-preprod-web:8080 } Caddy passes the client's Host on and sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto itself, which is all the API needs. An event stream stays open for up to an hour, until the token it was opened with expires, so nothing may cut a response off sooner: Caddy sets no such limit by default, but a read_timeout in the transport (which counts the upload too) or a timeouts { write ... } in the Caddyfile's global servers options would, so leave write out or make it more than an hour. The API believes the forwarded headers only from PROXY_TRUSTED_CIDR. Find the Caddy container's address on the proxy network with docker inspect <caddy> --format '{{(index .NetworkSettings.Networks "proxy").IPAddress}}' and set it as a /32 in both stacks' .env. Docker gives a container a new address when it is recreated, unless its own compose file fixes one (ipv4_address on the network, which needs a subnet on the network); otherwise check the address after recreating Caddy, since a stale one makes every client look like the proxy. Trusting the whole network's CIDR instead means any container on it can set a client address, which is acceptable only if nothing else runs on it. The DeployCompose workflow DeployCompose runs on manual dispatch only (Actions, DeployCompose, Run workflow). It has three inputs: Input What it does target Required: preprod or production, the stack to deploy to. The job runs in the GitHub environment of that name, so that environment's protection rules apply first, and DEPLOY_HOST, DEPLOY_USER, DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS and DEPLOY_SSH_KEY are that environment's: a preprod run can only reach the pre-prod gate, with the pre-prod key. The input has no default, but GitHub's run dialog always preselects the first choice, which is preprod, so production is only ever deployed by picking it image-tag Blank for the version of the commit the run is on; an older tag, with migrate off, rolls back migrate On by default; off for a rollback One run per stack deploys at a time: runs share the concurrency group deploy-compose-<target>, so a second deploy to the same stack waits rather than cancelling the first, and a pre-prod deploy never waits for a production one. The target accepts those two values only, checked again before anything signs in. The DeployCompose target checks the target and the tag, checks that the registry has all three images at that tag, and connects to the server as DEPLOY_USER, checking its host key against DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS. It sends deploy <tag> (with --no-migrate when migrate is off) and the job's token on standard input. The gate on the server signs in to the registry with the token in a temporary Docker configuration, which it deletes when it exits, so no credential stays on the server; a Compose plugin installed for the deploy user alone (~/.docker/cli-plugins) is linked into it, so it is still found. It takes the stack's deploy lock (/opt/passel/.deploy.lock; each stack has its own in its own directory), so a second deploy of the same stack, from the workflow or by hand, stops with another deploy is running before it touches anything, and holds it until deploy.sh ends. It pulls passel-deploy:<tag>, copies its files to /opt/passel/releases/<tag>/, and runs that release's deploy.sh, which: Pulls the images. Passel's own are pulled only when the server lacks them, since a version tag never moves. PostgreSQL's, busybox's, Caddy's and the dashboard's are pulled on every deploy, which brings their patches in, except with --no-migrate, when the server's own copies are used too. When Docker Hub or MCR can't be reached, the deploy goes on with the images the server has; only one it has never pulled fails it. Starts PostgreSQL and waits for it to be healthy. Runs db-roles, parcels-init and, unless --no-migrate, db-migrate, each to completion. Starts api, web and the profiles' services, and waits for them to be healthy. Fetches SMOKE_URL (https://<API_HOST>/health by default), retrying for about half a minute. Only when every step has succeeded does it record the release: release.env becomes release.env.previous, the new release.env names the tag, releases.log gets a line, current points at the release, and dangling images are pruned (tagged ones stay for a rollback). If a step fails, it prints the last 200 lines of the API's and the web app's logs, leaves release.env as it was and fails the run. Whatever had already started keeps running: a failed migration leaves the previous API serving, but an API that started and then failed the smoke check is the new one, so roll back as below. Each release deploys with its own compose files, because they come from the deploy image of the same tag. Rolling back to an earlier release Run DeployCompose with the stack's target, image-tag set to the release to go back to and migrate off; the other stack is not touched. releases.log on the server names the earlier tags (release.env.previous holds only the last one, which is the same tag after a repeat deploy or a restore); any tag the registry still has works, except that a second stack can't go below the first release that reads its per-stack settings (Pre-prod and production on one server). That release's images start with that release's compose files, on the database as the newer migration left it. That only works because of one rule for every change to the schema: a release may add tables and columns, but a new column must be nullable or have a default, so that the release before it, which doesn't know the column, can still insert rows. db-migrate never drops a column, an index or a foreign key, and the API's startup check accepts what a newer migration added. With migrate off, the older migration doesn't run either; run it (migrate on) only if the older release needs Marten functions put back, which its startup check would say. Deploying by hand On the server, as the deploy user, the gate does the same as the workflow; /opt/passel-preprod/deploy-gate.sh deploys pre-prod in the same way. Backups and the restore drill backup.sh writes three files with the same UTC timestamp: db-<time>.dump (pg_dump in the custom format), roles-<time>.sql (pg_dumpall --roles-only, for reference: db-roles recreates the logins) and parcels-<time>.tgz (the parcels volume). It writes them under temporary names and renames them only once all three are complete, so a failed run leaves no dump without its archive. The API keeps running throughout. The database is dumped first and the files archived second: a file uploaded in between is in the archive without a record, and the orphan scan removes it after a restore; a parcel deleted in between is in the dump without its file, and after a restore its download answers 404 (the API logs Parcel <id> has no blob). Uploads in flight (.uploading) are left out of the archive, and a file the API moves or deletes while the archive is written is skipped and named in the log; any other error from tar fails the run. Run it from the deploy user's crontab: 15 3 * * * /opt/passel/current/backup.sh /var/backups/passel >>/var/log/passel/backup.log 2>&1 The directory and the log's directory must exist and belong to the deploy user. Shipping the files off the server and pruning old ones is for an offsite tool such as restic or rclone, run after it. The database and the parcels are consistent only as a pair from the same run. The backups leave out /opt/passel/.env, which holds the passwords and ENCODING_ALPHABET: keep a copy of it off the server, apart from the backup files (step 5 of Server setup). The passwords can be set anew, but every packet, parcel and device id a client holds, and every shared link, depends on the alphabet, and a restore with another one brings the data back with none of them decoding. To restore, or to rehearse a restore on a spare server, from /opt/passel/current with dc standing for docker compose --env-file /opt/passel/.env --env-file /opt/passel/release.env and $backups for the directory the backup files are in (/var/backups/passel with the cron line above, /opt/passel/backups by default): On a new server, set it up as in Server setup, but put the kept copy of .env at /opt/passel/.env instead of a new one, with the same ENCODING_ALPHABET, and deploy the release the backup came from once, so that current and release.env exist. dc down, and for a full restore remove the old volumes too (dc down -v). dc up -d --wait postgres, which creates an empty database. dc run --rm --no-deps -T db-roles for the two logins. dc exec -T postgres sh -c 'pg_restore --username="$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname="$POSTGRES_DB" --no-owner --no-privileges --role=passel_owner' < "$backups"/db-<time>.dump. The tables then belong to passel_owner; the dump's grants are left out because passel_app doesn't exist yet. dc run --rm --no-deps -T db-migrate, which creates passel_app and puts back the grants and default privileges. dc run --rm --no-deps -T parcels-init, then dc run --rm --no-deps -T parcels-init sh -c 'cd /v && tar -xzf -' < "$backups"/parcels-<time>.tgz. Deploy the release again (deploy <tag> --no-migrate), which starts the rest and checks it. This redeploy makes release.env.previous name the same tag, so after a restore look in releases.log for the releases before it. Disk space df -h /var/lib/docker shows what is left for the images and the volumes, and docker system df -v what each volume takes. A full disk shows first as 503 on the file endpoints (the filesystem store's writes fail), then as a database that stops accepting writes. Each release keeps its images until removed: docker image ls 'ghcr.io/invex-games/*' lists them, and docker image rm removes those of releases you won't roll back to. Their directories under releases/ are small and can go too, except the current and previous ones. The Deploy workflow Deploy runs on manual dispatch only (Actions, Deploy, Run workflow), in the production environment, so its protection rules apply before anything runs. One run deploys at a time; a second one waits rather than cancelling the first. The workflow signs in to Azure with azure/login and the deployment identity's federated credential, then runs DeployWebApi, which: Checks that the Google client ids are real client ids and that the Sqids alphabet is set. Writes the Bicep with aspire publish and attaches it to the run as AzureInfrastructure, a record of what was provisioned. Runs aspire deploy --environment Production. Aspire provisions or updates every resource in the resource group, builds the two images with dotnet publish (the .NET SDK's container support) and pushes them with the version tag, updates the migration job and runs it, and only once the migration has succeeded updates the API's container app. Container Apps then starts the new revision and moves traffic to it when its readiness probe passes. If the migration fails, the deployment stops before the API is touched, and the running revision keeps serving. If a new revision never becomes ready (a missing setting, for example), or the deployment fails after the migration, the previous revision keeps serving too, and can still restart: the API's startup check accepts a schema a newer migration has added to, and only refuses one that lacks something it needs. To see the Bicep without deploying, run dotnet atom PublishAzureInfrastructure; it writes the files to atom-publish/AzureInfrastructure without signing in to anything. Every pull request runs it too, so a change that breaks the Azure model fails in review. One-off setup These are the steps of the checklist in ADR 0003, in order. They need someone who can create resource groups and role assignments in the subscription; the deployment identity itself only ever gets rights in the API's resource group. Azure Register the resource providers the deployment uses, once per subscription: az provider register --namespace Microsoft.App az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ContainerRegistry az provider register --namespace Microsoft.DBforPostgreSQL az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Insights az provider register --namespace Microsoft.KeyVault az provider register --namespace Microsoft.ManagedIdentity az provider register --namespace Microsoft.OperationalInsights az provider register --namespace Microsoft.Storage Create the API's resource group, and a separate one for the deployment identity. The identity lives apart so that its rights in the API's group don't include changing its own credentials: az group create --name <rg> --location <region> az group create --name <ops-rg> --location <region> az identity create --name passel-github-deploy --resource-group <ops-rg> Give the identity a federated credential that only a workflow job in the production environment of this repository can use: az identity federated-credential create --name github-production --identity-name passel-github-deploy --resource-group <ops-rg> --issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com --subject repo:Invex-Games/passel:environment:production --audiences api://AzureADTokenExchange Note the identity's clientId and principalId (az identity show --name passel-github-deploy --resource-group <ops-rg>), and the tenant id (az account show --query tenantId). The API checks at startup that the database has every table, column and function it needs and refuses to start otherwise, so a revision deployed without its migration never takes traffic. Anything more, such as a column or an index a newer release added, it accepts. A schema change reaches production at the next deployment, applied by the migration job while the previous revision is still serving. So a change must work with the code before it as well as after it: add a column or a table in one release, and stop using the old one in a later one. db-migrate never drops a table, or a column, index or foreign key the configuration no longer declares; it logs each one it leaves in place. A restore creates a new server rather than rewinding the existing one: az postgres flexible-server restore --resource-group <rg> --name <new-server> --source-server <server> --restore-time 2026-11-04T09:00:00Z The deployment keeps pointing at the original server, so copy what you need back from the restored one (pg_dump and pg_restore), then delete it. Rolling back The Deploy workflow deploys only from main: the production environment refuses any other branch, and the run dialog offers branches and tags, never a commit. So a rollback is a change on main: Revert the commits to undo (git revert) in a pull request, and merge it once Validate passes. Run the Deploy workflow from main. It deploys the reverted code under a new version, and its migration puts back the older release's Marten functions. Tables, columns, indexes and foreign keys the newer release added stay where they are, data included, and the older code ignores them. While that goes through review, the API alone can go back to an earlier image straight away, without a deployment. The older code starts on the newer schema, because the startup check accepts what a newer migration added. List the revisions with their images, then point the container app at the one to go back to: az containerapp revision list --name invex-passel-webapi --resource-group <rg> --query "[].{name:name, created:properties.createdTime, image:properties.template.containers[0].image}" --output table az containerapp update --name invex-passel-webapi --resource-group <rg> --image <image> The next Deploy run replaces that image with whatever main holds, so follow it with the revert. Logs and telemetry The API's requests, dependencies, exceptions and logs are in Application Insights (passel-insights). Container output, including the migration job's, is in the Log Analytics workspace (passel-logs), table ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL; each job run's status is also on the job's Execution history page in the portal. Both keep data for the workspace's default of 30 days. None of it holds what users send: requests are recorded by path (packet ids, never content) with the query redacted, SQL without parameter values, and logs name packet ids. The page fetches for link previews go to the hosts users link, so they are left out of the dependencies, the outgoing HTTP and DNS metrics carry no host name, and the reason a link got no preview is logged at Debug, which Production doesn't keep. A new outgoing request to a URL a user supplied must call ExcludeFromTelemetry on its HttpRequestMessage in the same way. Uploaded files stay out of it in the same way. The storage requests are recorded as dependencies by blob URI, and a blob is named after its parcel's Guid alone, never a user or a file name; requests to the API are recorded by path, which carries the public parcel id. File names are never logged, and the file sweep logs counts at Information and parcel ids at Warning. The Azure SDK's own event log, which logs every storage request at Information, is kept to warnings (Azure.Core in appsettings.json). The API in Production refuses to start on a database that hasn't been migrated, and starts with an Application Insights connection string set. The integration tests run the migration twice and the API on the DML-only role, and check that the role can't create or alter tables. They also run a newer release's migration, then this build's API on it, then this build's migration as a rollback, and check that the API serves throughout and the newer column survives. What can only be checked in Azure: the first aspire deploy, the Entra mapping of the API's role (a security label set by db-migrate), the probes' Host header, the custom-domain steps, the API's managed-identity sign-in to storage, and how much ephemeral disk the container has for uploads buffered while they are checked (at most four 25 MB files at once).

docs/guides/testing.html.title: Testing | Passel
docs/guides/testing.html.summary: Testing Each component has its own test suite. Only the Web API integration tests need Docker; nothing needs a running API. Suite Tooling Run directly Run with Atom Web API xUnit v3 on Microsoft.Testing.Platform dotnet test --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi.Tests/Invex.Passel.WebApi.Tests.csproj dotnet atom TestWebApi Web API integration xUnit v3, with PostgreSQL and Azurite in Docker containers (Testcontainers) dotnet test --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests/Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests.csproj dotnet atom TestWebApi, after the unit tests Shared TypeScript packages, the Chrome extension and the web app TypeScript type-check of every workspace member, then Vitest: src/packages/core/test for the platform-free logic, src/chrome-extension/test for the extension's own modules, against a stubbed chrome, and src/web/test for the web app npm run typecheck and npm test in src dotnet atom TestChromeExtension, with coverage Mobile app flutter analyze, then flutter test Both, in src/mobile_app dotnet atom TestMobileApp, with coverage dotnet atom Test runs all three. Notes global.json selects Microsoft.Testing.Platform. Pass the test project with --project; a bare dotnet test <path> is parsed differently in this mode. dotnet atom TestMobileApp uses whichever Flutter is on your PATH. Unlike BuildMobileAppAndroid, it never switches your SDK to the flutter-version the build pins. The extension's tests (src/chrome-extension/test) run its modules unbundled against test/chrome.ts, a stand-in for chrome.* with storage that keeps what is written, events a test can fire and vi.fn()s for the rest; test/setup.ts supplies the __CONFIG__ the build would. The service worker's modules run in Node, which like a service worker has fetch and streams but no DOM: sign-in (the authorization URL for each prompt mode, the state, nonce, audience and expiry checks, account changes, development users), the API client (the 401 refresh, retry and sign-out matrix, ProblemDetails messages, the endpoints, the event stream and its idle timeout, with fetch stubbed), the live connection's port lifecycle and backoff, and the worker's message routing, delete scheduling and undo, context menus, keyboard commands and the passel keyword, with fake timers. The popup's composer and controller run in jsdom on the real static/popup.html, as the popup and as the side panel. npm run test:coverage in src writes each package's line and branch coverage to its coverage/lcov.info (with an HTML report beside it), and dotnet atom TestChromeExtension keeps both as the ChromeExtensionCoverage artifact (atom-publish/ChromeExtensionCoverage/chrome-extension.lcov.info, core.lcov.info and web.lcov.info). The mobile app's widget tests (test/packets/*_test.dart, test/auth/login_page_test.dart) drive the screens with the fakes in test/fakes.dart: the feed page signed in and out with its sync label, the list's loading, failure and empty states and its loading of older items, the send sheet, the tiles (copy, share and links, with the plugin channels mocked) and delete with undo. dotnet atom TestMobileApp runs flutter test --coverage and keeps the line coverage of lib/, src/mobile_app/coverage/lcov.info, as the MobileAppCoverage artifact (atom-publish/MobileAppCoverage/lcov.info locally, attached to the workflow run in CI). The Web API unit tests cover endpoint helpers, the event hub, notification payloads, id encoding, the link preview guards and extractor (the table of refused and allowed addresses, the URL checks, redirects, and the size and time limits, against a fake handler and a stand-in for DNS), and the device registry's checks: what a registration, a name and a push token may be, the push key, the device cap, and that no device response or ToString shows a token, and the file pipeline's parts: type sniffing, file names, the counting stream, the image inspector on images generated in the tests (orientation, metadata stripping, an animated GIF, a decompression bomb), the file quota and options, the download headers and the sweep's selection and worker. The Marten mappings, the SQL, the live-update path, the preview fetch end to end, the device registry's unique keys and races, uploads, downloads and the sweep against real storage, and the contract files are covered by the integration tests, against a real PostgreSQL and Azurite; see Integration tests. Contracts contracts/ at the repository root is read by all three suites, so a change to the packet wire shape or to the feed rules fails a test on every side that has not followed it: The Web API integration tests generate contracts/openapi.json and contracts/fixtures/ from the running API and fail when the committed files differ. To regenerate them, run the integration tests with PASSEL_UPDATE_CONTRACTS=1 in the environment (Docker running): $env:PASSEL_UPDATE_CONTRACTS = "1"; dotnet test --project src/webapi/Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests/Invex.Passel.WebApi.IntegrationTests.csproj In a POSIX shell: PASSEL_UPDATE_CONTRACTS=1 dotnet test --project …. Review the diff and commit it with the change that caused it. The extension (test/contracts.test.ts) and the mobile app (test/contracts_test.dart) parse every fixture with their real parsers and run every scenario in contracts/feed-scenarios.json through their feed stores. A fixture file or a scenario action they do not know fails both suites until they handle it. contracts/feed-scenarios.json is written by hand and explains its own format. Add a scenario when a feed rule changes. See Contracts for what the files are and where the wire shape is declared.
